u.c: U U (ū), the twenty-first letter of the English alphabet, is a cursive form of the letter V, with which it was formerly used interchangeably, both letters being then used both as vowels and consonants. U and V are now, however, differentiated, U being used only as a vowel or semivowel, and V only as a consonant. The true primary vowel sound of U, in Anglo-Saxon, was the sound which it still retains in most of the languages of Europe, that of long oo, as in tool, and short oo, as in wood, answering to the French ou in tour. Etymologically U is most closely related to o, y (vowel), w, and v; as in two, duet, dyad, twice; top, tuft; sop, sup; auspice, aviary. See V, also O and Y.

uberous.c: Uberous U"ber*ous (?), a. [L. uber.] Fruitful; copious; abundant; plentiful. [Obs.] Sir T. Herbert.

uberty.c: Uberty U"ber*ty (?), n. [L. ubertas.] Fruitfulness; copiousness; abundance; plenty. [Obs.] Florio.

ubiety.c: Ubiety Ubication { U`bi*ca"tion (?), U*bi"e*ty (?), } n. [NL. ubicatio, ubietas, fr. L. ubi where.] The quality or state of being in a place; local relation; position or location; whereness. [R.] Glanvill.

ubiquitarian.c: Ubiquitarian Ubiquist { U"bi*quist (?), U*biq`ui*ta"ri*an (?), } n. [L. ubique everywhere: cf. F. ubiquiste, ubiquitaire. See Ubiquity.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a school of Lutheran divines which held that the body of Christ is present everywhere, and especially in the eucharist, in virtue of his omnipresence. Called also ubiquitist, and ubiquitary.

ubiquitariness.c: Ubiquitariness U*biq"ui*ta*ri*ness (u*bĭk"wĭ*ta*rĭ*nĕs), n. Quality or state of being ubiquitary, or ubiquitous. [R.] Fuller.

ubiquitary.c: Ubiquitary U*biq"ui*ta*ry (u*bĭk"wĭ*ta*ry̆), a. [L. ubique everywhere. See Ubiquitarian.] Ubiquitous. Howell.
Ubiquitary U*biq"ui*ta*ry, n.; pl. Ubiquitaries (?). 1. One who exists everywhere. B. Jonson.

ubiquitous.c: Ubiquitous U*biq"ui*tous (u*bĭk"wĭ*tŭs), a. [See Ubiquity.] Existing or being everywhere, or in all places, at the same time; omnipresent. -- U*biq"ui*tous*ly, adv.

ubiquity.c: Ubiquity U*biq"ui*ty (u*bĭk"wĭ*ty̆), n. [L. ubique everywhere, fr. ubi where, perhaps for cubi, quobi (cf. alicubi anywhere), and if so akin to E. who: cf. F. ubiquité.] 1. Existence everywhere, or in all places, at the same time; omnipresence; as, the ubiquity of God is not disputed by those who admit his existence.

uchees.c: Uchees U"chees (?), n. pl. (Ethnol.) A tribe of North American Indians belonging to the Creek confederation.

uckewallist.c: Uckewallist Uck`e*wal"list (?), prop. n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect of rigid Anabaptists, which originated in 1637, and whose tenets were essentially the same as those of the Mennonists. In addition, however, they held that Judas and the murderers of Christ were saved. So called from the founder of the sect, Ucke Wallis, a native of Friesland. Eadie.

udalman.c: Udalman Udaler Udalborn Udal U"dal (ū"dail), n. & a. U"dal*born`, U"dal*er, U"dal*man, etc. [Icel. ōðal allodium, an hereditary estate; akin to Sw. odal allodial, Dan. odel.] Vars. of Odal, etc.; property held by udal, or allodial, right -- Obs. exc. in Shetland and the Orkney Islands, where udal designates a freehold, land held in fee simple without any charter and free of any feudal character.
Udalman Udaler { U"dal*er (?), U"dal*man (?), } n. In the Shetland and Orkney Islands, one who holds property by udal, or allodial, right. Sir W. Scott.

udal.c: Udal U"dal, a. Allodial; -- a term used in Finland, Shetland, and Orkney. See Allodial. Burrill.

udder.c: Udder Ud"der (?), n. [OE. uddir, AS. ūder; akin to D. uijer, G. euter, OHG. ūtar, ūtiro, Icel. jūgr, Sw. jufver, jur, Dan. yver, L. uber, Gr. o"y^qar, Skr. ūdhar. √216. Cf. Exuberant.] 1. (Anat.) The glandular organ in which milk is secreted and stored; -- popularly called the bag in cows and other quadrupeds. See Mamma.

uddered.c: Uddered Ud"dered (?), a. Having an udder or udders.

udderless.c: Udderless Ud"der*less, a. 1. Destitute or deprived of an udder.

udometer.c: Udometer U*dom"e*ter (?), n. [L. udus wet, moist + -meter.] (Meteor.) A rain gauge.

ugh.c: Ugh Ugh (ŏo), interj. An exclamation expressive of disgust, horror, or recoil. Its utterance is usually accompanied by a shudder.

uglesome.c: Uglesome Ug"le*some (ŭg"'l*sŭm), a. [√3. See Ugly.] Ugly. [Obs.] “Such an uglesome countenance.” Latimer.

uglify.c: Uglify Ug"li*fy (?), v. t. [Ugly + -fy.] To disfigure; to make ugly. [R.] Mad. D'Arblay.

uglily.c: Uglily Ug"li*ly, adv. In an ugly manner; with deformity.

ugliness.c: Ugliness Ug"li*ness, n. The quality or state of being ugly.

ugly.c: Ugly Ug"ly (?), a. [Compar. Uglier (?); superl. Ugliest.] [Icel. uggligr fearful, dreadful; uggr fear (akin to ugga to fear) + -ligr (akin to E. -ly, like).??. Cf. Awe.] 1. Offensive to the sight; contrary to beauty; being of disagreeable or loathsome aspect; unsightly; repulsive; deformed.
Ugly Ug"ly (?), n. A shade for the face, projecting from the bonnet. [Colloq. Eng.] C. Kingsley.
Ugly Ug"ly, v. t. To make ugly. [R.] Richardson.

ugrian.c: Ugrian U"gri*an (?), n. pl. (Ethnol.) A Mongolian race, ancestors of the Finns. [Written also Uigrian.]

ugsome.c: Ugsome Ug"some (?), a. [??. See Ugly.] Ugly; offensive; loathsome. [Obs.] -- Ug"some*ness, n. [Obs.] “The horror and ugsomeness of death.” Latimer.

uhlan.c: Uhlan Uh"lan (?), n. [G. uhlan, Pol. ulan, hulan, from Turk. oglān a youth, lad; of Tartar origin.] [Written also ulan, and formerly hulan.] 1. One of a certain description of militia among the Tartars.

uintatherium.c: Uintatherium ‖U*in`ta*the"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Uinta, the Indian name of the region where the animals were discovered + Gr. qhri`on beast.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of large Eocene ungulates allied to Dinoceras. This name is sometimes used for nearly all the known species of the group. See Dinoceras.

uitlander.c: Uitlander ‖Uit"land`er (?), n. [D. Cf. Outlander.] A foreigner; an outlander. [South Africa]

ukase.c: Ukase U*kase" (?), n. [F., fr. Russ. ukas'; pref. u- + kazate to show, to say.] 1. In Russia, a published proclamation or imperial order, having the force of law.

ularburong.c: Ularburong U*lar"bu*rong (?), n. [From the native Malay name.] (Zool.) A large East Indian nocturnal tree snake (Dipsas dendrophila). It is not venomous.

ulcer.c: Ulcer Ul"cer (?), n. [F. ulcère, L. ulcus, gen. ulceris, akin to Gr.?.] 1. (Med.) A solution of continuity in any of the soft parts of the body, discharging purulent matter, found on a surface, especially one of the natural surfaces of the body, and originating generally in a constitutional disorder; a sore discharging pus. It is distinguished from an abscess, which has its beginning, at least, in the depth of the tissues.
Ulcer Ul"cer, v. t. To ulcerate. [R.] Fuller.

ulcerate.c: Ulcerate Ul"cer*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Ulcerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ulcerating.] [L. ulceratus, p. p. of ulcerare, fr. ulcus ulcer.] To be formed into an ulcer; to become ulcerous.
Ulcerate Ul"cer*ate, v. t. To affect with, or as with, an ulcer or ulcers. Harvey.

ulcerated.c: Ulcerated Ul"cer*a`ted (?), a. Affected with, or as with, an ulcer or ulcers; as, an ulcerated sore throat.

ulceration.c: Ulceration Ul`cer*a"tion (?), n. [L. ulceratio: cf. F. ulcération.] (Med.) The process of forming an ulcer, or of becoming ulcerous; the state of being ulcerated; also, an ulcer.

ulcerative.c: Ulcerative Ul"cer*a*tive (?), a. Of or pertaining to ulcers; as, an ulcerative process.

ulcerous.c: Ulcerous Ul"cer*ous (?), a. [L. ulcerosus: cf. F. ulcéreux.] 1. Having the nature or character of an ulcer; discharging purulent or other matter. R. Browning.

ulcuscule.c: Ulcuscule Ulcuscle { Ul"cus*cle (?), Ul*cus"cule (?), } n. [L. ulcusculum, dim. of ulcus. See Ulcer.] A little ulcer. [R.]

ule.c: Ule U"le (ū"le), n. [Sp.] (Bot.) A Mexican and Central American tree (Castilloa elastica and Castilloa Markhamiana) related to the breadfruit tree. Its milky juice contains caoutchouc. Called also ule tree.

ulema.c: Ulema ‖U`le*ma" (?), n. [Turk. & Ar. 'ulamā the wise or learned men, pl. of 'ālim wise, learned, fr. alima to know.] (Islam) A college or body composed of the hierarchy (the imams, or ministers of religion, the muftis, or doctors of law, and the cadis, or administrators of justice). That of Turkey alone now has political power; its head is the sheik ul Islam.

ulexite.c: Ulexite U"lex*ite (?), n. [After a German chemist.] (Min.) A mineral occurring in white rounded crystalline masses. It is a hydrous borate of lime and soda.

uliginous.c: Uliginous Uliginose { U*lig"i*nose` (?), U*lig"i*nous (?), } a. [L. uliginosus, fr. uligo, -inis, moisture, fr. uvere to be moist.] Muddy; oozy; slimy; also, growing in muddy places. [R.] Woodward.

ullage.c: ullage ul"lage (ŭl"laj; 48), n. [OF. eullage, ouillage, the filling up of a cask, fr. ouillier, oillier, euillier, to fill a wine cask; properly, to add oil to prevent evaporation, as to a flask that is nearly full, fr. OF. oile oil. See Oil.] (Com.) The amount which a vessel, as a cask, of liquor lacks of being full; wantage; deficiency.

ullet.c: ullet ul"let (ŭl"lĕt), n. [Cf. OF. hullote, E. howlet.] (Zool.) A European owl (Syrnium aluco) of a tawny color; -- called also uluia.

ullmannite.c: Ullmannite Ull"mann*ite (?), n. [So named after J. C. Ullman, a German chemist.] (Min.) A brittle mineral of a steel-gray color and metallic luster, containing antimony, arsenic, sulphur, and nickel.

ulmaceous.c: Ulmaceous Ul*ma"ceous (?), a. [L. ulmus an elm.] (Bot.) Of or pertaining to a suborder of urticaceous plants, of which the elm is the type.

ulmate.c: Ulmate Ul"mate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of ulmic acid.

ulmic.c: Ulmic Ul"mic (?), a. [L. ulmus an elm: cf. F. ulmique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to ulmin; designating an acid obtained from ulmin.

ulmin.c: Ulmin Ul"min (?), n. [L. ulmus an elm: cf. F. ulmine.] (Chem.) A brown amorphous substance found in decaying vegetation. Cf. Humin. [Formerly written ulmine.]

ulmus.c: Ulmus ‖Ul"mus (?), n. [L., an elm.] (Bot.) A genus of trees including the elm.

ulna.c: Ulna ‖Ul"na (ŭl"nȧ), n. [L., the elbow. See Ell.] 1. (Anat.) The postaxial bone of the forearm, or brachium, corresponding to the fibula of the hind limb. See Radius.

ulnage.c: Ulnage Ul"nage (?), n. [See Ulna, and cf. Alnage.] (Old Eng. Law) Measurement by the ell; alnage.

ulnar.c: Ulnar Ul"nar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the ulna, or the elbow; as, the ulnar nerve.

ulnare.c: Ulnare ‖Ul*na"re (?), n.; pl. Ulnaria (#). [NL. See Ulna.] (Anat.) One of the bones or cartilages of the carpus, which articulates with the ulna and corresponds to the cuneiform in man.

ulodendron.c: Ulodendron ‖U`lo*den"dron (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, for? whole +? tree.] (Paleon.) A genus of fossil trees.

uloid.c: Uloid U"loid (?), a. [Written also ouloid.] [Gr.? scar + -oid.] (Med.) Resembling a scar; scarlike.

ulonata.c: Ulonata ‖U`lo*na"ta (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A division of insects nearly equivalent to the true Orthoptera.

ulotrichan.c: Ulotrichan U*lot"ri*chan (?), a. (Anthropol.) Of or pertaining to the Ulotrichi. -- n. One of the Ulotrichi.

ulotrichi.c: Ulotrichi ‖U*lot"ri*chi (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?, woolly-haired;? woolly +?,?, hair.] (Anthropol.) The division of mankind which embraces the races having woolly or crispy hair. Cf. Leiotrichi.

ulotrichous.c: Ulotrichous U*lot"ri*chous (?), a. (Anthropol.) Having woolly or crispy hair; -- opposed to leiotrichous.

ulster.c: Ulster Ul"ster (?), n. A long, loose overcoat, worn by men and women, originally made of frieze from Ulster, Ireland.

ulterior.c: Ulterior Ul*te"ri*or (?), a. [L., comp. of ultra, ultro, beyond, on the other side, properly cases of an old adjective, formed with a comparative suffix, which is akin to OL. uls beyond, L. olim formerly, hereafter, orig., at that time, ille that, OL. olle, ollus. Cf. Outrage.] 1. Situated beyond, or on the farther side; thither; -- correlative with hither.
Ulterior Ul*te"ri*or, n. Ulterior side or part. [R.] Coleridge.

ulteriorly.c: Ulteriorly Ul*te"ri*or*ly, adv. More distantly or remotely.

ultima.c: Ultima ‖Ul"ti*ma (ŭl"iĭ*mȧ), a. [L., fem. of ultimus last.] Most remote; furthest; final; last.
Ultima Ul"ti*ma, n. [L., fem. of ultimus last.] (Gram. & Pros.) The last syllable of a word.

ultimate.c: Ultimate Ul"ti*mate (?), a. [LL. ultimatus last, extreme, fr. L. ultimare to come to an end, fr. ultimus the farthest, last, superl. from the same source as ulterior. See Ulterior, and cf. Ultimatum.] 1. Farthest; most remote in space or time; extreme; last; final.
Ultimate Ul"ti*mate (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Ultimated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ultimating.] 1. To come or bring to an end or issue; to eventuate; to end. [R.]

ultimately.c: Ultimately Ul"ti*mate*ly (?), adv. As a final consequence; at last; in the end; as, afflictions often tend to correct immoral habits, and ultimately prove blessings.

ultimation.c: Ultimation Ul`ti*ma"tion (ŭl`tĭ*mā"shŭn), n. State of being ultimate; that which is ultimate, or final; ultimatum. [R.] Swift.

ultimatum.c: Ultimatum Ul`ti*ma"tum (ŭl`tĭ*mā"tŭm), n.; pl. E. Ultimatums (ŭl`tĭ*mā"tŭmz), L. Ultimata (#). [NL. See Ultimate.] 1. A final proposition, concession, or condition; especially, the final propositions, conditions, or terms, offered by either of the parties in a diplomatic negotiation; the most favorable terms that a negotiator can offer, the rejection of which usually puts an end to the hesitation.

ultimity.c: Ultimity Ul*tim"i*ty (ŭl*tĭm"ĭ*ty̆), n. [LL. ultimitus extremity, fr. L. ultimus the last.] The last stage or consequence; finality. [Obs.] Bacon.

ultimo.c: Ultimo ‖Ul"ti*mo. [L. ultimo (mense) in the last month.] In the month immediately preceding the present; as, on the 1st ultimo; -- usually abbreviated to ult. Cf. Proximo.

ultion.c: Ultion Ul"tion (?), n. [L. ultio.] The act of taking vengeance; revenge. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

ultra.c: Ultra- Ul"tra- (?), a. A prefix from the Latin ultra beyond (see Ulterior), having in composition the signification beyond, on the other side, chiefly when joined with words expressing relations of place; as, ultramarine, ultramontane, ultramundane, ultratropical, etc. In other relations it has the sense of excessively, exceedingly, beyond what is common, natural, right, or proper; as, ultraconservative; ultrademocratic, ultradespotic, ultraliberal, ultraradical, etc.
Ultra Ul"tra, a. [See Ultra-.] Going beyond others, or beyond due limit; extreme; fanatical; uncompromising; as, an ultra reformer; ultra measures.
Ultra Ul"tra, n. One who advocates extreme measures; an ultraist; an extremist; a radical. Brougham.

Ultra vires ‖Ul`tra vi"res (?), [Law Latin, from L. prep. ultra beyond + vires, pl. of. vis strength.] Beyond power; transcending authority; -- a phrase used frequently in relation to acts or enactments by corporations in excess of their chartered or statutory rights.

ultragaseous.c: Ultragaseous Ul`tra*gas"e*ous (?), a. [Pref. ultra + gaseous.] (Physics) Having the properties exhibited by gases under very low pressures (one millionth of an atmosphere or less). Matter under this condition, which has been termed the fourth state of matter, is sometimes called radiant matter.

ultraism.c: Ultraism Ul"tra*ism (ŭl"trȧ*ĭz'm), n. [Cf. F. ultraïsme. See Ultra-.] The principles of those who advocate extreme measures, as radical reform, and the like. Dr. H. More.

ultraist.c: Ultraist Ul"tra*ist, n. One who pushes a principle or measure to extremes; an extremist; a radical; an ultra.

ultramarine.c: Ultramarine Ul`tra*ma*rine" (ŭl`trȧ*mȧ*rēn"), a. [Pref. ultra- + marine.] Situated or being beyond the sea. Burke.

Ultramarine Ul`tra*ma*rine", n. [Cf. Sp. ultramarino. So called because the lapis lazuli was originally brought from beyond the sea, -- from Asia.] (Chem.) A blue pigment formerly obtained by powdering lapis lazuli, but now produced in large quantities by fusing together silica, alumina, soda, and sulphur, thus forming a glass, colored blue by the sodium polysulphides made in the fusion. Also used adjectively.

ultramontane.c: Ultramontane Ul`tra*mon"tane (?), a. [LL. ultramontanus; L. ultra beyond + montanus belonging to a mountain, from mons, montis, mountain: cf. F. ultramontain, It. ultramontano. See Ultra-, and Mountain.] Being beyond the mountains; specifically, being beyond the Alps, in respect to the one who speaks.
Ultramontane Ul`tra*mon"tane, n. 1. One who resides beyond the mountains, especially beyond the Alps; a foreigner.

ultramontanism.c: Ultramontanism Ul`tra*mon"ta*nism (?), n. [Cf. F. ultramontanisme.] The principles of those within the Roman Catholic Church who maintain extreme views favoring the pope's supremacy; -- so used by those living north of the Alps in reference to the Italians; -- rarely used in an opposite sense, as referring to the views of those living north of the Alps and opposed to the papal claims. Cf. Gallicanism.

ultramontanist.c: Ultramontanist Ul`tra*mon"ta*nist (?), n. One who upholds ultramontanism.

ultramundane.c: Ultramundane Ul`tra*mun"dane (?), a. [L. ultramundanus. See Ultra-, and Mundane.] Being beyond the world, or beyond the limits of our system. Boyle.

ultrared.c: Ultrared Ul`tra*red" (?), a. [Pref. ultra- + red.] (Physics) Situated beyond or below the red rays; as, the ultrated rays of the spectrum, which are less refrangible than the red.

ultratropical.c: Ultratropical Ul`tra*trop"ic*al (?), a. [Pref. ultra- + tropical.] Situated beyond, or outside of, the tropics; extratropical; also, having an excessively tropical temperature; warmer than the tropics.

ultraviolet.c: Ultraviolet Ul`tra*vi"o*let (?), a. [Pref. ultra- + violet.] (Physics) Lying outside the visible spectrum at its blue-violet end; -- said of light more refrangible (i. e. having a shorter wavelength) than the extreme violet rays of the visible spectrum. Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than those of ultrviolet light are not usually considered as light waves, but are classified differently. The ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum is generally considered as comprising those electromagnetic emissions with wavelengths lying between those of visible light and those of X-rays, i. e. between 4000 Angstroms and 100 Angstroms.

ultrazodiacal.c: Ultrazodiacal Ul`tra*zo*di"a*cal (?), a. [Pref. ultra- + zodiacal.] (Astron.) Outside the zodiac; being in that part of the heavens that is more than eight degrees from the ecliptic; as, ultrazodiacal planets, that is, those planets which in part of their orbits go beyond the zodiac.

ultroneous.c: Ultroneous Ul*tro"ne*ous (?), a. [L. ultroneus, from ultro to the further side, on his part, of one's own accord. See Ultra-.] Spontaneous; voluntary. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor. -- Ul*tro"ne*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Ul*tro"ne*ous*ness, n. [Obs.]

ulula.c: Ulula ‖Ul"u*la (?), prop. n. [L., a screech owl.] (Zool.) A genus of owls including the great gray owl (Ulula cinerea) of Arctic America, and other similar species. See Illust. of Owl.

ululate.c: Ululate Ul"u*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Ululated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ululating.] [L. ululatus, p. p. of ululare to howl, yell, shriek.] To howl, as a dog or a wolf; to wail; as, ululating jackals. Sir T. Herbert.

ululation.c: Ululation Ul`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. ululatio.] A howling, as of a dog or wolf; a wailing.

ulva.c: Ulva ‖Ul"va (?), prop. n. [L., sedge.] (Bot.) A genus of thin papery bright green seaweeds including the kinds called sea lettuce.

umbe.c: Umbe Um"be (?), prep. [AS. ymbe; akin to OHG. umbi, G. um. Cf. Amb-.] About. [Obs.] Layamon.

umbecast.c: Umbecast Um"be*cast` (?), v. i. [Umbe + cast.] To cast about; to consider; to ponder. [Obs.] Sir T. Malory.

umbel.c: Umbel Um"bel (?), n. [L. umbella a little shadow, umbrella, dim. of umbra shade. See Umbrella.] (Bot.) A kind of flower cluster in which the flower stalks radiate from a common point, as in the carrot and milkweed. It is simple or compound; in the latter case, each peduncle bears another little umbel, called umbellet, or umbellule.

umbellar.c: Umbellar Um"bel*lar (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to an umbel; having the form of an umbel.

umbellated.c: Umbellated Umbellate { Um"bel*late (?), Um"bel*la`ted (?), } a. [NL. umbellatus.] (Bot.) Bearing umbels; pertaining to an umbel; umbel-like; as, umbellate plants or flowers.

umbellet.c: Umbellet Um"bel*let (?), n. (Bot.) A small or partial umbel; an umbellule.

umbellic.c: Umbellic Um*bel"lic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, certain umbelliferous plants; as, umbellic acid.

umbellifer.c: Umbellifer Um*bel"li*fer (?), n. [NL. See Umbelliferous.] (Bot.) A plant producing an umbel or umbels.

umbelliferone.c: Umbelliferone Um`bel*lif"er*one (?), n. (Chem.) A tasteless white crystalline substance, C9H6O3, found in the bark of a certain plant (Daphne Mezereum), and also obtained by the distillation of certain gums from the Umbelliferae, as galbanum, asafetida, etc. It is analogous to coumarin. Called also hydroxy-coumarin. Its strong fluorescence under ultraviolet light makes it useful in analytical biochemistry, as, for example, to detect phosphatase activity by hydrolysis of umbelliferyl phosphate.

umbelliferous.c: Umbelliferous Um`bel*lif"er*ous (?), a. [Umbel + -ferous: cf. F. ombellifère.] (Bot.) (a) Producing umbels. (b) Of or pertaining to a natural order (Umbelliferae) of plants, of which the parsley, carrot, parsnip, and fennel are well-known examples.

umbellularia.c: Umbellularia ‖Um*bel`lu*la"ri*a (?), prop. n. [NL. See Umbellule.] (Zool.) A genus of deep-sea alcyonaria consisting of a cluster of large flowerlike polyps situated at the summit of a long, slender stem which stands upright in the mud, supported by a bulbous base.

umbellule.c: Umbellule Um"bel*lule (?), n. [NL. umbellula, dim. of umbella: cf. F. ombellule.] (Bot.) An umbellet.

umber.c: Umber Um"ber (?), n. [F. ombre ocherous ore of iron, terre d'ombre, It. terra d'ombra, literally, earth of shadow or shade, L. umbra shadow, shade. Cf. Umber, 3 & 4, Umbrage.] 1. (Paint.) A brown or reddish pigment used in both oil and water colors, obtained from certain natural clays variously colored by the oxides of iron and manganese. It is commonly heated or burned before being used, and is then called burnt umber; when not heated, it is called raw umber. See Burnt umber, below.
Umber Um"ber, a. Of or pertaining to umber; resembling umber; olive-brown; dark brown; dark; dusky.
Umber Um"ber, v. t. To color with umber; to shade or darken; as, to umber over one's face. B. Jonson.

umbery.c: Umbery Um"ber*y (?), a. Of or pertaining to umber; like umber; as, umbery gold.

umbilic.c: Umbilic Um*bil"ic (?), n. [From L. umbilicus: cf. F. ombilic. See Navel.] 1. The navel; the center. [Obs.] “The umbilic of the world.” Sir T. Herbert.

umbilical.c: Umbilical Um*bil"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. ombilical. See Umbilic, n.] 1. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to an umbilicus, or umbilical cord; umbilic.

umbilicated.c: Umbilicated Umbilicate { Um*bil"i*cate (?), Um*bil"i*ca`ted (?), } a. [L. umbilicatus. See Umbilic.] (a) Depressed in the middle, like a navel, as a flower, fruit, or leaf; navel-shaped; having an umbilicus; as, an umbilicated smallpox vesicle. (b) (Bot.) Supported by a stalk at the central point.

umbilication.c: Umbilication Um*bil"i*ca"tion (?), n. A slight, navel-like depression, or dimpling, of the center of a rounded body; as, the umbilication of a smallpox vesicle; also, the condition of being umbilicated.

umbilicus.c: Umbilicus ‖Um`bi*li"cus (?), n. [L. See Umbilic.] 1. (Anat.) The depression, or mark, in the median line of the abdomen, which indicates the point where the umbilical cord separated from the fetus; the navel; the belly button, in humans.

umble.c: Umble pie Um"ble pie` (?). A pie made of umbles. See To eat humble pie, under Humble.

umbles.c: Umbles Um"bles (?), n. pl. [See Nombles.] The entrails and coarser parts of a deer; hence, sometimes, entrails, in general. [Written also humbles.] Johnson.

umbo.c: Umbo ‖Um"bo (?), n.; pl. L. Umbones (#), E. Umbos (#). [L.] 1. The boss of a shield, at or near the middle, and usually projecting, sometimes in a sharp spike.

umbonated.c: Umbonated Umbonate { Um"bo*nate (?), Um"bo*na`ted (?), } a. [NL. umbonatus. See Umbo.] Having a conical or rounded projection or protuberance, like a boss.

umbra.c: Umbra ‖Um"bra (?), n.; pl. Umbrae (#). [L., a shadow.] 1. (Astron.) (a) The conical shadow projected from a planet or satellite, on the side opposite to the sun, within which a spectator could see no portion of the sun's disk; -- used in contradistinction from penumbra. See Penumbra. (b) The central dark portion, or nucleus, of a sun spot. (c) The fainter part of a sun spot; -- now more commonly called penumbra.

umbraculiferous.c: Umbraculiferous Um*brac`u*lif"er*ous (ŭm*brăk`u*lĭf"ẽr*ŭs), a. [L. umbraculum umbrella (dim. of umbra shade) + -ferous.] (Bot.) Bearing something like an open umbrella.

umbraculiform.c: Umbraculiform Um*brac`u*li*form (ŭm*brăk"u*lĭ*fôrm), a. [L. umbraculum any thing that furnishes shade, a bower, umbrella (dim. of umbra a shade) + -form.] Having the form of anything that serves to shade, as a tree top, an umbrella, and the like; specifically (Bot.), having the form of an umbrella; umbrella-shaped.

umbrage.c: Umbrage Um"brage (ŭm"braj; 48), n. [F. ombrage shade, suspicion, umbrage, L. umbraticus belonging to shade, fr. umbra a shade. Cf. Umber, Umbratic.] 1. Shade; shadow; obscurity; hence, that which affords a shade, as a screen of trees or foliage.

umbrageous.c: umbrageous um*bra"geous (ŭm*brā"jŭs; 277), a. [Cf. F. ombrageux shy, skittish, suspicious, in OF. also, shady. See Umbrage.] 1. Forming or affording a shade; shady; shaded; as, umbrageous trees or foliage.

umbrate.c: Umbrate Um"brate (ŭm"brāt), v. t. [L. umbratus, p. p. of umbrare to shade, fr. umbra a shade.] To shade; to shadow; to foreshadow. [Obs.]

umbratical.c: Umbratical Umbratic { Um*brat"ic (ŭm*brăt"ĭk), Um*brat"ic*al (ŭm*brăt"ĭ*kail), } a. [L. umbraticus, from umbra shade. See Umbrage.] Of or pertaining to the shade or darkness; shadowy; unreal; secluded; retired. [R.] B. Jonson.

umbratile.c: Umbratile Um"bra*tile (?), a. [L. umbratilus, fr. umbra shade.] Umbratic. [R.] B. Jonson.

umbratious.c: Umbratious Um*bra"tious (?), a. [L. umbra a shade. Cf. Umbrageous.] Suspicious; captious; disposed to take umbrage. [Obs. & R.] Sir H. Wotton.

umbrel.c: Umbrel Um*brel" (?), n. An umbrella. [Obs. or Colloq.]

umbrella.c: Umbrella Um*brel"la (?), n. [It. ombrella, fr. ombra a shade, L. umbra; cf. L. umbella a sunshade, a parasol. Cf. Umbel, Umbrage.] 1. A shade, screen, or guard, carried in the hand for sheltering the person from the rays of the sun, or from rain or snow. It is formed of silk, cotton, or other fabric, extended on strips of whalebone, steel, or other elastic material, inserted in, or fastened to, a rod or stick by means of pivots or hinges, in such a way as to allow of being opened and closed with ease. See Parasol.

umbriere.c: Umbriere Umbrere { Um*brere, Um*briere } (?), n. [F. ombre a shade, L. umbra; cf. F. ombrelle a sunshade, OF. also ombrière. See Umbrella.] In ancient armor, a visor, or projection like the peak of a cap, to which a face guard was sometimes attached. This was sometimes fixed, and sometimes moved freely upon the helmet and could be raised like the beaver. Called also umber, and umbril. [Obs.]

umbriferous.c: Umbriferous Um*brif"er*ous (?), a. [L. umbrifer; umbra a shade + ferre to bear.] Casting or making a shade; umbrageous. -- Um*brif"er*ous*ly (#), adv.

umbrose.c: Umbrose Um"brose` (?), a. [L. umbrosus, fr. umbra a shade.] Shady; umbrageous. [Obs.]

umbrosity.c: Umbrosity Um*bros"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being umbrose; shadiness. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

umhofo.c: umhofo um*ho"fo (ŭm*hō"fo), n. (Zool.) An African two-horned rhinoceros (Atelodus simus or Rhinoceros simus); -- called also chukuru, and white rhinoceros.

umlaut.c: umlaut ‖um"laut (ōom"lout), n. [G., from um about + laut sound.] (Philol.) The euphonic modification of a root vowel sound by the influence of a, u, or especially i, in the syllable which formerly followed.

umlauted.c: Umlauted Um"laut*ed, a. (Philol.) Having the umlaut; as, umlauted vowels.

umpirage.c: Umpirage Um"pi*rage (?; 48), n. [From Umpire.] 1. The office of an umpire; the power, right, or authority of an umpire to decide.

umpire.c: Umpire Um"pire (?), n. [OE. nompere, nounpere (also impier, fr. F. impair uneven), fr. OF. nomper uneven, F. non-pair; hence the meaning, uneven, i. e., third person; non not + OF. per even, equal, peer, F. pair; cf. L. impar uneven, unequal. See Non-, and Peer, n.]
Umpire Um"pire, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Umpired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Umpiring.] 1. To decide as umpire; to arbitrate; to settle, as a dispute.
Umpire Um"pire, v. i. To act as umpire or arbitrator.

umquhile.c: umquhile um"quhile (ŭm"kwĭl), adv. [Cf. OF. umwhile for a time. See While.] Some time ago; formerly. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott. -- a. Former. [Scot.]

un.c: Un- Un-. [OE. un-, on-, the unaccented form of the accented prefix and- (cf. Answer); akin to D. ont-, G. ent-, OHG. int-, Goth. and-. See Anti-.] An inseparable verbal prefix or particle. It is prefixed: (a) To verbs to express the contrary, and not the simple negative, of the action of the verb to which it is prefixed; as in unbend, uncoil, undo, unfold. (b) To nouns to form verbs expressing privation of the thing, quality, or state expressed by the noun, or separation from it; as in unchild, unsex. Sometimes particles and participial adjectives formed with this prefix coincide in form with compounds of the negative prefix un- (see 2d Un-); as in undone (from undo), meaning unfastened, ruined; and undone (from 2d un- and done) meaning not done, not finished. Un- is sometimes used with an intensive force merely; as in unloose.

Un- Un-. [OE. & AS. un-; akin to OFries. un-, D. on-, OS., OHG., & G. un-, Icel. ō-, ū-, Sw. o-, Dan. u-, W. an-, L. in-, Gr.?,?, Skr. an-, a-. √193. Cf. A- not In- not, No, adv.] An inseparable prefix, or particle, signifying not; in-; non-. In- is prefixed mostly to words of Latin origin, or else to words formed by Latin suffixes; un- is of much wider application, and is attached at will to almost any adjective, or participle used adjectively, or adverb, from which it may be desired to form a corresponding negative adjective or adverb, and is also, but less freely, prefixed to nouns. Un- sometimes has merely an intensive force; as in unmerciless, unremorseless.

unable.c: Unable Un*a"ble (?), a. Not able; not having sufficient strength, means, knowledge, skill, or the like; impotent; weak; helpless; incapable; -- now usually followed by an infinitive or an adverbial phrase; as, unable for work; unable to bear fatigue.

una.c: Una boat U"na boat` (?). (Naut.) The English name for a catboat; -- so called because Una was the name of the first boat of this kind taken to England. D. Kemp.

unabridged.c: Unabridged Un`a*bridged" (?), a. Not abridged, or shortened; full; complete; entire; whole.

unabsorbable.c: Unabsorbable Un`ab*sorb"a*ble (?), a. Not absorbable; specifically (Physiol.), not capable of absorption; unable to pass by osmosis into the circulating blood; as, the unabsorbable portion of food.

unacceptability.c: Unacceptability Un`ac*cept`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being unacceptable; unacceptableness.

unacceptable.c: Unacceptable Un`ac*cept"a*ble (?), a. Not acceptable; not pleasing; not welcome; unpleasant; disagreeable; displeasing; offensive. -- Un`ac*cept"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`ac*cept"a*bly, adv.

unaccessible.c: Unaccessible Un`ac*cess"i*ble (?), a. Inaccessible. Herbert. -- Un`ac*cess"i*bleness, n. -- Un`ac*cess"i*bly, adv.

unaccomplished.c: Unaccomplished Un`ac*com"plished (?), a. Not accomplished or performed; unfinished; also, deficient in accomplishment; unrefined.

unaccomplishment.c: Unaccomplishment Un`ac*com"plish*ment (?), n. The state of being unaccomplished. [Obs.] Milton.

unaccountability.c: Unaccountability Un`ac*count`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unaccountable.

unaccountable.c: Unaccountable Un`ac*count"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not accountable or responsible; free from control. South.

unaccustomed.c: Unaccustomed Un`ac*cus"tomed (?), a. 1. Not used; not habituated; unfamiliar; unused; -- with to.

unacquaintance.c: Unacquaintance Un`ac*quaint"ance (?), n. The quality or state of being unacquainted; want of acquaintance; ignorance.

unactive.c: Unactive Un*ac"tive, v. t. [1st pref. un- + active; or from unactive, a.] To render inactive or listless. [Obs.] Fuller.

unadulterated.c: Unadulterated Unadulterate { Un`a*dul"ter*ate (?), Un`a*dul"ter*a`ted (?), } a. Not adulterated; pure. “Unadulterate air.” Cowper. -- Un`a*dul"ter*ate*ly, adv.

unadvisable.c: Unadvisable Un`ad*vis"a*ble (?), a. Not advisable; inadvisable; inexpedient. Lowth. -- Un`ad*vis"a*bly, adv.

unadvised.c: Unadvised Un`ad*vised" (?), a. 1. Not prudent; not discreet; ill advised. Shak.

unaffected.c: Unaffected Un`af*fect"ed (?), a. 1. Not affected or moved; destitute of affection or emotion; uninfluenced.

unaidable.c: Unaidable Un*aid"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being aided. “Her unaidable estate.” Shak.

unalienable.c: Unalienable Un*al"ien*a*ble (?), a. Inalienable; as, unalienable rights. Swift. -- Un*al"ien*a*bly, adv.

unalist.c: Unalist U"nal*ist (ū"nail*ĭst), n. [L. unus one.] (Eccl.) An ecclesiastic who holds but one benefice; -- distinguished from pluralist. [Eng.] V. Knox.

unallied.c: Unallied Un`al*lied" (ŭn`ăl*līd"), a. Not allied; having no ally; having no connection or relation; as, unallied species or genera.

unalloyed.c: Unalloyed Un`al*loyed" (ŭn`ăl*loid"), a. Not alloyed; not reduced by foreign admixture; unmixed; unqualified; pure; as, unalloyed metals; unalloyed happiness.

unalmsed.c: Unalmsed Un*almsed" (ŭn*ämzd"), a. Not having received alms. [Obs. & R.] Pollock.

unambiguity.c: Unambiguity Un*am`bi*gu"i*ty (?), n. Absence of ambiguity; clearness; perspicuity.

unambition.c: Unambition Un`am*bi"tion (?), n. The absence of ambition. [R.] F. W. Newman.

unamiability.c: Unamiability Un*a`mi*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unamiable; moroseness.

unamiable.c: Unamiable Un*a"mi*a*ble (?), a. Not amiable; morose; ill-natured; repulsive. -- Un*a"mi*a*bly, adv.

unanchor.c: Unanchor Un*an"chor (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + anchor.] To loose from the anchor, as a ship. De Quincey.

unaneled.c: Unaneled Un`a*neled" (?), a. Not aneled; not having received extreme unction. Shak.

unanimity.c: Unanimity U`na*nim"i*ty (?), n. [L. unanimitas: cf. F. unanimité.] The quality or state of being unanimous.

unanimous.c: Unanimous U*nan"i*mous (u*năn"ĭ*mŭs), a. [L. unanimus, unanimis; unus one + animus mind: cf. F. unanime. See Unit, and Animate.] 1. Being of one mind; agreeing in opinion, design, or determination; consentient; not discordant or dissentient; harmonious; as, the assembly was unanimous; the members of the council were unanimous. “Both in one faith unanimous.” Milton.

unanswerability.c: Unanswerability Un*an`swer*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being unanswerable; unanswerableness.

unanswerable.c: Unanswerable Un*an"swer*a*ble (?), a. Not answerable; irrefutable; conclusive; decisive; as, he gave an unanswerable argument. -- Un*an"swer*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*an"swer*a*bly, adv.

unanswered.c: Unanswered Un*an"swered (?), a. 1. Not answered; not replied to; as, an unanswered letter.

unappalled.c: Unappalled Un`ap*palled" (?), a. Not appalled; not frightened; dauntless; undaunted. Milton.

unapparel.c: Unapparel Un`ap*par"el (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + apparel.] To divest of clothing; to strip. [Obs.] Donne.

unappealable.c: Unappealable Un`ap*peal"a*ble, a. 1. Not appealable; that can not be carried to a higher tribunal by appeal; as, an unappealable suit or action.

unappropriate.c: Unappropriate Un`ap*pro"pri*ate (?), a. [Pref. un- not + appropriate, a.] 1. Inappropriate; unsuitable.

Unappropriate Un`ap*pro"pri*ate (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + appropriate, v. t.] To take from private possession; to restore to the possession or right of all; as, to unappropriate a monopoly. [R.] Milton.

unappropriated.c: Unappropriated Un`ap*pro"pri*a`ted (?), a. [Pref. un- not + appropriated.] 1. Not specially appropriate; having no special application. J. Warton.

unapt.c: Unapt Un*apt" (?), a. 1. Inapt; slow; dull. Bacon.

unaquit.c: Unaquit Un`a*quit" (?), a. [See Un- not, and Acquit.] Unrequited. [R. & Obs.] Gower.

unargued.c: Unargued Un*ar"gued (?), a. 1. Not argued or debated.

unarm.c: Unarm Un*arm" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + arm.] To disarm. Sir T. Browne.
Unarm Un*arm", v. i. To put off, or lay down, one's arms or armor. “I'll unarm again.” Shak.

unarmed.c: Unarmed Un*armed" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + armed.] 1. Not armed or armored; having no arms or weapons.

unarted.c: Unarted Un*art"ed (?), a. 1. Ignorant of the arts. [Obs.] E. Waterhouse.

unartful.c: unartful un*art"ful (?), a. Lacking art or skill; artless. Congreve. -- Un*art"ful*ly, adv. Swift. Burke.

unassented.c: Unassented Un`as*sent"ed (?), a. Not assented; -- said specif. of stocks or bonds the holders of which refuse to deposit them by way of assent to an agreement altering their status, as in a readjustment.

unassuming.c: Unassuming Un`as*sum"ing (?), a. Not assuming; not bold or forward; not arrogant or presuming; humble; modest; retiring; as, an unassuming youth; unassuming manners.

unassured.c: Unassured Un`as*sured" (?), a. 1. Not assured; not bold or confident.

unatonable.c: Unatonable Un`a*ton"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not capable of being brought into harmony; irreconcilable. “Unatonable matrimony.” [Obs.] Milton.

unattached.c: Unattached Un`at*tached" (?), a. 1. Not attached; not adhering; having no engagement; free.

unattire.c: Unattire Un`at*tire" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + attire.] To divest of attire; to undress.

unau.c: Unau U*nau" (u*nä"), n. [Brazilian.] (Zool.) The two-toed sloth (Cholopus didactylus), native of South America. It is about two feet long. Its color is a uniform grayish brown, sometimes with a reddish tint.

unaudienced.c: Unaudienced Un*au"di*enced (?), a. Not given an audience; not received or heard.

unauthorize.c: Unauthorize Un*au"thor*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + authorize.] To disown the authority of; to repudiate.

unavoidable.c: Unavoidable Un`a*void"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not avoidable; incapable of being shunned or prevented; inevitable; necessary; as, unavoidable troubles.

unavoided.c: Unavoided Un`a*void"ed, a. 1. Not avoided or shunned. Shak.

unaware.c: Unaware Un`a*ware" (?), a. Not aware; not noticing; giving no heed; thoughtless; inattentive. Swift.

unawares.c: Unawares Un`a*wares" (?), adv. Without design or preparation; suddenly; without premeditation, unexpectedly. “Mercies lighting unawares.” J. H. Newman.

unbacked.c: Unbacked Un*backed" (?), a. 1. Never mounted by a rider; unbroken. “Unbacked colts.” Shak.

unbag.c: Unbag Un*bag" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bag.] To pour, or take, or let go, out of a bag or bags.

unbalanced.c: Unbalanced Un*bal"anced (?), a. [In senses 1 and 2, pref. un- not + balanced; in sense 3, 1st pref. un- + balance.] 1. Not balanced; not in equipoise; having no counterpoise, or having insufficient counterpoise.

unballast.c: Unballast Un*bal"last (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + ballast.] To free from ballast; to discharge ballast from. Totten.
Unballast Un*bal"last, a. Not ballasted. [Obs. & R.] Addison.

unballasted.c: Unballasted Un*bal"last*ed, a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unballast.] Freed from ballast; having discharged ballast.

unbanded.c: Unbanded Un*band"ed (?), a. [1st un- + band + -ed.] Wanting a band or string; unfastened. [Obs.] Shak.

unbank.c: Unbank Un*bank" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bank.] To remove a bank from; to open by, or as if by, the removal of a bank. H. Taylor.

unbar.c: Unbar Un*bar" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bar.] To remove a bar or bars from; to unbolt; to open; as, to unbar a gate. Heber.

unbark.c: Unbark Un*bark" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bark rind.] To deprive of the bark; to decorticate; to strip; as, to unbark a tree. Bacon.
Unbark Un*bark", v. t. [1st pref. un- + bark the vessel.] To cause to disembark; to land. [Obs.] Hakluyt.

unbarrel.c: Unbarrel Un*bar"rel (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + barrel.] To remove or release from a barrel or barrels.

unbarricade.c: Unbarricade Un*bar`ri*cade" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + barricade.] To unbolt; to unbar; to open.

unbarricadoed.c: Unbarricadoed Un*bar`ri*ca"doed (?), a. Not obstructed by barricades; open; as, unbarricadoed streets. Burke.

unbashful.c: Unbashful Un*bash"ful (?), a. Not bashful or modest; bold; impudent; shameless. Shak.

unbay.c: Unbay Un*bay" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bay to dam.] To free from the restraint of anything that surrounds or incloses; to let loose; to open. [Obs.]

unbe.c: Unbe Un*be" (ŭn*bē"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + be.] To cause not to be; to cause to be another. [Obs. & R.]

unbear.c: Unbear Un*bear" (ŭn*bâr"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bear to support.] To remove or loose the bearing rein of (a horse).

unbeast.c: Unbeast Un*beast" (ŭn*bēst"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + beast.] To deliver from the form or nature of a beast.

unbecome.c: Unbecome Un`be*come" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + become.] To misbecome. [Obs.] Bp. Sherlock.

unbecoming.c: Unbecoming Un`be*com"ing (?), a. [Pref. un- not + becoming.] Not becoming; unsuitable; unfit; indecorous; improper.

unbed.c: Unbed Un*bed" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bed.] To raise or rouse from bed.

unbedinned.c: Unbedinned Un`be*dinned" (?), a. Not filled with din.

unbefool.c: Unbefool Un`be*fool" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + befool.] To deliver from the state of a fool; to awaken the mind of; to undeceive.

unbeget.c: Unbeget Un`be*get" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + beget.] To deprive of existence. Dryden.

unbegilt.c: Unbegilt Un`be*gilt" (?), a. Not gilded; hence, not rewarded with gold.

unbegotten.c: Unbegotten Unbegot { Un`be*got" (?), Un`be*got"ten (?), } a. [Pref. un- not + begot, begotten.] Not begot; not yet generated; also, having never been generated; self-existent; eternal.

unbeguile.c: Unbeguile Un`be*guile" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbeguiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unbeguiling.] [1st pref. un- + beguile.] To set free from the influence of guile; to undeceive. “Then unbeguile thyself.” Donne.

unbegun.c: Unbegun Un`be*gun" (?), a. Not yet begun; also, existing without a beginning.

unbehovely.c: Unbehovely Un`be*hove"ly (?), a. Not behooving or becoming; unseemly. [Obs. & R.] Gower.

unbeing.c: Unbeing Un*be"ing (?), a. Not existing. [Obs.] “Beings yet unbeing.” Sir T. Browne.

unbelief.c: Unbelief Un`be*lief" (?), n. [Pref. un- not + belief: cf. AS. ungeleáfa.] 1. The withholding of belief; doubt; incredulity; skepticism.

unbeliever.c: Unbeliever Un`be*liev"er (?), n. 1. One who does not believe; an incredulous person; a doubter; a skeptic.

unbelieving.c: Unbelieving Un`be*liev"ing, a. 1. Not believing; incredulous; doubting; distrusting; skeptical.

unbelt.c: Unbelt Un*belt" (ŭn*bĕlt"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + belt.] To remove or loose the belt of; to ungird.

unbend.c: Unbend Un*bend" (ŭn*bĕnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbent (ŭn*bĕnt"); p. pr. & vb. n. Unbending.] [1st pref. un- + bend.] 1. To free from flexure; to make, or allow to become, straight; to loosen; as, to unbend a bow.
Unbend Un*bend", v. i. 1. To cease to be bent; to become straight or relaxed.

unbending.c: Unbending Un*bend"ing, a. [In senses 1, 2, and 3, pref. un- not + bending; in sense 4, properly p. pr. of unbend.] 1. Not bending; not suffering flexure; not yielding to pressure; stiff; -- applied to material things.

unbenevolence.c: Unbenevolence Un`be*nev"o*lence (?), n. Absence or want of benevolence; ill will.

unbenumb.c: Unbenumb Un`be*numb" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + benumb.] To relieve of numbness; to restore sensation to.

unbereft.c: Unbereft Un`be*reft" (?), a. Not bereft; not taken away.

unbeseem.c: Unbeseem Un`be*seem" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + beseem.] To be unbecoming or unsuitable to; to misbecome.

unbeseeming.c: Unbeseeming Un`be*seem"ing, a. [Pref. un- not + beseeming.] Unbecoming; not befitting. -- Un`be*seem"ing*ly, adv. -- Un`be*seem"ing*ness, n.

unbespeak.c: Unbespeak Un`be*speak" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bespeak.] To unsay; hence, to annul or cancel. [Obs.] Pepys.

unbethink.c: Unbethink Un`be*think" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bethink.] To change the mind of (one's self). [Obs.]

unbewitch.c: Unbewitch Un`be*witch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bewitch.] To free from a spell; to disenchant. [R.] South.

unbias.c: Unbias Un*bi"as (ŭn*bī"ais), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bias.] To free from bias or prejudice. Swift.

unbiased.c: Unbiased Un*bi"ased (ŭn*bī"aist), a. [Pref. un- not + biased.] Free from bias or prejudice; unprejudiced; impartial. -- Un*bi"ased*ly, adv. --Un*bi"ased*ness, n.

unbidden.c: Unbidden Unbid { Un*bid" (ŭn*bĭd"), Un*bid"den (?), } a. 1. Not bidden; not commanded.

unbind.c: Unbind Un*bind" (ŭn*bīnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbound (ŭn*bound"); p. pr. & vb. n. Unbinding.] [AS. unbindan. See Un-, and Bind.] To remove a band from; to set free from shackles or fastenings; to untie; to unfasten; to loose; as, unbind your fillets; to unbind a prisoner's arms; to unbind a load.

unbishop.c: Unbishop Un*bish"op (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bishop.] To deprive, as a city, of a bishop; to deprive, as a clergyman, of episcopal dignity or rights. [R.] “Then he unbishops himself.” Milton.

unbit.c: Unbit Un*bit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Unbitting.] [1st pref. un- + bit.] (Naut.) To remove the turns of (a rope or cable) from the bits; as, to unbit a cable. Totten.

unblemished.c: Unblemished Un*blem"ished (?), a. Not blemished; pure; spotless; as, an unblemished reputation or life. Addison.

unbless.c: Unbless Un*bless" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bless.] To deprive of blessings; to make wretched. [Obs.] Shak.

unblest.c: Unblest Unblessed { Un*blessed", Un*blest } (?), a. [Pref. un- not + blessed, blest.] Not blest; excluded from benediction; hence, accursed; wretched. “Unblessed enchanter.” Milton.

unblind.c: Unblind Un*blind" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + blind.] To free from blindness; to give or restore sight to; to open the eyes of. [R.] J. Webster (1607).

unblindfold.c: Unblindfold Un*blind"fold` (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + blindfold.] To free from that which blindfolds. Spenser.

unblushing.c: Unblushing Un*blush"ing (?), a. Not blushing; shameless. -- Un*blush"ing*ly, adv.

unbody.c: Unbody Un*bod"y (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + body.] To free from the body; to disembody.
Unbody Un*bod"y, v. i. To leave the body; to be disembodied; -- said of the soul or spirit. [R.] Chaucer.

unbolt.c: Unbolt Un*bolt" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bolt.] To remove a bolt from; to unfasten; to unbar; to open. “He shall unbolt the gates.” Shak.
Unbolt Un*bolt", v. i. To explain or unfold a matter; to make a revelation. [Obs.] “I will unbolt to you.” Shak.

unbone.c: Unbone Un*bone" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bone.]

unbonnet.c: Unbonnet Un*bon"net (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + bonnet.] To take a bonnet from; to take off one's bonnet; to uncover; as, to unbonnet one's head. Sir W. Scott.

unbooked.c: Unbooked Un*booked" (?), a. Not written in a book; unrecorded. “UnbookedEnglish life.” Masson.

unboot.c: Unboot Un*boot" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + boot.] To take off the boots from.

unborn.c: Unborn Un*born" (?), a. Not born; not yet brought into life; being still to appear; future.

unborrowed.c: Unborrowed Un*bor"rowed (?), a. Not borrowed; being one's own; native; original.

unbosom.c: Unbosom Un*bos"om (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbosomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unbosoming.] [1st pref. un- + bosom.] To disclose freely; to reveal in confidence, as secrets; to confess; -- often used reflexively; as, to unbosom one's self. Milton.

unbosomer.c: Unbosomer Un*bos"om*er (?), n. One who unbosoms, or discloses. [R.] “An unbosomer of secrets.” Thackeray.

unbottomed.c: Unbottomed Un*bot"tomed (?), a. 1. [1st pref. un- + bottom + -ed.] Deprived of a bottom.

unbound.c: Unbound Un*bound" (?), imp. & p. p. of Unbind.

unbounded.c: Unbounded Un*bound"ed, a. Having no bound or limit; as, unbounded space; an, unbounded ambition. Addison. -- Un*bound"ed*ly, adv. -- Un*bound"ed*ness, n.

unbow.c: Unbow Un*bow" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bow.] To unbend. [R.] Fuller.

unbowed.c: Unbowed Un*bowed" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + bowed.] Not bent or arched; not bowed down. Byron.

unbowel.c: Unbowel Un*bow"el (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unboweled (?) or Unbowelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Unboweling or Unbowelling.] [1st pref. un- + bowel.] To deprive of the entrails; to disembowel. Dr. H. More.

unbox.c: Unbox Un*box" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + box.] To remove from a box or boxes.

unboy.c: Unboy Un*boy" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + boy.] To divest of the traits of a boy. [R.] Clarendon.

unbrace.c: Unbrace Un*brace" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + brace.] To free from tension; to relax; to loose; as, to unbrace a drum; to unbrace the nerves. Spenser.

unbraid.c: Unbraid Un*braid" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + braid.] To separate the strands of; to undo, as a braid; to unravel; to disentangle.

unbreast.c: Unbreast Un*breast" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + breast.] To disclose, or lay open; to unbosom. [Obs.] P. Fletcher,

unbred.c: Unbred Un*bred" (?), a. 1. Not begotten; unborn. [Obs.] “Thou age unbred.” Shak.

unbreech.c: Unbreech Un*breech" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unbreeched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unbreeching.] [1st pref. un- + breech.] 1. To remove the breeches of; to divest or strip of breeches. Shak.

unbrewed.c: Unbrewed Un*brewed" (?), a. Not made by brewing; unmixed; pure; genuine. [R.] Young.

unbridle.c: Unbridle Un*bri"dle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bridle.] To free from the bridle; to set loose.

unbridled.c: Unbridled Un*bri"dled (?), a. [Pref. un- not + bridled.] Loosed from the bridle, or as from the bridle; hence, unrestrained; licentious; violent; as, unbridled passions. “Unbridled boldness.” B. Jonson.

unbroken.c: Unbroken Un*bro"ken (?), a. Not broken; continuous; unsubdued; as, an unbroken colt.

unbuckle.c: Unbuckle Un*buc"kle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + buckle.] To loose the buckles of; to unfasten; as, to unbuckle a shoe. “Unbuckle anon thy purse.” Chaucer.

unbuild.c: Unbuild Un*build (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + build.] To demolish; to raze. “To unbuild the city.” Shak.

unbundle.c: Unbundle Un*bun"dle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bundle.] To release, as from a bundle; to disclose.

unbung.c: Unbung Un*bung" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bung.] To remove the bung from; as, to unbung a cask.

unburden.c: Unburden Un*bur"den (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + burden.] 1. To relieve from a burden.

unburiable.c: Unburiable Un*bur"i*a*ble (?), a. Not ready or not proper to be buried. Tennyson.

unburrow.c: Unburrow Un*bur"row (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + burrow.] To force from a burrow; to unearth.

unburthen.c: Unburthen Un*bur"then (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + burthen.] To unburden; to unload.

unbury.c: Unbury Un*bur"y (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + bury.] To disinter; to exhume; fig., to disclose.

unbusied.c: Unbusied Un*bus"ied (?), a. Not required to work; unemployed; not busy. [R.]

unbutton.c: Unbutton Un*but"ton (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + button.] To loose the buttons of; to unfasten.

unbuxom.c: Unbuxom Un*bux"om (?), a. Disobedient. [Obs.] Piers Plowman. -- Un*bux"om*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Un*bux"om*ness, n. [Obs.]

uncage.c: Uncage Un*cage" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cage.] To loose, or release, from, or as from, a cage.

uncalledfor.c: Uncalled-for Un*called"-for` (?), a. Not called for; not required or needed; improper; gratuitous; wanton.

uncalm.c: Uncalm Un*calm" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + calm.] To disturb; to disquiet. Dryden.

uncamp.c: Uncamp Un*camp" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + camp.] To break up the camp of; to dislodge from camp. [R.]

uncanny.c: Uncanny Un*can"ny (?), a. Not canny; unsafe; strange; weird; ghostly. Sir W. Scott. -- Un*can"ni*ness, n. G. Eliot.

uncanonize.c: Uncanonize Un*can"on*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + canonize.] 1. To deprive of canonical authority.

uncap.c: Uncap Un*cap" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cap.] To remove a cap or cover from.

uncapable.c: Uncapable Un*ca"pa*ble (?), a. Incapable. [Obs.] “Uncapable of conviction.” Locke.

uncape.c: Uncape Un*cape" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cape.] To remove a cap or cape from. [Obs.]

uncapper.c: Uncapper Un*cap"per (?), n. An instrument for removing an exploded cap from a cartridge shell.

uncardinal.c: Uncardinal Un*car"di*nal (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cardinal.] To degrade from the cardinalship.

uncared.c: Uncared Un*cared" (?), a. Not cared for; not heeded; -- with for.

uncarnate.c: Uncarnate Un*car"nate (?), a. Not fleshly; specifically, not made flesh; not incarnate. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
Uncarnate Un*car"nate (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + carnate.] To divest of flesh.

uncart.c: Uncart Un*cart" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cart.] To take from, or set free from, a cart; to unload.

uncase.c: Uncase Un*case" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + case.]

uncastle.c: Uncastle Un*cas"tle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + castle.] To take a castle from; to turn out of a castle.

uncaused.c: Uncaused Un*caused" (?), a. Having no antecedent cause; uncreated; self-existent; eternal. A. Baxter.

unce.c: Unce Unce (?), n. [L. uncus hook.] A claw. [Obs.]
Unce Unce, n. [L. uncia ounce. See Ounce a weight.] An ounce; a small portion. [Obs.] “By unces hung his locks.” Chaucer.

unceasable.c: Unceasable Un*ceas"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being ended; unceasing. [R.]

uncentre.c: Uncentre Uncenter { Un*cen"ter, Un*cen"tre } (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + center.] To throw from its center.

uncentury.c: Uncentury Un*cen"tu*ry (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + century.] To remove from its actual century. [R.]

uncertain.c: Uncertain Un*cer"tain (ŭn*sẽr"tĭn), a. [Pref. un- not + certain. Cf. Incertain.] 1. Not certain; not having certain knowledge; not assured in mind; distrustful. Chaucer.
Uncertain Un*cer"tain, v. t. [1st pref. un- + certain; or fr. uncertain, a.] To make uncertain. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

uncertainly.c: Uncertainly Un*cer"tain*ly, adv. In an uncertain manner.

uncessant.c: Uncessant Un*ces"sant (?), a. Incessant. [Obs.] Dr. H. More. -- Un*ces"sant*ly, adv. [Obs.]

unchain.c: Unchain Un*chain" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + chain.] To free from chains or slavery; to let loose. Prior.

unchancy.c: Unchancy Un*chan"cy (?), a. [Pref un- + Scot. chancy fortunate, safe.] 1. Happening at a bad time; unseasonable; inconvenient. A. Trollope.

unchaplain.c: Unchaplain Un*chap"lain (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + chaplain.] To remove from a chaplaincy.

uncharge.c: Uncharge Un*charge" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + charge.]

unchariot.c: Unchariot Un*char"i*ot (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + chariot.] To throw out of a chariot. Pope.

uncharitable.c: Uncharitable Un*char"i*ta*ble (?), a. Not charitable; contrary to charity; severe in judging; harsh; censorious; as, uncharitable opinions or zeal. Addison. -- Un*char"i*ta*ble*ness, n. -- Un*char"i*ta*bly, adv.

uncharm.c: Uncharm Un*charm" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + charm.] To release from a charm, fascination, or secret power; to disenchant. Beau. & Fl.

uncharnel.c: Uncharnel Un*char"nel (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Uncharneled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Uncharneling.] [1st pref. un- + charnel.] To remove from a charnel house; to raise from the grave; to exhume. Byron.

unchaste.c: Unchaste Un*chaste" (?), a. Not chaste; not continent; lewd. -- Un*chaste"ly, adv. -- Un*chaste"ness, n.

unchastity.c: Unchastity Un*chas"ti*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unchaste; lewdness; incontinence.

uncheckable.c: Uncheckable Un*check"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being checked or stopped. [R.]

unchild.c: Unchild Un*child" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + child.]

unchristen.c: Unchristen Un*chris"ten (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + christen.] To render unchristian. [Obs. & R.] Milton.

unchristened.c: Unchristened Un*chris"tened (?), a. [Pref. un- not + christened.] Not christened; as, an unchristened child.

unchristian.c: Unchristian Un*chris"tian (?), a. [Pref. un- not + Christian.] 1. Not Christian; not converted to the Christian faith; infidel.
Unchristian Un*chris"tian, v. t. [1st pref. un- + Christian.] To make unchristian. [Obs.] South.

unchristianize.c: Unchristianize Un*chris"tian*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + Christianize.] To turn from the Christian faith; to cause to abandon the belief and profession of Christianity.

unchristianly.c: Unchristianly Un*chris"tian*ly, adv. In an unchristian manner.

unchristianness.c: Unchristianness Un*chris"tian*ness, n. The quality or state of being unchristian. [R.] Eikon Basilike.

unchurch.c: Unchurch Un*church" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + church.] 1. To expel, or cause to separate, from a church; to excommunicate. Sir M. Hale.

uncia.c: Uncia ‖Un"ci*a (?), n.; pl. Unciae (#). [L. See Ounce a measure of weight.] 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A twelfth part, as of the Roman as; an ounce.

uncial.c: Uncial Un"cial (?), a. [L. uncialis amounting to the twelfth part of a pound or a foot, from uncia the twelfth part of a pound or of a foot, an ounce, an inch: cf. F. oncial. See Inch a measure.] Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain style of letters used in ancient manuscripts, esp. in Greek and Latin manuscripts. The letters are somewhat rounded, and the upstrokes and downstrokes usually have a slight inclination. These letters were used as early as the 1st century b. c., and were seldom used after the 10th century a. d., being superseded by the cursive style.

unciform.c: Unciform Un"ci*form (ŭn"sĭ*fôrm), a. [L. uncus a hook + -form.] Having the shape of a hook; being of a curved or hooked form; hooklike.
Unciform Un"ci*form, n. (Anat.) The unciform bone. See Illust. of Perissodactyla.

uncinata.c: Uncinata ‖Un`ci*na"ta (ŭn"sĭ*nā"tȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. uncinus a hook.] (Zool.) A division of marine chaetopod annelids which are furnished with uncini, as the serpulas and sabellas.

uncinate.c: Uncinate Un"ci*nate (?), a. [L. uncinatus, from uncinus a hook, from uncus a hook.] Hooked; bent at the tip in the form of a hook; as, an uncinate process.

uncinatum.c: Uncinatum ‖Un`ci*na"tum (?), n. [NL., from L. uncinatus hooked.] (Anat.) The unciform bone.

uncinus.c: Uncinus ‖Un*ci"nus (?), n.; pl. Uncini (#). [L., a hook.] (Zool.) One of the peculiar minute chitinous hooks found in large numbers in the tori of tubicolous annelids belonging to the Uncinata.

uncipher.c: Uncipher Un*ci"pher (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cipher.] To decipher; as, to uncipher a letter. [Obs.] Sir W. Temple.

uncircumcised.c: Uncircumcised Un*cir"cum*cised (?), n. Not circumcised; hence, not of the Israelites. “This uncircumcised Philistine.” 1 Sam. xvii. 26.

uncircumcision.c: Uncircumcision Un*cir`cum*ci"sion (?), n. 1. The absence or want of circumcision.

uncircumstandtial.c: Uncircumstandtial Un*cir`cum*stand"tial (?), a. 1. Not circumstantial; not entering into minute particulars.

uncity.c: Uncity Un*cit"y (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + city.] To deprive of the rank or rights of a city. [Obs.]

uncivil.c: Uncivil Un*civ"il (?), a. 1. Not civilized; savage; barbarous; uncivilized.

uncivilization.c: Uncivilization Un*civ`i*li*za"tion (?), n. The state of being uncivilized; savagery or barbarism. [R.]

uncivilized.c: Uncivilized Un*civ"i*lized (?), a. 1. Not civilized; not reclaimed from savage life; rude; barbarous; savage; as, the uncivilized inhabitants of Central Africa.

uncivilty.c: Uncivilty Un*civ"il*ty, adv. In an uncivil manner.

unclasp.c: Unclasp Un*clasp" (ŭn*klȧsp"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clasp.] To loose the clasp of; to open, as something that is fastened with, or as with, a clasp; as, to unclasp a book; to unclasp the hands; to unclasp one's heart.

uncle.c: Uncle Un"cle (?), n. [OE. uncle, OF. oncle, uncle, F. oncle, fr. L. avunculus a maternal uncle, dim. of avus a grandfather; akin to Lith. avynas uncle, Goth. aw? grandmother, Icel. āi great grandfather.] 1. The brother of one's father or mother; also applied to an aunt's husband; -- the correlative of aunt in sex, and of nephew and niece in relationship.

unclean.c: Unclean Un*clean" (ŭn*klēn"), a. [AS. unclǣne. See Unnot, and Clean.] 1. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy.

uncleansable.c: Uncleansable Un*cleans"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being cleansed or cleaned.

unclench.c: Unclench Un*clench" (?), v. t. Same as Unclinch.

uncleship.c: Uncleship Un"cle*ship (?), n. The office or position of an uncle. Lamb.

unclew.c: Unclew Un*clew" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clew.] To unwind, unfold, or untie; hence, to undo; to ruin. Shak.

unclinch.c: Unclinch Un*clinch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clinch.] To cause to be no longer clinched; to open; as, to unclinch the fist. [Written also unclench.]

uncling.c: Uncling Un*cling" (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + cling.] To cease from clinging or adhering. [Obs.] Milton.

uncloak.c: Uncloak Un*cloak" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cloak.] To remove a cloak or cover from; to deprive of a cloak or cover; to unmask; to reveal.
Uncloak Un*cloak", v. i. To remove, or take off, one's cloak.

unclog.c: Unclog Un*clog", v. t. [1st pref. un- + clog.] To disencumber of a clog, or of difficulties and obstructions; to free from encumbrances; to set at liberty. Shak.

uncloister.c: Uncloister Un*clois"ter (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cloister.] To release from a cloister, or from confinement or seclusion; to set free; to liberate.

unclose.c: Unclose Un*close" (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + close.] 1. To open; to separate the parts of; as, to unclose a letter; to unclose one's eyes.

unclosed.c: Unclosed Un*closed" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + closed.] 1. Not separated by inclosures; open. Clarendon.

unclothe.c: Unclothe Un*clothe" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clothe.] To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked. I. Watts.

unclothed.c: Unclothed Un*clothed" (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unclothe.] Divested or stripped of clothing. Byron.

uncloud.c: Uncloud Un*cloud" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cloud.] To free from clouds; to unvail; to clear from obscurity, gloom, sorrow, or the like. Beau. & Fl.

unclue.c: Unclue Un*clue" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clue.] To unwind; to untangle.

unclutch.c: Unclutch Un*clutch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + clutch.] 1. To open, as something closely shut. “Unclutch his griping hand.” Dr. H. More.

unco.c: Unco Un"co (?), a. [Scot. The same word as E. uncouth.] Unknown; strange, or foreign; unusual, or surprising; distant in manner; reserved. [Scot.]
Unco Un"co, adv. In a high degree; to a great extent; greatly; very. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Unco Un"co, n. A strange thing or person. [Scot.]

uncoach.c: Uncoach Un*coach" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + coach.] To detach or loose from a coach. [Obs.] Chapman.

uncock.c: Uncock Un*cock" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cock.] 1. To let down the cock of, as a firearm.

uncoffle.c: Uncoffle Un*cof"fle (?; 115), v. t. [1st pref. un- + coffle.] To release from a coffle.

uncoif.c: Uncoif Un*coif" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + coif.] To deprive of the coif or cap. Young.

uncoil.c: Uncoil Un*coil" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + coil.] To unwind or open, as a coil of rope. Derham.

uncoined.c: Uncoined Un*coined" (?), a. 1. Not coined, or minted; as, uncoined silver. Locke.

uncolt.c: Uncolt Un*colt" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + colt.] To unhorse. [Obs. & R.] Shak.

uncombine.c: Uncombine Un`com*bine" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + combine.] To separate, as substances in combination; to release from combination or union. [R.] Daniel.

uncomeatable.c: Uncomeatable Un`come*at"a*ble (?), a. Not to be come at, or reached; inaccessible. [Colloq.] Addison.

uncomely.c: Uncomely Un*come"ly (?), a. Not comely. -- adv. In an uncomely manner. 1 Cor. vii. 36.

uncomfortable.c: Uncomfortable Un*com"fort*a*ble (?), a. 1. Feeling discomfort; uneasy; as, to be uncomfortable on account of one's position.

uncommon.c: Uncommon Un*com"mon (?), a. Not common; unusual; infrequent; rare; hence, remarkable; strange; as, an uncommon season; an uncommon degree of cold or heat; uncommon courage.

uncomprehend.c: Uncomprehend Un*com`pre*hend (?), v. t. [1st un- + comprehend.] To fail to comprehend. [R.] Daniel.

uncompromising.c: Uncompromising Un*com"pro*mi`sing (?), a. Not admitting of compromise; making no truce or concessions; obstinate; unyielding; inflexible. -- Un*com"pro*mi`sing*ly, adv.

unconceivable.c: Unconceivable Un`con*ceiv"a*ble (?), a. Inconceivable. [Obs.] Locke. -- Un`con*ceiv"a*ble*ness, n. [Obs.] -- Un`con*ceiv"a*bly, adv. [Obs.]

unconcern.c: Unconcern Un`con*cern" (?), n. Want of concern; absence of anxiety; freedom from solicitude; indifference.

unconcerned.c: Unconcerned Un`con*cerned" (?), a. Not concerned; not anxious or solicitous; easy in mind; carelessly secure; indifferent; as, to be unconcerned at what has happened; to be unconcerned about the future. -- Un`con*cern"ed*ly (#), adv. -- Un`con*cern"ed*ness, n.

unconcerning.c: Unconcerning Un`con*cern"ing, a. Not interesting or affecting; insignificant; not belonging to one. [Obs.] Addison.

unconcernment.c: Unconcernment Un`con*cern"ment (?), n. The state of being unconcerned, or of having no share or concern; unconcernedness. [Obs.] South.

unconcluding.c: Unconcluding Unconcludent { Un`con*clud"ent (?), Un`con*clud"ing (?), } a. Inconclusive. [Obs.] Locke.

unconditional.c: Unconditional Un`con*di"tion*al (?), a. Not conditional, limited, or conditioned; made without condition; absolute; unreserved; as, an unconditional surrender.

unconditioned.c: Unconditioned Un`con*di"tioned (?), a. 1. Not conditioned or subject to conditions; unconditional.

unconfidence.c: Unconfidence Un*con"fi*dence (?), n. Absence of confidence; uncertainty; doubt.

unconformability.c: Unconformability Un`con*form`a*bil"i*ty, n. 1. The quality or state of being unconformable; unconformableness.

unconformable.c: Unconformable Un`con*form"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not conformable; not agreeable; not conforming.

unconformity.c: Unconformity Un`con*form"i*ty, n. 1. Want of conformity; incongruity; inconsistency. South.

unconfound.c: Unconfound Un`con*found" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + confound.] To free from a state of confusion, or of being confounded. Milton.

unconfounded.c: Unconfounded Un`con*found"ed (?), a. [Pref. un- not + confounded.] Not confounded. Bp. Warburton.

uncongeal.c: Uncongeal Un`con*geal" (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + congeal.] To thaw; to become liquid again. Tennyson.

unconning.c: Unconning Un*con"ning (?), a. Not knowing; ignorant. [Obs.] Chaucer. -- n. Ignorance. [Obs.]

unconquerable.c: Unconquerable Un*con"quer*a*ble (?), a. Not conquerable; indomitable. -- Un*con"quer*a*bly, adv.

unconscionable.c: Unconscionable Un*con"scion*a*ble (ŭn*kŏn"shŭn*ȧ*b'l), a. 1. Not conscionable; exceeding the limits of any reasonable claim or expectation; not conforming to reason; unreasonable; inordinate; extravagant; as, an unconscionable person or demand; unconscionable size.

unconscious.c: unconscious un*con"scious (ŭn*kŏn"shŭs), a. 1. Not conscious; having no consciousness or power of mental perception; without cerebral appreciation; hence, not knowing or regarding; ignorant; as, an unconscious man. Cowper.

unconsecrate.c: Unconsecrate Un*con"se*crate (ŭn*kŏn"se*krāt), v. t. [1st pref. un- + consecrate.] To render not sacred; to deprive of sanctity; to desecrate. [Obs.] South.

unconsiderate.c: Unconsiderate Un`con*sid"er*ate (?), a. Inconsiderate; heedless; careless. [Obs.] Daniel. -- Un`con*sid"er*ate*ness, n. [Obs.] Hales.

unconsidered.c: Unconsidered Un`con*sid"ered (?), a. Not considered or attended to; not regarded; inconsiderable; trifling.

unconsonant.c: Unconsonant Un*con"so*nant (?), a. Incongruous; inconsistent. “A thing unconsonant.” Hooker.

unconstancy.c: Unconstancy Un*con"stan*cy (?), n. Inconstancy. [Obs.] “The unconstancy of the foundation.” Fuller.

unconstant.c: Unconstant Un*con"stant (?), a. Not constant; inconstant; fickle; changeable. [Obs.] Shak. -- Un*con"stant*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Un*con"stant*ness, n. [Obs.]

unconstitutional.c: Unconstitutional Un*con`sti*tu"tion*al (?), a. Not constitutional; not according to, or consistent with, the terms of a constitution of government; contrary to the constitution; as, an unconstitutional law, or act of an officer. Burke. -- Un*con`sti*tu"tion*al"i*ty (#), n. -- Un*con`sti*tu"tion*al-ly (#), adv.

unconstraint.c: Unconstraint Un`con*straint" (?), n. Freedom from constraint; ease. Felton.

unconsummate.c: Unconsummate Un`con*sum"mate (?), a. Not consummated; not accomplished. [Obs.] Dryden.

uncontinent.c: Uncontinent Un*con"ti*nent (?), a. Not continent; incontinent. Wyclif (2 Tim. iii. 3).

uncontrollable.c: Uncontrollable Un`con*trol"la*ble (?), a. 1. Incapable of being controlled; ungovernable; irresistible; as, an uncontrollable temper; uncontrollable events.

uncontroversory.c: Uncontroversory Un*con`tro*ver"so*ry (?), a. Not involving controversy. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

unconvenient.c: Unconvenient Un`con*ven"ient (?), a. Inconvenient. Bale. -- Un`con*ven"ient*ly, adv. Udall.

unconversion.c: Unconversion Un`con*ver"sion (?), n. The state of being unconverted; impenitence. [R.]

unconverted.c: Unconverted Un`con*vert"ed (?), a. 1. Not converted or exchanged.

uncord.c: Uncord Un*cord" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cord.] To release from cords; to loosen the cord or cords of; to unfasten or unbind; as, to uncord a package.

uncork.c: Uncork Un*cork" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cork.] To draw the cork from; as, to uncork a bottle.

uncorrigible.c: Uncorrigible Un*cor"ri*gi*ble (?), a. Incorrigible; not capable of correction. [Obs.]

uncorruptible.c: Uncorruptible Un`cor*rupt"i*ble (?), a. Incorruptible. “The glory of the uncorruptible God.” Rom. i. 23.

uncouple.c: Uncouple Un*cou"ple (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + couple.] To loose, as dogs, from their couples; also, to set loose; to disconnect; to disjoin; as, to uncouple railroad cars.
Uncouple Un*cou"ple, v. i. To roam at liberty. [Obs.] Chaucer.

uncourtliness.c: Uncourtliness Un*court"li*ness (?), n. Absence of courtliness; rudeness; rusticity. Addison.

uncous.c: Uncous Un"cous (?), a. [L. uncus hooked, as n., a hook.] Hooklike; hooked. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

uncouth.c: Uncouth Un*couth" (ŭn*kōoth"), a. [OE. uncouth, AS. uncūð unknown, strange: un- (see Un- not) + cūð known, p. p. of cunnan to know. See Can to be able, and cf. Unco, Unked.] 1. Unknown. [Obs.] “This uncouth errand.” Milton.

uncovenable.c: Uncovenable Un*cov"e*na*ble (?), a. Not covenable; inconvenient. [Obs.] Wyclif (1 Tim. iv. 7).

uncovenanted.c: Uncovenanted Un*cov"e*nant*ed (?), a. 1. Not covenanted; not granted or entered into under a covenant, agreement, or contract. Bp. Horsley.

uncover.c: Uncover Un*cov"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Uncovered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Uncovering.] [1st pref. un- + cover.] 1. To take the cover from; to divest of covering; as, to uncover a box, bed, house, or the like; to uncover one's body.
Uncover Un*cov"er (?), v. i. 1. To take off the hat or cap; to bare the head in token of respect.

uncowl.c: Uncowl Un*cowl" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + cowl.] To divest or deprive of a cowl. Pope.

uncreate.c: Uncreate Un`cre*ate" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + create.] To deprive of existence; to annihilate.
Uncreate Un`cre*ate" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + create, a.] Uncreated; self-existent. Book of Common Prayer.

uncreated.c: Uncreated Un`cre*at"ed, a. [In sense 1, properly p. p. of uncreate; in senses 2 and 3, pref. un- not + created.] 1. Deprived of existence; annihilated. Beau. & Fl.

uncreatedness.c: Uncreatedness Un`cre*at"ed*ness, n. The quality or state of being uncreated.

uncredit.c: Uncredit Un*cred"it (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + credit.] To cause to be disbelieved; to discredit. [Obs.] Fuller.

uncrown.c: Uncrown Un*crown" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + crown.] To deprive of a crown; to take the crown from; hence, to discrown; to dethrone.

uncrudded.c: Uncrudded Un*crud"ded (?), a. [See Un- not, and Curd.] Not cruddled, or curdled. [Obs.]

unction.c: Unction Unc"tion (?), n. [OE. unccioun, uncioun, OF. oncion, onction, F. onction, fr. L. unctio, fr. ungere, unctum, to anoint. See Unguent.] 1. The act of anointing, smearing, or rubbing with an unguent, oil, or ointment, especially for medical purposes, or as a symbol of consecration; as, mercurial unction.

unctuosity.c: Unctuosity Unc`tu*os"i*ty (?; 135), n. [Cf. F. onctuosité.] Quality or state of being unctuous. Sir T. Browne.

unctuous.c: Unctuous Unc"tu*ous (?; 135), a. [F. onctueux, LL. unctuosus, fr. L. unctus anointment, fr. ungere, unctum, to anoint. See Unguent.] 1. Of the nature or quality of an unguent or ointment; fatty; oily; greasy. “The unctuous cheese.” Longfellow.

unculpable.c: Unculpable Un*cul"pa*ble (?), a. Inculpable; not blameworthy. [R.] Hooker.

uncult.c: Uncult Un*cult" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + L. cultus, p. p. of colere to cultivate. Cf. Incult.] Not cultivated; rude; illiterate. [Obs.]

unculture.c: Unculture Un*cul"ture (?; 135), n. Want of culture. “Idleness, ill husbandry... unculture.” Bp. Hall.

uncurably.c: Uncurably Un*cur"a*bly, adv. In an uncurable manner.

uncurbable.c: Uncurbable Un*curb"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being curbed. Shak.

uncurl.c: Uncurl Un*curl" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + curl.] To loose from curls, or ringlets; to straighten out, as anything curled or curly.
Uncurl Un*curl", v. i. To become uncurled, or straight.

uncurrent.c: Uncurrent Un*cur"rent (?), a. Not current. Specifically: Not passing in common payment; not receivable at par or full value; as, uncurrent notes. Shak.

uncurse.c: Uncurse Un*curse" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + curse.] To free from a curse or an execration. Shak.

uncurtain.c: Uncurtain Un*cur"tain (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + curtain.] To remove a curtain from; to reveal. Moore.

uncus.c: Uncus ‖Un"cus (?), n.; pl. Unci (#). [L.] (Zool.) A hook or claw.

uncustomable.c: Uncustomable Un*cus"tom*a*ble (?), a. Not customable, or subject to customs duties.

uncustomed.c: Uncustomed Un*cus"tomed (?), a. Uncustomable; also, not having paid duty or customs. Smollett.

uncut.c: Uncut Un*cut" (?), a. 1. Not cut; not separated or divided by cutting or otherwise; -- said especially of books, periodicals, and the like, when the leaves have not been separated by trimming in binding.
Uncut velvet Un*cut" vel"vet. A fabric woven like velvet, but with the loops of the warp threads uncut.

uncuth.c: Uncuth Un*cuth" (?), a. Unknown; strange. [Obs.] -- n. A stranger. [Obs.]

uncypher.c: Uncypher Un*cy"pher (?), v. t. alternate spelling of Uncipher; same as decipher.

undam.c: Undam Un*dam" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dam.] To free from a dam, mound, or other obstruction. Dryden.

undated.c: Undated Un"da*ted (ŭn"da*tĕd), a. [L. undatus, p. p. of undare to rise in waves, to wave, to undulate, fr. unda a wave. See Undulate.] (Bot.) Rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved.
Undated Un*dat"ed (ŭn*dāt"ĕd), a. [Pref. un- not + dated.] Not dated; having no date; of unknown age; as, an undated letter.

undauntable.c: Undauntable Un*daunt"a*ble (ŭn*dänt"ȧ*b'l), a. Incapable of being daunted; intrepid; fearless; indomitable. Bp. Hall.

undaunted.c: Undaunted Un*daunt"ed (?), a. Not daunted; not subdued or depressed by fear. Shak.

unde.c: Unde Un"dé (?), a. [F. ondé.] (Her.) Waving or wavy; -- applied to ordinaries, or division lines.

undeadly.c: Undeadly Un*dead"ly (?), a. Not subject to death; immortal. [Obs.] -- Un*dead"li*ness, n. [Obs.] Wyclif.

undeaf.c: Undeaf Un*deaf" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + deaf.] To free from deafness; to cause to hear. [Obs.] Shak.

undecagon.c: Undecagon Un*dec"a*gon (?), n. [L. undecim eleven + Gr.? an angle.] (Geom.) A figure having eleven angles and eleven sides.

undecane.c: Undecane Un"de*cane (?), n. [L. undecim eleven.] (Chem.) A liquid hydrocarbon, C11H24, of the methane series, found in petroleum; -- so called from its containing eleven carbon atoms in the molecule.

undeceive.c: Undeceive Un`de*ceive" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + deceive.] To cause to be no longer deceived; to free from deception, fraud, fallacy, or mistake. South.

undecency.c: Undecency Un*de"cen*cy (?), n. Indecency. [Obs.] “Decency and undecency.” Jer. Taylor.

undecennary.c: Undecennary Un`de*cen"na*ry (?), a. [L. undecim eleven (unus one + decem ten) + -ennary as in decennary. Cf. Undecennial.] Occurring once in every period of eleven years; undecennial.

undecennial.c: Undecennial Un`de*cen"ni*al (?), a. [See Undecennary, and cf. Decennial.] Occurring or observed every eleventh year; belonging to, or continuing, a period of eleven years; undecennary; as, an undecennial festival.

undecide.c: Undecide Un`de*cide" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + decide.] To reverse or recant, as a previous decision.

undeck.c: Undeck Un*deck" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + deck.] To divest of ornaments. Shak.

undecolic.c: Undecolic Un`de*col"ic (?), a. [Undecylenic + propiolic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C11H18O2, of the propiolic acid series, obtained indirectly from undecylenic acid as a white crystalline substance.

undecreed.c: Undecreed Un`de*creed" (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + decreed.] Not decreed.

undecyl.c: Undecyl Un"de*cyl (?), n. [Undecane + -yl.] (Chem.) The radical regarded as characteristic of undecylic acid.

undecylenic.c: Undecylenic Un*dec`y*len"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid C11H20O2, homologous with acrylic acid, and obtained as a white crystalline substance by the distillation of castor oil.

undecylic.c: Undecylic Un`de*cyl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Related to, derived from, or containing, the undecyl radical; specifically, designating that member of the fatty acids which corresponds to undecane, and is obtained as a white crystalline substance, C10H21.CO2H.

undeeded.c: Undeeded Un*deed"ed (?), a. 1. Not deeded or transferred by deed; as, undeeded land.

undefine.c: Undefine Un`de*fine" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + define.] To make indefinite; to obliterate or confuse the definition or limitations of.

undeify.c: Undeify Un*de"i*fy (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + deify.] To degrade from the state of deity; to deprive of the character or qualities of a god; to deprive of the reverence due to a god. Addison.

undeniable.c: Undeniable Un`de*ni"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not deniable; incapable of denial; palpably true; indisputable; obvious; as, undeniable evidence.

undeniably.c: Undeniably Un`de*ni"a*bly, adv. In an undeniable manner.

undepartable.c: Undepartable Un`de*part"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being parted; inseparable. [Obs.] Chaucer. Wyclif.

under.c: Under Un"der (ŭn"dẽr), prep. [AS. under, prep. & adv.; akin to OFries. under, OS. undar, D. onder, G. unter, OHG. untar, Icel. undir, Sw. & Dan. under, Goth. undar, L. infra below, inferior lower, Skr. adhas below. √201. Cf. Inferior.] 1. Below or lower, in place or position, with the idea of being covered; lower than; beneath; -- opposed to over; as, he stood under a tree; the carriage is under cover; a cellar extends under the whole house.

Under Un"der (ŭn"dẽr), adv. In a lower, subject, or subordinate condition; in subjection; -- used chiefly in a few idiomatic phrases; as, to bring under, to reduce to subjection; to subdue; to keep under, to keep in subjection; to control; to go under, to be unsuccessful; to fail; to go bankrupt.
