Under Un"der, a. Lower in position, intensity, rank, or degree; subject; subordinate; -- generally in composition with a noun, and written with or without the hyphen; as, an undercurrent; undertone; underdose; under-garment; underofficer; undersheriff.

underact.c: Underact Un`der*act" (?), v. t. To perform inefficiently, as a play; to act feebly.

underaction.c: Underaction Un"der*ac`tion (?), n. Subordinate action; a minor action incidental or subsidiary to the main story; an episode.

underage.c: underage un"der*age` (ŭn"dẽr*ĭj), a. Shortage or deficiency in amount; shortfall. [Obs.]

underaid.c: Underaid Un`der*aid" (?), v. t. To aid clandestinely. [Obs.]

underarm.c: Under-arm Un"der-arm (?), a. (Cricket) 1. Done (as bowling) with the arm not raised above the elbow, that is, not swung far out from the body; underhand. Cf. Over-arm and Round-Arm.

underback.c: Underback Un"der*back` (?), n. (Brewing) A vessel which receives the wort as it flows from the mashing tub.

underbear.c: Underbear Un`der*bear" (?), v. t. [AS. underberan. See Under, and Bear to support.] 1. To support; to endure. [Obs.] Shak.

underbearer.c: Underbearer Un"der*bear`er (?), n. One who supports or sustains; especially, at a funeral, one of those who bear the corpse, as distinguished from a bearer, or pallbearer, who helps to hold up the pall.

underbid.c: Underbid Un`der*bid" (?), v. t. To bid less than, as when a contract or service is offered to the lowest bidder; to offer to contract, sell, or do for a lower price than.

underbind.c: Underbind Un`der*bind" (?), v. t. To bind beneath. Fairfax.

underboard.c: Underboard Un"der*board` (?), adv. Under the board, or table; hence, secretly; unfairly; underhand. See the Note under Aboveboard.

underbrace.c: Underbrace Un`der*brace (?), v. t. To brace, fasten, or bind underneath or below. Cowper.

underbred.c: Underbred Un"der*bred` (?), a. Not thoroughly bred; ill-bred; as, an underbred fellow. Goldsmith.

underbrush.c: Underbrush Un"der*brush` (?), n. Shrubs, small trees, and the like, in a wood or forest, growing beneath large trees; undergrowth.

underbuilder.c: Underbuilder Un"der*build`er (?), n. A subordinate or assistant builder.

underbuy.c: Underbuy Un`der*buy" (?), v. t. To buy at less than the real value or worth; to buy cheaper than. [R.] J. Fletcher.

undercast.c: Undercast Un`der*cast" (?), v. t. To cast under or beneath.

underchamberlain.c: Underchamberlain Un`der*cham"ber*lain (?), n. A deputy chamberlain of the exchequer.

underchaps.c: Underchaps Un"der*chaps` (?), n. pl. The lower chaps or jaw. Paley.

undercharge.c: Undercharge Un`der*charge" (?), v. t. 1. To charge below or under; to charge less than is usual or suitable for; as, to undercharge goods or services.
Undercharge Un"der*charge` (?), n. A charge that is less than is usual or suitable.

underclay.c: Underclay Un"der*clay` (?), n. (Geol.) A stratum of clay lying beneath a coal bed, often containing the roots of coal plants, especially the Stigmaria.

undercliff.c: Undercliff Un"der*cliff` (?), n. A subordinate cliff on a shore, consisting of material that has fallen from the higher cliff above.

underclothes.c: Underclothes Un"der*clothes` (?), n. pl. Clothes worn under others, especially those worn next the skin for warmth; underwear.

undercoat.c: Undercoat Un"der*coat` (?), n. 1. A coat worn under another; a light coat, as distinguished from an overcoat, or a greatcoat.

underconduct.c: Underconduct Un"der*con`duct (?), n. A lower conduit; a subterranean conduit. [Obs.] Sir H. Wotton.

underconsumption.c: Underconsumption Un`der*con*sump"tion (?), n. (Polit. Econ.) Consumption of less than is produced; consumption of less than the usual amount. F. A. Walker.

undercraft.c: Undercraft Un"der*craft` (?), n. A sly trick or device; as, an undercraft of authors. [R.] Sterne.

undercreep.c: Undercreep Un`der*creep" (?), v. i. To creep secretly or privily. [Obs.] Wyclif.

undercrest.c: Undercrest Un`der*crest" (?), v. t. To support as a crest; to bear. [Obs. & R.] Shak.

undercroft.c: Undercroft Un"der*croft (?), n. [Under + Prov. E. croft a vault; cf. OD. krochte crypt, and E. crypt.] (Arch.) A subterranean room of any kind; esp., one under a church (see Crypt), or one used as a chapel or for any sacred purpose.

undercry.c: Undercry Un`der*cry" (?), v. i. To cry aloud. [Obs.] Wyclif.

undercurrent.c: Undercurrent Un"der*cur`rent (?), n. 1. A current below the surface of water, sometimes flowing in a contrary direction to that on the surface. Totten.
Undercurrent Un"der*cur`rent, a. Running beneath the surface; hidden. [R.] “Undercurrent woe.” Tennyson.

undercut.c: Undercut Un"der*cut` (?), n. The lower or under side of a sirloin of beef; the fillet.
Undercut Un`der*cut" (?), v. t. 1. To cut away, as the side of an object, so as to leave an overhanging portion.
Undercut Un"der*cut` (?), p. a. Cut away below.

underdealing.c: Underdealing Un"der*deal`ing (?), n. Crafty, unfair, or underhand dealing; unfair practice; trickery. Milton.

underdelve.c: Underdelve Un`der*delve" (?), v. t. To delve under. [Obs.]

underdig.c: Underdig Un`der*dig" (?), v. t. To dig under or beneath; to undermine. [Obs.] Wyclif.

underditch.c: Underditch Un`der*ditch" (?), v. t. To dig an underground ditch or ditches in, so as to drain the surface; to underdrain; as, to underditch a field or a farm.

underdo.c: Underdo Un`der*do" (?), v. i. To do less than is requisite or proper; -- opposed to overdo. Grew.
Underdo Un`der*do", v. t. To do less thoroughly than is requisite; specifically, to cook insufficiently; as, to underdo the meat; -- opposed to overdo.

underdoer.c: Underdoer Un"der*do`er (?), n. One who underdoes; a shirk.

underdolven.c: Underdolven Un`der*dolv"en (?), obs. p. p. of Underdelve.

underdose.c: Underdose Un"der*dose` (?), n. A dose which is less than required; a small or insufficient dose.
Underdose Un`der*dose" (?), v. t. & i. To give an underdose or underdoses to; to practice giving insufficient doses.

underdrain.c: Underdrain Un"der*drain` (?), n. An underground drain or trench with openings through which the water may percolate from the soil or ground above.
Underdrain Un`der*drain" (?), v. t. To drain by forming an underdrain or underdrains in; as, to underdrain land.

underestimate.c: Underestimate Un`der*es"ti*mate (?), v. t. To set too low a value on; to estimate below the truth.
Underestimate Un`der*es"ti*mate (?), n. The act of underestimating; too low an estimate.

underfaction.c: Underfaction Un"der*fac`tion (?), n. A subordinate party or faction.

underfaculty.c: Underfaculty Un"der*fac`ul*ty (?), n. An inferior or subordinate faculty.

underfeed.c: Underfeed Un`der*feed" (?), v. t. To feed with too little food; to supply with an insufficient quantity of food.

underfellow.c: Underfellow Un"der*fel`low (?), n. An underling; a mean, low fellow. [R.] Sir P. Sidney.

underfilling.c: Underfilling Un"der*fill`ing (?), n. The filling below or beneath; the under part of a building. Sir H. Wotton.

underfollow.c: Underfollow Un`der*fol"low (?), v. t. To follow closely or immediately after. [Obs.] Wyclif.

underfong.c: Underfong Un`der*fong" (?), v. t. [AS. underfongen, p. p. of underfōn to undertake; under under + fōn to take. See Fang to seize.] 1. To undertake; to take in hand; to receive. [Obs.] Piers Plowman. Rom. of R.

underfoot.c: Underfoot Un`der*foot" (?), adv. Under the feet; underneath; below. See Under foot, under Foot, n.
Underfoot Un`der*foot", a. Low; base; abject; trodden down.

underfringe.c: Underfringe Un"der*fringe` (?), n. A lower fringe; a fringe underneath something.

underfurnish.c: Underfurnish Un`der*fur"nish (?), v. t. To supply with less than enough; to furnish insufficiently. Collier.

underfurrow.c: Underfurrow Un`der*fur"row (?), v. t. To cover as under a furrow; to plow in; as, to underfurrow seed or manure.

undergarment.c: Under-garment Un"der-gar`ment (?), n. A garment worn below another.

underget.c: Underget Un`der*get" (?), v. t. To get under or beneath; also, to understand. [Obs.] R. of Gloucester.

undergird.c: Undergird Un`der*gird" (?), v. t. To bind below; to gird round the bottom.

underglaze.c: Underglaze Un"der*glaze` (?), a. Applied under the glaze, that is, before the glaze is put on; fitted to be so applied; -- said of colors in porcelain painting.

undergo.c: Undergo Un`der*go" (?), v. t. [imp. Underwent (?); p. p. Undergone (?; 115); p. pr. & vb. n. Undergoing.] [AS. undergān. See Under, and Go.] 1. To go or move below or under. [Obs.]

undergod.c: Undergod Un"der*god` (?), n. A lower or inferior god; a subordinate deity; a demigod.

undergore.c: Undergore Un`der*gore" (?), v. t. To gore underneath.

undergown.c: Undergown Un"der*gown` (?), n. A gown worn under another, or under some other article of dress.

undergraduate.c: Undergraduate Un`der*grad"u*ate (?), n. A member of a university or a college who has not taken his first degree; a student in any school who has not completed his course. Contrasted with graduate student.
Undergraduate Un`der*grad"u*ate, a. Of or pertaining to an undergraduate, or the body of undergraduates.

undergraduateship.c: Undergraduateship Un`der*grad"u*ate*ship, n. The position or condition of an undergraduate.

undergroan.c: Undergroan Un`der*groan (?), v. t. To groan beneath. [Obs.]

underground.c: Underground Un"der*ground` (?), n. 1. The place or space beneath the surface of the ground; subterranean space.
Underground Un"der*ground`, a. 1. Being below the surface of the ground; as, an underground story or apartment.
Underground Un"der*ground`, adv. Beneath the surface of the earth.

undergrove.c: Undergrove Un"der*grove` (?), n. A grove of shrubs or low trees under taller ones. Wordsworth.

undergrow.c: Undergrow Un`der*grow" (?), v. i. To grow to an inferior, or less than the usual, size or height. Wyclif.

undergrown.c: Undergrown Un`der*grown" (?), a. Of small stature; not grown to a full height or size.

undergrowth.c: Undergrowth Un"der*growth` (?), n. That which grows under trees; specifically, shrubs or small trees growing among large trees. Milton.

undergrub.c: Undergrub Un`der*grub" (?), v. t. To undermine. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

underhand.c: Underhand Un"der*hand` (ŭn"dẽr*hănd`), a. 1. Secret; clandestine; hence, mean; unfair; fraudulent. Addison.
Underhand Un"der*hand` (ŭn"dẽr*hănd`), adv. 1. By secret means; in a clandestine manner; hence, by fraud; unfairly; dishonorably.

underhandedly.c: Underhandedly Un"der*hand`ed*ly (ŭn"dẽr*hănd`ĕd*ly̆), adv. In an underhand manner.

underhang.c: Underhang Un`der*hang" (ŭn`dẽr*hăng"), v. t. & i. To hang under or down; to suspend. Holland.

underhangman.c: Underhangman Un"der*hang`man (?), n. An assistant or deputy hangman. Shak.

underhead.c: Underhead Un"der*head` (?), n. A blockhead, or stupid person; a dunderhead. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

underheave.c: Underheave Un`der*heave" (?), v. i. To heave or lift from below. [Obs.] Wyclif.

underhew.c: Underhew Un`der*hew" (?), v. t. To hew less than is usual or proper; specifically, to hew, as a piece of timber which should be square, in such a manner that it appears to contain a greater number of cubic feet than it really does contain. Haldeman.

underhonest.c: Underhonest Un`der*hon"est (?), a. Not entirely honest. [R.] “We think him overproud and underhonest.” Shak.

underhung.c: Underhung Un`der*hung" (?), a. 1. (Carp.) Resting on a track at the bottom, instead of being suspended; -- said of a sliding door. Forney.

Underhung Underslung { Un"der*slung` (?), Un"der*hung" (?) }, a. Of an automobile body, suspended from the springs in such a manner that the frame of the chassis is below the axles, the object being to lower the center of gravity of the car.

underjaw.c: Underjaw Un"der*jaw` (?), n. The lower jaw. Paley.

underjoin.c: Underjoin Un`der*join" (?), v. t. To join below or beneath; to subjoin. Wyclif.

underkeep.c: Underkeep Un`der*keep" (?), v. t. To keep under, or in subjection; to suppress. [Obs.] Spenser.

underkeeper.c: Underkeeper Un"der*keep`er (?), n. A subordinate keeper or guardian. Gray.

underkind.c: Underkind Un"der*kind` (?), n. An inferior kind. Dryden.

underkingdom.c: Underkingdom Un"der*king`dom (?), n. A subordinate or dependent kingdom. Tennyson.

underlaborer.c: Underlaborer Un"der*la`bor*er (?), n. An assistant or subordinate laborer. Locke.

underlaid.c: Underlaid Un`der*laid" (?), a. Laid or placed underneath; also, having something laid or lying underneath.

underlay.c: Underlay Un`der*lay" (?), v. t. [AS. underlecgan. See Under, and Lay, v. t.] 1. To lay beneath; to put under.
Underlay Un`der*lay", v. i. (Mining) To incline from the vertical; to hade; -- said of a vein, fault, or lode.
Underlay Un"der*lay` (?), n. 1. (Mining) The inclination of a vein, fault, or lode from the vertical; a hade; -- called also underlie.

underlayer.c: Underlayer Un"der*lay`er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, underlays or is underlaid; a lower layer.

underleaf.c: Underleaf Un"der*leaf` (?), n. A prolific sort of apple, good for cider. [Obs.] Mortimer.

underlease.c: Underlease Un"der*lease (?), n. (Law) A lease granted by a tenant or lessee; especially, a lease granted by one who is himself a lessee for years, for any fewer or less number of years than he himself holds; a sublease. Burrill.

underlet.c: Underlet Un`der*let" (?), v. t. 1. To let below the value.

underletter.c: Underletter Un"der*let`ter (?), n. A tenant or lessee who grants a lease to another.

underlie.c: Underlie Un`der*lie" (?), v. t. [AS. underlicgan. See Under, and Lie to be prostrate.] 1. To lie under; to rest beneath; to be situated under; as, a stratum of clay underlies the surface gravel.
Underlie Un`der*lie", v. i. To lie below or under.

underline.c: Underline Un`der*line" (?), v. t. 1. To mark a line below, as words; to underscore.

underling.c: Underling Un"der*ling (?), n. [Under + -ling.] 1. An inferior person or agent; a subordinate; a low-ranking employee. Milton.

underload.c: Underload starter Un"der*load start`er. (Elec.) A motor starter provided with an underload switch.

Underload switch Underload switch. (Elec.) A switch which opens a circuit when the current falls below a certain predetermined value, used to protect certain types of motors from running at excessive speed upon decrease of load.

underlock.c: underlock un"der*lock` (?), n. A lock of wool hanging under the belly of a sheep.

underlooker.c: underlooker un"der*look`er (?), n. (Mining) A person who inspects a mine daily; -- called also underviewer.

underlying.c: underlying un`der*ly"ing (?), a. 1. Lying under or beneath; as, the underlying strata of a locality.

undermanned.c: Undermanned Un`der*manned" (?), a. (Naut.) Insufficiently furnished with men; short-handed.

undermasted.c: Undermasted Un"der*mast`ed (?), a. (Naut.) Having masts smaller than the usual dimension; -- said of vessels. Totten.

undermaster.c: Undermaster Un"der*mas`ter (?), n. A master subordinate to the principal master; an assistant master.

undermatch.c: Undermatch Un"der*match` (?), n. One who is not a match for another. Fuller.

undermeal.c: Undermeal Un"der*meal` (?), n. [AS. under under + m?l part or portion; cf. AS. underm?l midday. See Under, Meal a part, and cf. Undern.] 1. The inferior, or after, part of the day; the afternoon. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

undermine.c: Undermine Un`der*mine" (?), v. t. 1. To excavate the earth beneath, or the part of, especially for the purpose of causing to fall or be overthrown; to form a mine under; to sap; as, to undermine a wall.

underminister.c: Underminister Un`der*min"is*ter (?), v. t. To serve, or minister to, in a subordinate relation. [Obs.] Wyclif.

underministry.c: Underministry Un`der*min"is*try (?), n. A subordinate or inferior ministry. Jer. Taylor.

undermirth.c: Undermirth Un"der*mirth` (?), n. Suppressed or concealed mirth. [Obs.] The Coronation.

undermost.c: Undermost Un"der*most (?), a. [From Under; cf. Aftermost.] Lowest, as in place, rank, or condition. Addison.

undern.c: Undern Un"dern (?), n. [AS. undern; akin to OS. undorn, OHG. untarn, untorn, Icel. undorn mid afternoon, mid forenoon, Goth. undaúrnimats the midday meal. Cf. Undermeal, Undertime.] The time between; the time between sunrise and noon; specifically, the third hour of the day, or nine o'clock in the morning, according to ancient reckoning; hence, mealtime, because formerly the principal meal was eaten at that hour; also, later, the afternoon; the time between dinner and supper. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

underneath.c: Underneath Un`der*neath" (?), adv. [OE. undirnepe. See Under, and Beneath.] Beneath; below; in a lower place; under; as, a channel underneath the soil.

underniceness.c: Underniceness Un`der*nice"ness (?), n. A want of niceness; indelicacy; impropriety.

undernime.c: Undernime Un`der*nime" (?), v. t. [imp. Undernom (?).] [OE. undernimen. See Under, and Nim.] 1. To receive; to perceive. [Obs.]

underpay.c: Underpay Un`der*pay" (?), v. t. To pay inadequately.

underpeep.c: Underpeep Un`der*peep" (?), v. t. To peep under. “The flame... would underpeep her lids.” [R.] Shak.

underpeer.c: Underpeer Un`der*peer" (?), v. t. To peer under. [R.]

underpin.c: Underpin Un`der*pin" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Underpinned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Underpinning.] 1. To lay stones, masonry, etc., under, as the sills of a building, on which it is to rest.

underpinning.c: Underpinning Un"der*pin`ning (?), n. 1. The act of one who underpins; the act of supporting by stones, masonry, or the like.

underpitch.c: Underpitch Un`der*pitch" (?), v. t. [imp. Underpight.] [OE. underpicchen. See Under, and Pitch to throw, fix.] To fill underneath; to stuff. [Obs.]

underplant.c: Underplant Un`der*plant" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Underplanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Underplanting.] To plant under; specif. (Forestry), to plant (young trees) under an existing stand.

underplay.c: Underplay Un`der*play" (?), v. i. 1. To play in a subordinate, or in an inferior manner; to underact a part.
Underplay Un"der*play` (?), n. (Card Playing) The act of underplaying.

underplot.c: Underplot Un"der*plot` (?), n. 1. A series of events in a play, proceeding collaterally with the main story, and subservient to it. Dryden.

underpoise.c: Underpoise Un`der*poise" (?), v. t. To weigh, estimate, or rate below desert; to undervalue. [R.] Marston.

underpossessor.c: Underpossessor Un"der*pos*sess`or (?), n. One who possesses or holds anything subject to the superior of another. Jer. Taylor.

underpraise.c: Underpraise Un`der*praise" (?), v. t. To praise below desert.

underprize.c: Underprize Un`der*prize" (?), v. t. To undervalue; to underestimate. Shak.

underproduction.c: Underproduction Un`der*pro*duc"tion (?), n. (Polit. Econ.) The production of less than is demanded or of less than the usual supply. F. A. Walker.

underproof.c: Underproof Un"der*proof` (?), a. Containing less alcohol than proof spirit. See Proof spirit, under Spirit.

underprop.c: Underprop Un`der*prop" (?), v. t. To prop from beneath; to put a prop under; to support; to uphold.

underproportioned.c: Underproportioned Un`der*pro*por"tioned (?), a. Of inadequate or inferior proportions; small; poor.

underpropper.c: Underpropper Un"der*prop`per (?), n. One who, or that which, underprops or supports.

underpull.c: Underpull Un`der*pull" (?), v. i. To exert one's influence secretly. [Obs.] Ld. North.

underput.c: Underput Un`der*put" (?), v. t. To put or send under. [Obs.]

underrate.c: Underrate Un`der*rate" (?), v. t. To rate too low; to rate below the value; to undervalue. Burke.
Underrate Un"der*rate` (?), n. A price less than the value; as, to sell a thing at an underrate. Cowley.

underreckon.c: Underreckon Un`der*reck"on (?), v. t. To reckon below what is right or proper; to underrate. Bp. Hall.

underrun.c: Underrun Un`der*run" (?), v. t. To run or pass under; especially (Naut.), to pass along and under, as a cable, for the purpose of taking it in, or of examining it.

undersail.c: Undersail Un`der*sail" (?), v. i. To sail alongshore. [Obs.]

undersailed.c: Undersailed Un"der*sailed` (?), a. Inadequately equipped with sails. [Obs.]

undersaturated.c: Undersaturated Un`der*sat"u*ra`ted (?), a. Not fully saturated; imperfectly saturated.

undersay.c: Undersay Un`der*say" (?), v. t. To say by way of derogation or contradiction. [Obs.] Spenser.

underscore.c: Underscore Un`der*score" (?), v. t. To draw a mark or line under; to underline. J. Tucker.

undersecretary.c: Undersecretary Un`der*sec"re*ta*ry (?), n. A secretary who is subordinate to the chief secretary; an assistant secretary; as, an undersecretary of the Treasury.

undersell.c: Undersell Un`der*sell" (?), v. t. To sell the same articles at a lower price than; to sell cheaper than.

underset.c: Underset Un`der*set" (?), v. t. To prop or support. Bacon.

undersetter.c: Undersetter Un"der*set`ter (?), n. One who, or that which, undersets or supports; a prop; a support; a pedestal.

undersetting.c: Undersetting Un"der*set`ting (?), n. Something set or built under as a support; a pedestal. Sir H. Wotton.

undershapen.c: Undershapen Un"der*shap`en (?), a. Under the usual shape or size; small; dwarfish. [Poetic]

undershirt.c: Undershirt Un"der*shirt` (?), n. A shirt worn next the skin, under another shirt; -- called also undervest.

undershoot.c: Undershoot Un`der*shoot" (?), v. t. To shoot short of (a mark).

undershot.c: Undershot Un"der*shot` (?), a. 1. (Zool.) Having the lower incisor teeth projecting beyond the upper ones, as in the bulldog.

undershrievalty.c: Undershrievalty Un"der*shriev"al*ty (?), n. The office or position of an undersheriff.

undershrieve.c: Undershrieve Un"der*shrieve` (?), n. (Bot.) A low shrub; a woody plant of low stature.

underside.c: Underside Un"der*side` (?), n. The lower or lowest side of anything. Paley.

undersign.c: Undersign Un`der*sign" (?), v. t. To write one's name at the foot or end of, as a letter or any legal instrument.

undersized.c: Undersized Un"der*sized` (?), a. Of a size less than is common.

underskirt.c: Underskirt Un"der*skirt` (?), n. A petticoat; the foundation skirt of a draped dress.

undersky.c: Undersky Un"der*sky` (?), n. The lower region of the sky.

undersleeve.c: Undersleeve Un"der*sleeve` (?), n. A sleeve of an under-garment; a sleeve worn under another,

undersoil.c: Undersoil Un"der*soil` (?), n. The soil beneath the surface; understratum; subsoil.

undersong.c: Undersong Un"der*song` (?), n. 1. The burden of a song; the chorus; the refrain. Dryden.

undersparred.c: Undersparred Un"der*sparred` (?), a. (Naut.) Having spars smaller than the usual dimension; -- said of vessels.

underspend.c: Underspend Un`der*spend" (?), v. t. To spend less than.

undersphere.c: Undersphere Un"der*sphere` (?), n. 1. A sphere which is smaller than, and in its movements subject to, another; a satellite.

underspore.c: Underspore Un`der*spore" (?), v. t. To raise with a spar, or piece of wood, used as a lever. [Obs.]

understair.c: Understair Un"der*stair` (?), a. Of or pertaining to the kitchen, or the servants' quarters; hence, subordinate; menial. [Obs.]

understairs.c: Understairs Un"der*stairs` (?), n. The basement or cellar.

understand.c: Understand Un`der*stand" (ŭn`dẽr*stănd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Understood (ŭn`dẽr*stŏod"), and Archaic Understanded; p. pr. & vb. n. Understanding.] [OE. understanden, AS. understandan, literally, to stand under; cf. AS. forstandan to understand, G. verstehen. The development of sense is not clear. See Under, and Stand.] 1. To have just and adequate ideas of; to apprehended the meaning or intention of; to have knowledge of; to comprehend; to know; as, to understand a problem in Euclid; to understand a proposition or a declaration; the court understands the advocate or his argument; to understand the sacred oracles; to understand a nod or a wink.
Understand Un`der*stand", v. i. 1. To have the use of the intellectual faculties; to be an intelligent being.

understandable.c: Understandable Un`der*stand"a*ble (ŭn`dẽr*stănd"ȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being understood; intelligible. Chillingworth.

understander.c: Understander Un`der*stand"er (ŭn`dẽr*stănd"ẽr), n. One who understands, or knows by experience. [R.] Dryden.

understanding.c: Understanding Un`der*stand"ing (ŭn`dẽr*stănd"ĭng), a. Knowing; intelligent; skillful; as, he is an understanding man.
Understanding Un`der*stand"ing, n. 1. The act of one who understands a thing, in any sense of the verb; knowledge; discernment; comprehension; interpretation; explanation.

understandingly.c: Understandingly Un`der*stand"ing*ly, adv. In an understanding manner; intelligibly; with full knowledge or comprehension; intelligently; as, to vote upon a question understandingly; to act or judge understandingly.

understate.c: Understate Un`der*state" (?), v. t. To state or represent less strongly than may be done truthfully.

understatement.c: Understatement Un"der*state`ment (?), n. The act of understating, or the condition of being understated; that which is understated; a statement below the truth.

understock.c: Understock Un`der*stock" (?), v. t. To supply insufficiently with stock. A. Smith.

understood.c: Understood Un`der*stood" (?), imp. & p. p. of Understand.

understrapper.c: Understrapper Un"der*strap`per (?), n. A petty fellow; an inferior agent; an underling.

understrapping.c: Understrapping Un"der*strap`ping, a. Becoming an understrapper; subservient. [R.] Sterne.

understratum.c: Understratum Un"der*stra`tum (?), n.; pl. L. Understrata (?), E. Understratums (?). The layer, or stratum, of earth on which the mold, or soil, rests; subsoil.

understroke.c: Understroke Un`der*stroke" (?), v. t. To underline or underscore. Swift.

understudy.c: Understudy Un"der*stud`y (?), v. t. & i. (Theater) To study, as another actor's part, in order to be his substitute in an emergency; to study another actor's part.
Understudy Un"der*stud`y, n. One who studies another's part with a view to assuming it in an emergency.

undersuit.c: Undersuit Un"der*suit` (?), n. A suit worn under another suit; a suit of underclothes.

undertakable.c: Undertakable Un`der*tak"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being undertaken; practicable.

undertake.c: Undertake Un`der*take" (?), v. t. [imp. Undertook (?); p. p. Undertaken (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Undertaking.] [Under + take.] 1. To take upon one's self; to engage in; to enter upon; to take in hand; to begin to perform; to set about; to attempt.
Undertake Un`der*take", v. i. 1. To take upon one's self, or assume, any business, duty, or province.

undertaker.c: Undertaker Un`der*tak"er (?), n. 1. One who undertakes; one who engages in any project or business. Beau. & Fl.

undertaking.c: Undertaking Un`der*tak"ing, n. 1. The act of one who undertakes, or engages in, any project or business. Hakluyt.

undertapster.c: Undertapster Un`der*tap"ster (?), n. Assistant to a tapster.

undertaxed.c: Undertaxed Un"der*taxed` (?), a. Taxed too little, or at a lower rate than others.

undertenancy.c: Undertenancy Un"der*ten`an*cy (?), n. Tenancy or tenure under a tenant or lessee; the tenure of an undertenant.

undertenant.c: Undertenant Un"der*ten`ant (?), n. The tenant of a tenant; one who holds lands or tenements of a tenant or lessee.

underthing.c: Underthing Un"der**thing` (?), n. Something that is inferior and of little worth. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

undertime.c: Undertime Undertide { Un"der*tide` (?), Un"der*time` (?), } n. [Under + tide, time. Cf. Undern.] The under or after part of the day; undermeal; evening. [Obs.]

undertone.c: Undertone Un"der*tone` (?), n. A low or subdued tone or utterance; a tone less loud than usual.

undertow.c: Undertow Un"der*tow` (?), n. (Naut.) The current that sets seaward near the bottom when waves are breaking upon the shore.

underturn.c: Underturn Un`der*turn (?), v. t. To turn upside down; to subvert; to upset. [Obs.] Wyclif.

undervaluation.c: Undervaluation Un`der*val`u*a"tion (?), n. The act of undervaluing; a rate or value not equal to the real worth.

undervalue.c: Undervalue Un`der*val"ue (?), v. t. 1. To value, rate, or estimate below the real worth; to depreciate.
Undervalue Un`der*val"ue, n. A low rate or price; a price less than the real worth; undervaluation. Milton.

underverse.c: Underverse Un"der*verse` (?), n. The lower or second verse. [Obs.]

underwear.c: Underwear Un"der*wear` (?), n. That which is worn under the outside clothing; underclothes.

underwing.c: Underwing Un"der*wing` (?), n. 1. (Zool.) One of the posterior wings of an insect.

underwitted.c: Underwitted Un"der*wit`ted (?), a. Weak in intellect; half-witted; silly. [R.] Bp. Kennet.

underwood.c: Underwood Un"der*wood` (?), n. Small trees and bushes that grow among large trees; coppice; underbrush; -- formerly used in the plural.

underwork.c: Underwork Un`der*work" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Underworked (?) or Underwrought (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Underworking.] 1. To injure by working secretly; to destroy or overthrow by clandestine measure; to undermine.
Underwork Un`der*work", v. i. 1. To work or operate in secret or clandestinely. B. Jonson.
Underwork Un"der*work` (?), n. Inferior or subordinate work; petty business. Addison.

underworld.c: Underworld Un"der*world` (?), n. 1. The lower of inferior world; the world which is under the heavens; the earth.

underwrite.c: Underwrite Un`der*write" (?), v. t. [imp. Underwrote (?), Obs. Underwrit (?); p. p. Underwritten (?), Obs. Underwrit; p. pr. & vb. n. Underwriting.] 1. To write under something else; to subscribe.
Underwrite Un`der*write", v. i. To practice the business of insuring; to take a risk of insurance on a vessel or the like.

underwriter.c: Underwriter Un"der*writ`er (?), n. One who underwrites his name to the conditions of an insurance policy, especially of a marine policy; an insurer.

underwriting.c: Underwriting Un"der*writ`ing, n. The business of an underwriter,

underyoke.c: Underyoke Un`der*yoke" (?), v. t. To subject to the yoke; to make subject. Wyclif.

undeserve.c: Undeserve Un`de*serve" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + deserve.] To fail to deserve. [Obs.] Milton.

undeserver.c: Undeserver Un`de*serv"er (?), n. One of no merit; one who is nor deserving or worthy. [Obs.] Shak.

undesigning.c: Undesigning Un`de*sign"ing (?), a. Having no artful, ulterior, or fraudulent purpose; sincere; artless; simple.

undeterminable.c: Undeterminable Un`de*ter"mi*na*ble (?), a. Not determinable; indeterminable. Locke.

undeterminate.c: Undeterminate Un`de*ter"mi*nate (?), a. Nor determinate; not settled or certain; indeterminate. South. -- Un`de*ter"mi*nate*ness, n. Dr. H. More.

undetermination.c: Undetermination Un`de*ter`mi*na"tion (?), n. Indetermination. Sir M. Hale.

undevil.c: Undevil Un*dev"il (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + devil.] To free from possession by a devil or evil spirit; to exorcise. [Obs.]

undevotion.c: Undevotion Un`de*vo"tion (?), n. Absence or want of devotion.

undifferentiated.c: Undifferentiated Un*dif`fer*en"ti*a`ted (?), a. Not differentiated; specifically (Biol.), homogenous, or nearly so; -- said especially of young or embryonic tissues which have not yet undergone differentiation (see Differentiation, 3), that is, which show no visible separation into their different structural parts.

undigenous.c: Undigenous Un*dig"e*nous (?), a. [L. unda a wave + -genous.] Generated by water. [R.] Kirwan.

undight.c: Undight Un*dight" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dight.] To put off; to lay aside, as a garment. [Obs.] Spenser.

undine.c: Undine Un*dine" (?), n. [G. undine, or F. ondin, ondine, from L. unda a wave, water.] One of a class of fabled female water spirits who might receive a human soul by intermarrying with a mortal.

undiocesed.c: Undiocesed Un*di"o*cesed (?), a. Unprovided with a diocese; having no diocese. Milton.

undirect.c: Undirect Un`di*rect" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + direct, v. t.] To misdirect; to mislead. [Obs.]
Undirect Un`di*rect", a. [Pref. un- not + direct.] Indirect.

undirected.c: Undirected Un`di*rect"ed, a. [In senses 1 and 2, pref. un- not + directed; in sense 3 properly p. p. of undirect.] 1. Not directed; not guided; left without direction.

undiscerning.c: Undiscerning Un`dis*cern"ing (?), n. Want of discernment. [R.] Spectator.

undisclose.c: Undisclose Un`dis*close" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + disclose.] To keep close or secret. [Obs.] Daniel.

undisputable.c: Undisputable Un*dis"pu*ta*ble (?), a. Indisputable. Addison. -- Un*dis"pu*ta*ble*ness, n.

undistinctive.c: Undistinctive Un`dis*tinc"tive (?), a. Making no distinctions; not discriminating; impartial.

undivided.c: Undivided Un`di*vid"ed (?), a. 1. Not divided; not separated or disunited; unbroken; whole; continuous; as, plains undivided by rivers or mountains.

undo.c: Undo Un*do" (?), v. t. [AS. und?n. See 1st Un-, and Do to perform.] 1. To reverse, as what has been done; to annul; to bring to naught.

undock.c: Undock Un*dock" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dock.] (Naut.) To take out of dock; as, to undock a ship.

undoer.c: Undoer Un*do"er (?), n. One who undoes anything; especially, one who ruins another.

undoing.c: Undoing Un*do"ing, n. 1. The reversal of what has been done.

undomesticate.c: Undomesticate Un`do*mes"ti*cate (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + domesticate.] To make wild or roving.

undone.c: Undone Un*done", a. [Pref. un- not + done.] Not done or performed; neglected.

undouble.c: Undouble Un*dou"ble (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + double.] To unfold, or render single.

undoubted.c: Undoubted Un*doubt"ed, a. Not doubted; not called in question; indubitable; indisputable; as, undoubted proof; undoubted hero. -- Un*doubt"ed*ly, adv.

undrape.c: Undrape Un*drape" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + drape.] To strip of drapery; to uncover or unveil.

undraw.c: Undraw Un*draw" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + draw.] To draw aside or open; to draw back.

undreamt.c: Undreamt Undreamed { Un*dreamed" (?), Un*dreamt" (?), } a. Not dreamed, or dreamed of; not th?ught of; not imagined; -- often followed by of.

undress.c: Undress Un*dress" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dress.]
Undress Un"dress (?), n. 1. A loose, negligent dress; ordinary dress, as distinguished from full dress.

undubitable.c: Undubitable Un*du"bi*ta*ble (?), a. Indubitable; as, an undubitable principle. [Obs.] Locke.

undue.c: Undue Un*due" (?), a. 1. Not due; not yet owing; as, an undue debt, note, or bond.

undueness.c: Undueness Un*due"ness, n. The quality of being undue.

unduke.c: Unduke Un*duke" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + duke.] To deprive of dukedom. Swift.

undulary.c: Undulary Un"du*la*ry (?), a. [See Undulate.] Moving like waves; undulatory. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

undulate.c: Undulate Un"du*late (?), a. [L. undulatus undulated, wavy, a dim. from unda a wave; cf. AS.??, Icel. unnr; perhaps akin to E. water. Cf. Abound, Inundate, Redound, Surround.] Same as Undulated.
Undulate Un"du*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Undulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Undulating.] To cause to move backward and forward, or up and down, in undulations or waves; to cause to vibrate.
Undulate Un"du*late, v. i. To move in, or have, undulations or waves; to vibrate; to wave; as, undulating air.

undulated.c: Undulated Un"du*la`ted (?), a. 1. Resembling, or in the nature of, waves; having a wavy surface; undulatory.

undulating.c: Undulating Un"du*la`ting, a. Rising and falling like waves; resembling wave form or motion; undulatory; rolling; wavy; as, an undulating medium; undulating ground. -- Un"du*la`ting*ly. adv.

undulation.c: Undulation Un`du*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. ondulation.] 1. The act of undulating; a waving motion or vibration; as, the undulations of a fluid, of water, or of air; the undulations of sound.

undulationist.c: Undulationist Un`du*la"tion*ist, n. One who advocates the undulatory theory of light. Whewell.

undulative.c: Undulative Un"du*la*tive (?), a. Consisting in, or accompanied by, undulations; undulatory.

undulatory.c: Undulatory Un"du*la*to*ry (?; 277), a. [Cf. F. ondulatoire.] Moving in the manner of undulations, or waves; resembling the motion of waves, which successively rise or swell rise or swell and fall; pertaining to a propagated alternating motion, similar to that of waves.

undull.c: Undull Un*dull" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dull.] To remove the dullness of; to clear. [Obs.] Whitlock.

unduly.c: Unduly Un*du"ly (?), adv. In an undue manner.

undumpish.c: Undumpish Un*dump"ish (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dumpish.] To relieve from the dumps. [Obs.] Fuller.

undust.c: Undust Un*dust" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + dust.] To free from dust. [Obs.]

undwellable.c: Undwellable Un*dwell"a*ble (?), a. Uninhabitable. [Obs.] “A land undwellable.” Wyclif.

undwelt.c: Undwelt Un*dwelt" (?), a. Not lived (in); -- with in.

undying.c: Undying Un*dy"ing (?), a. Not dying; imperishable; unending; immortal; as, the undying souls of men.

uneared.c: Uneared Un*eared" (?), a. Not eared, or plowed. Shak.

unearned.c: Unearned Un*earned" (?), a. Not earned; not gained by labor or service.

unearth.c: Unearth Un*earth" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unearthed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unearthing.] [1st pref. un- + earth.] To drive or draw from the earth; hence, to uncover; to bring out from concealment; to bring to light; to disclose; as, to unearth a secret.

unearthly.c: Unearthly Un*earth"ly, a. Not terrestrial; supernatural; preternatural; hence, weird; appalling; terrific; as, an unearthly sight or sound. -- Un*earth"li*ness (#), n.

unease.c: Unease Un*ease" (?), n. Want of ease; uneasiness. [Obs.]

uneasily.c: Uneasily Un*eas"i*ly (?), adv. In an easy manner.

uneasiness.c: Uneasiness Un*eas"i*ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being uneasy; restlessness; disquietude; anxiety.

uneath.c: Uneath Un*eath" (?), a. [AS. uneá?e; un- not + eá?? easily, easy; akin to OS.??i easy, OHG.?di.] Not easy; difficult; hard. [Obs.]
Uneath Un*eath", adv. Not easily; hardly; scarcely. [Obs.]

unedge.c: Unedge Un*edge" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + edge.] To deprive of the edge; to blunt. J. Fletcher.

unefectual.c: Unefectual Un`e*fec"tu*al (?), a. Ineffectual. “His uneffectual fire.” Shak.

unembodied.c: Unembodied Un`em*bod"ied (?), a. 1. Free from a corporeal body; disembodied; as, unembodied spirits. Byron.

unempirically.c: Unempirically Un`em*pir"ic*al*ly (?), adv. Not empirically; without experiment or experience.

unemployed.c: Unemployed Un`em*ployed" (?), a. 1. Not employed in manual or other labor; having no regular work.

unemployment.c: Unemployment Un`em*ploy"ment (?), n. Quality or state of being not employed; -- used esp. in economics, of the condition of various social classes when temporarily thrown out of employment, as those engaged for short periods, those whose trade is decaying, and those least competent.

unencumber.c: Unencumber Un`en*cum"ber (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + encumber.] To free from incumbrance; to disencumber.

unendly.c: Unendly Un*end"ly (?), a. [Pref. un- not + end + -ly.] Unending; endless. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

unentangle.c: Unentangle Un`en*tan"gle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + entangle.] To disentangle.

unequal.c: Unequal Un*e"qual (?), a. [Cf. Inequal.] 1. Not equal; not matched; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity, strength, talents, acquirements, age, station, or the like; as, the fingers are of unequal length; peers and commoners are unequal in rank.

unequalable.c: Unequalable Un*e"qual*a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being equaled or paralleled. [Obs.] Boyle.

unequaled.c: Unequaled Un*e"qualed (?), a. Not equaled; unmatched; unparalleled; unrivaled; exceeding; surpassing; -- in a good or bad sense; as, unequaled excellence; unequaled ingratitude or baseness. [Written also unequalled.]

unequally.c: Unequally Un*e"qual*ly (?), adv. In an unequal manner.

unequalness.c: Unequalness Un*e"qual*ness, n. The quality or state of being unequal; inequality; unevenness. Jer. Taylor.

unequity.c: Unequity Un*eq"ui*ty (?), n. Want of equity or uprightness; injustice; wickedness; iniquity. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unequivocal.c: Unequivocal Un`e*quiv"o*cal (?), a. Not equivocal; not doubtful; not ambiguous; evident; sincere; plain; as, unequivocal evidence; unequivocal words. -- Un`e*quiv"o*cal*ly, adv. -- Un`e*quiv"o*cal*ness, n.

unerring.c: Unerring Un*err"ing (?), a. Committing no mistake; incapable or error or failure certain; sure; unfailing; as, the unerring wisdom of God.

unerringly.c: Unerringly Un*err"ing*ly, adv. In an unerring manner.

unessential.c: Unessential Un`es*sen"tial (?), a. 1. Not essential; not of prime importance; not indispensable; unimportant. Addison.
Unessential Un`es*sen"tial, n. Something not constituting essence, or something which is not of absolute necessity; as, forms are among the unessentials of religion.

unessentially.c: Unessentially Un`es*sen"tial*ly, adv. In an unessential manner.

unestablish.c: Unestablish Un`es*tab"lish (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + establish.] To disestablish. [R.]

unethes.c: Unethes Uneth { Un*eth" (ŭn*ĕth"), Un*ethes" (?) }, adv. With difficulty; scarcely. See Uneath. [Written also unethe, unneth, unnethe, unnethes, etc.] [Obs.] Chaucer.

uneven.c: Uneven Un*e"ven (?), a. [AS. unefen. See Un- not, and Even, a.] 1. Not even; not level; not uniform; rough; as, an uneven road or way; uneven ground.

unexampled.c: Unexampled Un`ex*am"pled (?), a. Having no example or similar case; being without precedent; unprecedented; unparalleled. “A revolution... unexampled for grandeur of results.” De Quincey.

unexceptionable.c: Unexceptionable Un`ex*cep"tion*a*ble (?), a. Not liable to any exception or objection; unobjectionable; faultless; good; excellent; as, a man of most unexceptionable character. -- Un`ex*cep"tion*a*ble*ness (#), n. -- Un`ex*cep"tion*a*bly, adv.

unexceptive.c: Unexceptive Un`ex*cept"ive (?), a. Not exceptive; not including, admitting, or being, an exception.

unexcusable.c: Unexcusable Un`ex*cus"a*ble (?), a. Inexcusable. Hayward. -- Un`ex*cus"a*ble*ness, n.

unexpectation.c: Unexpectation Un*ex`pec*ta"tion (?), n. Absence of expectation; want of foresight. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

unexpected.c: Unexpected Un`ex*pect"ed (?), a. Not expected; coming without warning; sudden. -- Un`ex*pect"ed*ly, adv. -- Un`ex*pect"ed*ness, n.

unexperienced.c: Unexperienced Un`ex*pe"ri*enced (?), a. 1. Not experienced; being without experience; inexperienced. Swift.

unexpert.c: Unexpert Un`ex*pert" (?), a. Not expert; inexpert. Milton.

unexpertly.c: Unexpertly Un`ex*pert"ly, adv. In an unexpert manner.

unexpressible.c: Unexpressible Un`ex*press"i*ble (?), a. Inexpressible. Tillotson. -- Un`ex*press"i*bly, adv.

unexpressive.c: Unexpressive Un`ex*press"ive (?), a. 1. Not expressive; not having the power of utterance; inexpressive.

unextricable.c: Unextricable Un*ex"tri*ca*ble (?), a. Not extricable; inextricable. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

unface.c: Unface Un*face" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + face.] To remove the face or cover from; to unmask; to expose.

unfailable.c: Unfailable Un*fail"a*ble (?), a. Infallible. [Obs.] “This unfailable word of truth.” Bp. Hall.

unfailing.c: Unfailing Un*fail"ing, a. Not failing; not liable to fail; inexhaustible; certain; sure. Dryden. -- Un*fail"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*fail"ing*ness, n.

unfair.c: Unfair Un*fair" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fair.] To deprive of fairness or beauty. [R.] Shak.
Unfair Un*fair", a. [AS. unfæger unlovely. See Un- not, and Fair, a.] Not fair; not honest; not impartial; disingenuous; using or involving trick or artifice; dishonest; unjust; unequal.

unfaith.c: Unfaith Un*faith" (?), n. Absence or want of faith; faithlessness; distrust; unbelief. [R.]

unfaithful.c: Unfaithful Un*faith"ful (?), a. 1. Not faithful; not observant of promises, vows, allegiance, or duty; violating trust or confidence; treacherous; perfidious; as, an unfaithful subject; an unfaithful agent or servant.

unfalcated.c: Unfalcated Un*fal"ca*ted (?), a. 1. Not falcated, or hooked.

unfasten.c: Unfasten Un*fas"ten (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fasten.] To loose; to unfix; to unbind; to untie.

unfathered.c: Unfathered Un*fa"thered (?), a. 1. Having no father; fatherless; hence, born contrary to nature. Shak.

unfavorable.c: Unfavorable Un*fa"vor*a*ble (?), a. Not favorable; not propitious; adverse; contrary; discouraging. -- Un*fa"vor*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*fa"vor*a*bly, adv.

unfeather.c: Unfeather Un*feath"er (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + feather.] To deprive of feathers; to strip. [R.]

unfeatured.c: Unfeatured Un*fea"tured (?; 135), a. Wanting regular features; deformed. “Visage rough, deformed, unfeatured, and a skin of buff.” Dryden.

unfeaty.c: Unfeaty Un*feat"y (?), a. [Un- not + feat, a.] Not feat; not dexterous; unskillful; clumsy. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

unfeeling.c: Unfeeling Un*feel"ing (?), a. 1. Destitute of feeling; void of sensibility; insensible; insensate.

unfeigned.c: Unfeigned Un*feigned" (?), a. Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere; genuine; as, unfeigned piety; unfeigned love to man. “Good faith unfeigned.” Chaucer. -- Un*feign"ed*ly (#), adv. -- Un*feign"ed*ness, n.

unfellow.c: Unfellow Un*fel"low (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fellow.] To prevent from being a fellow or companion; to separate from one's fellows; to dissever.

unfellowed.c: Unfellowed Un*fel"lowed (?), a. [Pref. un- + fellowed.] Being without a fellow; unmatched; unmated. Shak.

unfence.c: Unfence Un*fence" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fence.] To strip of a fence; to remove a fence from.

unfertile.c: Unfertile Un*fer"tile (?), a. Not fertile; infertile; barren. -- Un*fer"tile*ness, n.

unfestlich.c: Unfestlich Un*fest"lich (?), a. Unfit for a feast; hence, jaded; worn. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unfetter.c: Unfetter Un*fet"ter (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fetter.] To loose from fetters or from restraint; to unchain; to unshackle; to liberate; as, to unfetter the mind.

unfeudalize.c: Unfeudalize Un*feu"dal*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + feudalize.] To free from feudal customs or character; to make not feudal. Carlyle.

unfile.c: Unfile Un*file" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + file.] To remove from a file or record.

unfiled.c: Unfiled Un*filed" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + filed, p. p. of file to defile.] Not defiled; pure. [Obs.] Surrey.

unfilial.c: Unfilial Un*fil"ial (?), a. Unsuitable to a son or a daughter; undutiful; not becoming a child. -- Un*fil"ial*ly, adv.

unfinished.c: Unfinished Un*fin"ished (?), a. Not finished, not brought to an end; imperfect; incomplete; left in the rough; wanting the last hand or touch; as, an unfinished house; an unfinished picture; an unfinished iron casting.

unfit.c: Unfit Un*fit" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fit.] To make unsuitable or incompetent; to deprive of the strength, skill, or proper qualities for anything; to disable; to incapacitate; to disqualify; as, sickness unfits a man for labor; sin unfits us for the society of holy beings.
Unfit Un*fit", a. [Pref. un- + fit.] Not fit; unsuitable. -- Un*fit"ly, adv. -- Un*fit"ness, n.

unfix.c: Unfix Un*fix" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fix.] 1. To loosen from a fastening; to detach from anything that holds; to unsettle; as, to unfix a bayonet; to unfix the mind or affections.

unfledged.c: Unfledged Un*fledged" (?), a. Not fledged; not feathered; hence, not fully developed; immature. Dryden.

unflesh.c: Unflesh Un*flesh" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + flesh.] To deprive of flesh; to reduce a skeleton. “Unfleshed humanity.” Wordsworth.

unfleshly.c: Unfleshly Un*flesh"ly (?), a. Not pertaining to the flesh; spiritual.

unflinching.c: Unflinching Un*flinch"ing (?), a. Not flinching or shrinking; unyielding. -- Un*flinch"ing*ly, adv.

unflower.c: Unflower Un*flow"er (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + flower.] To strip of flowers. [R.] G. Fletcher.

unfold.c: Unfold Un*fold" (?), v. t. [AS. unfealdan. See 1st Un-, and Fold, v. t.] 1. To open the folds of; to expand; to spread out; as, to unfold a tablecloth.
Unfold Un*fold", v. i. To open; to expand; to become disclosed or developed.

unfolder.c: Unfolder Un*fold"er (?), n. One who, or that which, unfolds.

unfoldment.c: Unfoldment Un*fold"ment (?), n. The acct of unfolding, or the state of being unfolded.

unfool.c: Unfool Un*fool" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fool.] To restore from folly, or from being a fool. [Obs.] Shak.

unforesee.c: Unforesee Un`fore*see" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + foresee.] To fail to foresee. Bp. Hacket.

unforeseeable.c: Unforeseeable Un`fore*see"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being foreseen. South.

unforeskinned.c: Unforeskinned Un*fore"skinned (?), a. [1st pref. un- + foreskin + -ed.] Deprived of the foreskin; circumcised. [R.] Milton.

unforgettable.c: Unforgettable Un`for*get"ta*ble (?), a. Not forgettable; enduring in memory.

unform.c: Unform Un*form" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + form.] To decompose, or resolve into parts; to destroy the form of; to unmake. [R.] Good.

unformed.c: Unformed Un*formed" (?), a. [In sense 1 properly p. p. of un form; in senses 2 and 3 pref. un- not + formed.]

unfortunate.c: Unfortunate Un*for"tu*nate (?), a. Not fortunate; unsuccessful; not prosperous; unlucky; attended with misfortune; unhappy; as, an unfortunate adventure; an unfortunate man; an unfortunate commander; unfortunate business. -- n. An unfortunate person. Hood.

unfounded.c: Unfounded Un*found"ed (?), a. 1. Not founded; not built or established. Milton.

unframe.c: Unframe Un*frame" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + frame.] To take apart, or destroy the frame of. Dryden.

unfrangible.c: Unfrangible Un*fran"gi*ble (?), a. Infrangible. [Obs.] “Impassible and unfrangible.” Jer. Taylor.

unfrankable.c: Unfrankable Un*frank"a*ble (?), a. Not frankable; incapable of being sent free by public conveyance.

unfraught.c: Unfraught Un*fraught" (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + fraught.] Not fraught; not burdened.

unfree.c: Unfree Un*free" (?), a. Not free; held in bondage.

unfreeze.c: Unfreeze Un*freeze" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + freeze.] To thaw. [Obs.]

unfrequent.c: Unfrequent Un*fre"quent (?), a. [Pref. un- not + frequent.] Infrequent. J. H. Newman. -- Un*fre"quent*ly adv.
Unfrequent Un`fre*quent" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + frequent.] To cease to frequent. [Obs.]

unfrequented.c: Unfrequented Un`fre*quent"ed, a. [Pref. un- + frequented.] Rarely visited; seldom or never resorted to by human beings; as, an unfrequented place or forest. Addison.

unfret.c: Unfret Un*fret" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + fret.] To smooth after being fretted. [Obs.]

unfriend.c: Unfriend Un*friend" (?), n. One not a friend; an enemy. [R.] Carlyle.

unfriended.c: Unfriended Un*friend"ed, a. Wanting friends; not befriended; not countenanced or supported. Goldsmith.

unfriendly.c: Unfriendly Un*friend"ly, a. 1. Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; hostile; as, an unfriendly neighbor.

unfriendship.c: Unfriendship Un*friend"ship, n. The state or quality of being unfriendly; unfriendliness; enmity.

unfrock.c: Unfrock Un*frock" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + frock.] To deprive or divest or a frock; specifically, to deprive of priestly character or privilege; as, to unfrock a priest.

unfruitful.c: Unfruitful Un*fruit"ful (?), a. Not producing fruit or offspring; unproductive; infertile; barren; sterile; as, an unfruitful tree or animal; unfruitful soil; an unfruitful life or effort. -- Un*fruit"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*fruit"ful*ness, n.

unfumed.c: Unfumed Un*fumed" (?), a. Not exposed to fumes; not fumigated. Milton.

unfurl.c: Unfurl Un*furl" (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + furl.] To loose from a furled state; to unfold; to expand; to open or spread; as, to unfurl sails; to unfurl a flag.

unfurnish.c: Unfurnish Un*fur"nish (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + furnish.] To strip of furniture; to divest; to strip.

ungain.c: Ungain Un*gain" (?), a. [OE. ungein. See Ungainly.] Ungainly; clumsy; awkward; also, troublesome; inconvenient. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Beau. & Pl.

ungainliness.c: Ungainliness Un*gain"li*ness, n. The state or quality of being ungainly; awkwardness.

ungainly.c: Ungainly Un*gain"ly, a. [OE. ungeinliche, adv., fr. ungein inconvenient; un- + Icel. gegn ready, serviceable; adv., against, opposite. See Un- not, and Gain, a., Again.]
Ungainly Un*gain"ly, adv. In an ungainly manner.

ungear.c: Ungear Un*gear" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + gear.] To strip of gear; to unharness; to throw out of gear.

ungeld.c: Ungeld Un*geld" (?), n. [Pref. un- not + geld payment.] (Anglo-Sax. Law) A person so far out of the protection of the law, that if he were murdered, no geld, or fine, should be paid, or composition made by him that killed him. Cowell. Burrill.

ungenerous.c: Ungenerous Un*gen"er*ous (?), a. Not generous; illiberal; ignoble; unkind; dishonorable.

ungenerously.c: Ungenerously Un*gen"er*ous*ly, adv. In an ungenerous manner.

ungenitured.c: Ungenitured Un*gen"i*tured (?), a. [Pref. un- not + geniture.] Destitute of genitals; impotent. [R.] Shak.

ungentle.c: Ungentle Un*gen"tle (?), a. Not gentle; lacking good breeding or delicacy; harsh.

unget.c: Unget Un*get" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + get.] To cause to be unbegotten or unborn, or as if unbegotten or unborn. [R.]

ungifted.c: Ungifted Un*gift"ed (?), a. Being without gifts, especially native gifts or endowments. Cowper.

ungird.c: Ungird Un*gird" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + gird.] To loose the girdle or band of; to unbind; to unload.

ungive.c: Ungive Un*give" (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + give.] To yield; to relax; to give way. [Obs.]

ungka.c: Ungka Ung"ka (?), n. (Zool.) The siamang; -- called also ungka ape.

ungkaputi.c: Ungka-puti Ung"ka-pu`ti (?), n. (Zool.) The agile gibbon; -- called also ungka-pati, and ungka-etam. See Gibbon.

unglaze.c: Unglaze Un*glaze" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + glaze.] To strip of glass; to remove the glazing, or glass, from, as a window.

unglorify.c: Unglorify Un*glo"ri*fy (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + glorify.] To deprive of glory. [R.] I. Watts.

unglove.c: Unglove Un*glove" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + glove.] To take off the glove or gloves of; as, to unglove the hand. Beau. & Fl.

unglue.c: Unglue Un*glue" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + glue.] To separate, part, or open, as anything fastened with glue.

ungod.c: Ungod Un*god" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + god.] 1. To deprive of divinity; to undeify. [R.] Donne.

ungodly.c: Ungodly Un*god"ly, a. 1. Not godly; not having regard for God; disobedient to God; wicked; impious; sinful.

ungored.c: Ungored Un*gored" (?), a. [Pref. un- + gore blood.] Not stained with gore; not bloodied. Sylvester.
Ungored Un*gored" (?), a. [Pref. un- + gored, p. p. of 3d gore.] Not gored or pierced.

ungotten.c: Ungotten Ungot { Un*got" (?), Un*got"ten (?), } a. 1. Not gotten; not acquired.

ungovernable.c: Ungovernable Un*gov"ern*a*ble (?), a. Not governable; not capable of being governed, ruled, or restrained; licentious; wild; unbridled; as, ungovernable passions. -- Un*gov"ern*a*bly, adv. Goldsmith.

ungown.c: Ungown Un*gown" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + gown.] To strip of a gown; to unfrock.

ungowned.c: Ungowned Un*gowned" (?), a. 1. [1st pref. un- + gown.] Stripped of a gown; unfrocked.

ungraceful.c: Ungraceful Un*grace"ful (?), a. Not graceful; not marked with ease and dignity; deficient in beauty and elegance; inelegant; awkward; as, ungraceful manners; ungraceful speech.

ungracious.c: Ungracious Un*gra"cious (?), a. 1. Not gracious; showing no grace or kindness; being without good will; unfeeling. Shak.

ungrate.c: Ungrate Un*grate" (?), a. Displeasing; ungrateful; ingrate. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

ungrateful.c: Ungrateful Un*grate"ful (?), a. 1. Not grateful; not thankful for favors; making no returns, or making ill return for kindness, attention, etc.; ingrateful. South.

ungrave.c: Ungrave Un*grave" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + grave.] To raise or remove from the grave; to disinter; to untomb; to exhume. [Obs.] Fuller.

ungual.c: Ungual Un"gual (?), a. [L. unguis a nail, claw, hoof.]

unguard.c: Unguard Un*guard" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + guard.] To deprive of a guard; to leave unprotected. [R.] Sterne.

ungueal.c: Ungueal Un"gue*al (?), a. [Cf. F. onguéal. See Ungual.] Ungual.

unguent.c: Unguent Un"guent (?; 277), n. [L. unguentum, from unguere, ungere, to anoint: cf. F. onguent. See Ointment, and cf. Unction, Unctuous.] A lubricant or salve for sores, burns, or the like; an ointment. Cowper.

unguentary.c: Unguentary Un"guen*ta*ry (?), a. [L. unguentarius.] Like an unguent, or partaking of its qualities.

unguestlike.c: Unguestlike Un*guest"like (?), adv. In a manner not becoming to a guest. [R.] Milton.

unguical.c: Unguical Un"guic*al (?), a. [L. unguis a nail or claw. Cf. Ungual.] Ungual.

unguicular.c: Unguicular Un*guic"u*lar (?), a. [L. unguiculus, dim. of unguis a nail.] Of or pertaining to a claw or a nail; ungual.

unguiculata.c: Unguiculata ‖Un*guic`u*la"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. unguiculus a finger nail.] (Zool.) An extensive division of Mammalia including those having claws or nails, as distinguished from the hoofed animals (Ungulata).

unguiculate.c: Unguiculate Un*guic"u*late (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Unguiculata.

unguiculated.c: Unguiculated Unguiculate { Un*guic"u*late, Un*guic"u*la`ted (?), } a. 1. Furnished with nails, claws, or hooks; clawed. See the Note under Nail, n., 1.

unguiferous.c: Unguiferous Un*guif"er*ous (?), a. [L. unguis nail or claw + -ferous.] Producing, having, or supporting nails or claws.

unguiform.c: Unguiform Un"gui*form (?), a. [L. unguis a nail or claw + -form.] Having the form of a claw or claws.

unguinous.c: Unguinous Un"gui*nous (?), a. [L. unguinosus, fr. unguen, -inis, fat, ointment.] Consisting of, or resembling, fat or oil; oily; unctuous; oleaginous.

unguis.c: Unguis ‖Un"guis (?), n.; pl. Ungues (#). [L., nail, claw, or hoof.] 1. The nail, claw, talon, or hoof of a finger, toe, or other appendage.

ungula.c: Ungula ‖Un"gu*la (?), n.; pl. Ungulae (#). [L., a claw, hoof, from unguis a nail, claw, hoof.] 1. A hoof, claw, or talon.

ungular.c: Ungular Un"gu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a hoof, claw, or talon; ungual.

ungulata.c: Ungulata ‖Un`gu*la"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. ungula hoof.] (Zool.) An extensive group of mammals including all those that have hoofs. It comprises the Artiodactyla and Perissodactyla.

ungulate.c: Ungulate Un"gu*late (?), a. [L. ungulatus. See Ungula.] 1. Shaped like a hoof.
Ungulate Un"gu*late, n. (Zool.) Any hoofed quadruped; one of the Ungulata.

unguled.c: Unguled Un"guled (?), a. [L. ungula a claw.] (Her.) Hoofed, or bearing hoofs; -- used only when these are of a tincture different from the body.

unguligrade.c: Unguligrade Un"gu*li*grade (?), a. [L. ungula hoof + gradi to walk.] (Zool.) Having, or walking on, hoofs.

ungulous.c: Ungulous Un"gu*lous (?), a. [See Ungula.] (Zool.) Same as Ungulate.

unhair.c: Unhair Un*hair" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hair.] To deprive of hair, or of hairs; as, to unhair hides for leather.

unhallow.c: Unhallow Un*hal"low (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hallow.] To profane; to desecrate.

unhallowed.c: Unhallowed Un*hal"lowed (?), a. [Pref. un- not + hallowed.] Not consecrated; hence, profane; unholy; impious; wicked.

unhand.c: Unhand Un*hand" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hand.] To loose from the hand; to let go.

unhandsome.c: Unhandsome Un*hand"some (?), a. 1. Not handsome; not beautiful; ungraceful; not comely or pleasing; plain; homely.

unhandy.c: Unhandy Un*hand"y (?), a. Clumsy; awkward; as, an Unhandy man.

unhang.c: Unhang Un*hang" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hang.]

unhap.c: Unhap Un*hap" (?), n. Ill luck; misfortune. [Obs.] “The cause of her unhap.” Sir P. Sidney.

unhappy.c: Unhappy Un*hap"py (?), a. 1. Not happy or fortunate; unfortunate; unlucky; as, affairs have taken an unhappy turn.

unharbor.c: Unharbor Un*har"bor (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + harbor.] To drive from harbor or shelter.

unharbored.c: Unharbored Un*har"bored (?), a. [Pref. un- not + harbored.] 1. Having no harbor or shelter; unprotected.

unharmonious.c: Unharmonious Un`har*mo"ni*ous (?), a. Inharmonious; unsymmetrical; also, unmusical; discordant. Swift. -- Un`har*mo"ni*ous*ly, adv.

unharness.c: Unharness Un*har"ness (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + harness.] 1. To strip of harness; to loose from harness or gear; as, to unharness horses or oxen. Cowper.

unhasp.c: Unhasp Un*hasp" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hasp.] To unloose the hasp of; to unclose.

unhat.c: Unhat Un*hat" (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + hat.] To take off the hat of; to remove one's hat, especially as a mark of respect. H. Spenser.

unhead.c: Unhead Un*head" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + head.]

unheal.c: Unheal Un*heal" (?), n. [Pref. un- not + heal health.] Misfortune; calamity; sickness. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Unheal Un*heal", v. t. To uncover. See Unhele. [Obs.]

unheard.c: Unheard Un*heard" (?), a. 1. Not heard; not perceived by the ear; as, words unheard by those present.

unheardof.c: Unheard-of Un*heard"-of (?), a. New; unprecedented; unparalleled. Swift.

unheart.c: Unheart Un*heart" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + heart.] To cause to lose heart; to dishearten. [Obs.] Shak.

unheedy.c: Unheedy Un*heed"y (?), a. Incautious; precipitate; heedless. [Obs.] Milton.

unheired.c: Unheired Un*heired" (?), a. Destitute of an heir.

unhele.c: Unhele Un*hele" (?), n. Same as Unheal, n. [Obs.]
Unhele Un*hele", v. t. [AS. unhelian. See 1st Un-, and Hele to cover.] To uncover. [Obs.] Spenser. Marston.

unhelm.c: Unhelm Un*helm" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + helm.] To deprive of the helm or helmet. Sir W. Scott.

unhelmed.c: Unhelmed Un*helmed" (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unhelm.] Divested or deprived of the helm or helmet.

unhelmet.c: Unhelmet Un*hel"met (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + helmet.] To deprive of the helmet. Sir W. Scott.

unhide.c: Unhide Un*hide" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hide.] To bring out from concealment; to discover. [Obs.] P. Fletcher.

unhinge.c: Unhinge Un*hinge" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hinge.]

unhingement.c: Unhingement Un*hinge"ment (?), n. The act unhinging, or the state of being unhinged.

unhitch.c: unhitch un*hitch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hitch.] To free from being hitched, or as if from being hitched; to unfasten; to loose; as, to unhitch a horse, or a trace.

unhive.c: unhive un*hive" (ŭn*hīv"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hive.]

unhoard.c: unhoard un*hoard" (ŭn*hōrd"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hoard.] To take or steal from a hoard; to pilfer. Milton.

unhold.c: unhold un*hold" (ŭn*hōld"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hold.] To cease to hold; to unhand; to release. [Obs.] Otway.

unholy.c: unholy un*ho"ly (ŭn*hō"ly̆), a. Not holy; unhallowed; not consecrated; hence, profane; wicked; impious. -- un*ho"li*ly (#), adv. -- un*ho"li*ness, n.

unhonest.c: unhonest un*hon"est (?), a. Dishonest; dishonorable. Ascham. -- Un*hon"est*ly, adv. Udall.

unhood.c: unhood un*hood" (ŭn*hŏod"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hood.] To remove a hood or disguise from. Quarterly Rev.

unhook.c: Unhook Un*hook" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hook.] To loose from a hook; to undo or open by loosening or unfastening the hooks of; as, to unhook a fish; to unhook a dress.

unhoop.c: Unhoop Un*hoop" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + hoop.] To strip or deprive of hoops; to take away the hoops of.

unhoped.c: Unhoped Un*hoped" (?), a. Not hoped or expected. “With unhoped success.” Dryden.

unhorse.c: Unhorse Un*horse" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + horse.] To throw from a horse; to cause to dismount; also, to take a horse or horses from; as, to unhorse a rider; to unhorse a carriage. Cowper.

unhouse.c: Unhouse Un*house" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + house.] To drive from a house or habitation; to dislodge; hence, to deprive of shelter.

unhoused.c: Unhoused Un*housed" (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unhouse.] Driven from a house; deprived of shelter.

unhouseled.c: Unhouseled Un*hou"seled (?), a. Not having received the sacrament. [Obs.] [Written also unhouselled.]

unhumanize.c: Unhumanize Un*hu"man*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + humanize.] To render inhuman or barbarous. J. Barlow.

unhusked.c: Unhusked Un*husked" (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + husked.] Not husked; having the husk on.

uni.c: Uni- U"ni- (?). [L. unus one. See One.] A prefix signifying one, once; as in uniaxial, unicellular.

uniate.c: Uniate Uniat { U"ni*at (?), U"ni*ate (?), } n. (Eccl.) A member of the Greek Church, who nevertheless acknowledges the supremacy of the Pope of Rome; one of the United Greeks. Also used adjectively.

uniaxal.c: Uniaxal U`ni*ax"al (?), a. [Uni + axal.] Uniaxial. -- U`ni*ax"al*ly, adv.

uniaxial.c: Uniaxial U`ni*ax"i*al (?), a. [Uni + axial.] 1. (Crystallog.) Having but one optic axis, or line of no double refraction.

uniaxially.c: Uniaxially U`ni*ax"i*al*ly, adv. In a uniaxial manner.

unibranchiate.c: Unibranchiate U`ni*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [Uni- + branchiate.] (Zool.) Having but one gill, as certain molluscs.

unicameral.c: Unicameral U`ni*cam"e*ral (?), a. [Uni- + L. camera vault.] Having, or consisting of, a single chamber; -- said of a legislative assembly. [R.] F. Lieber.

unicapsular.c: Unicapsular U`ni*cap"su*lar (?). [Uni- + capsular: cf. F. unicapsulaire.] (Bot.) Having but one capsule to each flower.

unicarinated.c: Unicarinated U`ni*car"i*na`ted (?), a. [Uni- + carinated.] Having one ridge or keel. Craig.

unicellular.c: Unicellular U`ni*cel"lu*lar (?), a. [Uni- + cellular.] Having, or consisting of, but a single cell; as, a unicellular organism.

unicentral.c: Unicentral U`ni*cen"tral (?), a. [Uni- + central.] (Biol.) Having a single center of growth.

unicity.c: Unicity U*nic"i*ty (?), n. [L. unicus single. See Unique.] The condition of being united; quality of the unique; unification.

uniclinal.c: Uniclinal U`ni*cli"nal (?), a. [Uni- + Gr.? to incline.] (Geol.) See Nonoclinal.

unicolorous.c: Unicolorous U`ni*col"or*ous (?), a. [Uni- + color.] (Zool.) Having the surface of a uniform color.

unicorn.c: Unicorn U"ni*corn (?), n. [OE. unicorne, F. unicorne, L. unicornis one-horned, having a single horn; unus one + cornu a horn; cf. L. unicornuus a unicorn. See One, and Horn.] 1. A fabulous animal with one horn; the monoceros; -- often represented in heraldry as a supporter.

unicornous.c: Unicornous U`ni*cor"nous (?), a. [See Unicorn.] (Zool.) Having but a single horn; -- said of certain insects. “Unicornous beetles.” Sir T. Browne.

unicostate.c: Unicostate U`ni*cos"tate (?), a. [Uni- + costate.] (Bot.) Having a single rib or strong nerve running upward from the base; -- said of a leaf.

unicursal.c: Unicursal U`ni*cur"sal (?), a. [Uni- + L. currere, cursum, to run.] (Geom.) That can be passed over in a single course; -- said of a curve when the coordinates of the point on the curve can be expressed as rational algebraic functions of a single parameter θ.

unideaed.c: Unideaed Un`i*de"aed (?), a. Having no ideas; senseless; frivolous. “Unideaed girls.” Mrs. Hemans.

unideal.c: Unideal Un`i*de"al (?), a. 1. Not ideal; real; unimaginative.

unidimensional.c: Unidimensional Un`i*di*men"sion*al (?), a. [Uni- + dimensional.] (Math.) Having but one dimension. See Dimension.

unifacial.c: Unifacial U`ni*fa"cial (?), a. [Uni- + facial.] Having but one front surface; as, some foliaceous corals are unifacial, the polyp mouths being confined to one surface.

unific.c: Unific U*nif"ic (?), a. Making one or unity; unifying.

unification.c: Unification U`ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [See Unify.] The act of unifying, or the state of being unified.

unifier.c: Unifier U"ni*fi`er (?), n. One who, or that which, unifies; as, a natural law is a unifier of phenomena.

unifilar.c: Unifilar U`ni*fi"lar (?), a. [Uni- + L. filum a thread.] Having only one thread; involving the use of only one thread, wire, fiber, or the like; as, unifilar suspension.

uniflagellate.c: Uniflagellate U`ni*fla*gel"late (?), a. [Uni- + flagellate.] (Biol.) Having but one flagellum; as, uniflagellate organisms.

uniflorous.c: Uniflorous U`ni*flo"rous (?), a. [Uni- + L. flos, floris, a flower: cf. F. uniflore.] (Bot.) Bearing one flower only; as, a uniflorous peduncle.

unifolliate.c: Unifolliate U`ni*fol"li*ate (?), a. [Uni- + foliate.] (Bot.) Having only one leaf.

unifollilate.c: Unifollilate U`ni*fol"li*late (?), a. [Uni- + foliolate.] (Bot.) Having only one leaflet, as the leaves of the orange tree.

uniform.c: Uniform U"ni*form (?), a. [L. uniformis; unus one + forma from: cf. F. uniforme.]

Uniform U"ni*form, n. [F. uniforme. See Uniform, a.] A dress of a particular style or fashion worn by persons in the same service or order by means of which they have a distinctive appearance; as, the uniform of the artillery, of the police, of the Freemasons, etc.
Uniform U"ni*form, v. t. 1. To clothe with a uniform; as, to uniform a company of soldiers.

uniformism.c: Uniformism U"ni*form`ism (?), n. [From Uniform.] (Geol.) The doctrine of uniformity in the geological history of the earth; -- in part equivalent to uniformitarianism, but also used, more broadly, as opposed to catastrophism.

uniformitarian.c: Uniformitarian U`ni*form`i*ta"ri*an (?), a. (Geol.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, the view or doctrine that existing causes, acting in the same manner and with essentially the same intensity as at the present time, are sufficient to account for all geological changes.
Uniformitarian U`ni*form`i*ta"ri*an, n. (Geol.) One who accepts uniformitarianism, or the uniformitarian doctrine.

uniformity.c: Uniformity U`ni*form"i*ty (?), n. [L. uniformitas: cf. F. uniformité.] 1. The quality or state of being uniform; freedom from variation or difference; resemblance to itself at all times; sameness of action, effect, etc., under like conditions; even tenor; as, the uniformity of design in a poem; the uniformity of nature.

uniformly.c: Uniformly U"ni*form`ly (?), adv. In a uniform manner; without variation or diversity; by a regular, constant, or common ratio of change; with even tenor; as, a temper uniformly mild.

unifromness.c: Unifromness U"ni*from`ness, n. The quality or state of being uniform; uniformity.

unify.c: Unify U"ni*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unifying (?).] [Uni- + -fy: cf. F. unifier.] To cause to be one; to make into a unit; to unite; to view as one.

unigeniture.c: Unigeniture U`ni*gen"i*ture (?), n. [L. unigenitus only-begotten; unus one + gignere, genitum, to beget.] The state of being the only begotten. [R.] Bp. Pearson.

unigenous.c: Unigenous U*nig"e*nous (?), a. [L. unigena; unus one + genere, gignere, to beget.] (Biol.) Being of one kind; being of the same genus.

unijugate.c: Unijugate U*nij"u*gate (?), a. [Uni- + L. jugum yoke, pair: cf. L. unijugus having one yoke.] (Bot.) Having but one pair of leaflets; -- said of a pinnate leaf.

unilabiate.c: Unilabiate U`ni*la"bi*ate (?), a. [Uni- + labiate.] (Bot.) Having one lip only; as, a unilabiate corolla.

unilateral.c: Unilateral U`ni*lat"er*al (?), a. [Uni- + lateral: cf. F. unilatéral.] 1. Being on one side only; affecting but one side; one-sided.

uniliteral.c: Uniliteral U`ni*lit"er*al (?), a. [Uni- + literal.] Consisting of one letter only; as, a uniliteral word or sign.

unilobar.c: Unilobar U`ni*lo"bar (?), a. [Uni- + lobar.] Consisting of a single lobe.

unilocular.c: Unilocular U`ni*loc"u*lar (?), a. [Uni- + locular: cf. F. uniloculaire.] (Biol.) Having one cell or cavity only; as, a unilocular capsule or shell.

unimpairable.c: Unimpairable Un`im*pair"a*ble (?), a. That can not be impaired. Hakewill.

unimpeachable.c: Unimpeachable Un`im*peach"a*ble (?), a. Not impeachable; not to be called in question; exempt from liability to accusation; free from stain, guilt, or fault; irreproachable; blameless; as, an unimpeachable reputation; unimpeachable testimony. Burke. -- Un`im*peach"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`im*peach"a*bly, adv.

unimplicate.c: Unimplicate Un*im"pli*cate (?), a. Not implicated. “Unimplicate in folly.” R. Browning.

unimportance.c: Unimportance Un`im*por"tance (?), n. Want of importance; triviality. Johnson.

unimproved.c: Unimproved Un`im*proved" (?), a. 1. Not improved; not made better or wiser; not advanced in knowledge, manners, or excellence.

unimuscular.c: Unimuscular U`ni*mus"cu*lar (?), a. [Uni- muscular.] (Zool.) Having only one adductor muscle, and one muscular impression on each valve, as the oyster; monomyarian.

unincumbered.c: Unincumbered Un`in*cum"bered (?), a. 1. Not incumbered; not burdened.

uninfringible.c: Uninfringible Un`in*frin"gi*ble (?), a. That may not be infringed; as, an uninfringible monopoly.

unintelligence.c: Unintelligence Un`in*tel"li*gence (?), n. Absence or lack of intelligence; unwisdom; ignorance. Bp. Hall.

uninterested.c: Uninterested Un*in"ter*est*ed (?), a. 1. Not interested; not having any interest or property in; having nothing at stake; as, to be uninterested in any business.

unintermission.c: Unintermission Un*in`ter*mis"sion (?), n. Want or failure of intermission. [R.] Bp. Parker.

uninucleated.c: Uninucleated U`ni*nu"cle*a`ted (?), a. [Uni- + nucleated.] (Biol.) Possessed of but a single nucleus; as, a uninucleated cell.

unio.c: Unio U"ni*o (?), n. [NL., fr. L. unio unity, union, a single large pearl. See Union.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of fresh-water mussels belonging to Unio and many allied genera.

uniocular.c: Uniocular U`ni*oc"u*lar (?), a. [Uni- + ocular.] Of, pertaining to, or seated in, one eye; monocular.

union.c: Union Un"ion (?; 277), n. [F., from L. unio oneness, union, a single large pearl, a kind of onion, fr. unus one. See One, and cf. Onion, Unit.] 1. The act of uniting or joining two or more things into one, or the state of being united or joined; junction; coalition; combination.

unionism.c: Unionism Un"ion*ism (?), n. 1. The sentiment of attachment to a federal union, especially to the federal union of the United States.

unionist.c: Unionist Un"ion*ist, n. 1. One who advocates or promotes union; especially a loyal supporter of a federal union, as that of the United States.

unionistic.c: Unionistic Un`ion*is"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to union or unionists; tending to promote or preserve union.

uniovulate.c: Uniovulate U`ni*o"vu*late (?), a. [Uni- + ovulate.] (Bot.) Containing but one ovule.

unipara.c: Unipara ‖U*nip"a*ra (?), n. [NL. See Uniparous.] A woman who has borne one child.

uniparous.c: Uniparous U*nip"a*rous (?), a. [Uni- + L. parere to bring forth.] 1. (Zool.) Producing but one egg or young at a time.

uniped.c: Uniped U"ni*ped (?), a. [Uni- + L. pes, pedis, foot.] Having only one foot. Wright.

unipersonalist.c: Unipersonalist U`ni*per"so*nal*ist, n. (Theol.) One who believes that the Deity is unipersonal.

uniphonous.c: Uniphonous U*niph"o*nous (?), a. [Uni- + Gr.? sound.] Having but one sound, as the drum. [R.]

uniplicate.c: Uniplicate U*nip"li*cate (?), a. [Uni- + plicate.] Having, or consisting of, but one fold.

unipolar.c: Unipolar U`ni*po"lar (?), a. [Uni- + polar.] 1. (Physics) Having, or acting by means of, one pole only.

unique.c: Unique U*nique" (?), a. [F. unique; cf. It. unico; from L. unicus, from unus one. See One.] Being without a like or equal; unmatched; unequaled; unparalleled; single in kind or excellence; sole. -- U*nique"ly, adv. -- U*nique"ness, n.
Unique U*nique", n. A thing without a like; something unequaled or unparalleled. [R.]

uniquity.c: Uniquity U*niq"ui*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unique; uniqueness. [R.] Walpole.

uniradiated.c: Uniradiated U`ni*ra"di*a`ted (?), a. [Uni- + radiated.] Having but one ray.

uniramous.c: Uniramous U`ni*ra"mous (?), a. [Uni- + L. ramus branch.] (Biol.) Having but one branch.

uniseptate.c: Uniseptate U`ni*sep"tate (?), a. [Uni- + septate.] (Bot.) Having but one septum, or partition; -- said of two-celled fruits, such as the silicles of cruciferous plants.

uniserial.c: Uniserial U`ni*se"ri*al (?), a. [Uni- + serial.] Having only one row or series.

uniseriate.c: Uniseriate U`ni*se"ri*ate (?), a. [Uni- + seriate.] Having one line or series; uniserial. -- U`ni*se"ri*ate*ly, adv.

unisexual.c: Unisexual U`ni*sex"u*al (?), a. [Uni- + sexual: cf. F. unisexuel.] (Biol.) Having one sex only, as plants which have the male and female flowers on separate individuals, or animals in which the sexes are in separate individuals; diœcious; -- distinguished from bisexual, or hermaphrodite. See Diœcious.

unisilicate.c: Unisilicate U`ni*sil"i*cate (?), n. [Uni- + silicate.] (Min.) A salt of orthosilicic acid, H4SiO4; -- so called because the ratio of the oxygen atoms united to the basic metals and silicon respectively is 1:1; for example, Mg2SiO4 or 2MgO.SiO2.

unison.c: Unison U"ni*son (?; 277), n. [LL. unisonus having the same sound; L. unus one + sonus a sound: cf. F. unisson, It. unisono. See One, and Sound a noise.] 1. Harmony; agreement; concord; union.
Unison U"ni*son (?; 277), a. [Cf. It. unisono. See Unison, n.] 1. Sounding alone. [Obs.]

unisonal.c: Unisonal U*nis"o*nal (?), a. Being in unison; unisonant. -- U*nis"o*nal*ly, adv.

unisonance.c: Unisonance U*nis"o*nance (?), n. [See Unisonant.] Accordance of sounds; unison.

unisonant.c: Unisonant U*nis"o*nant (?), a. [Uni- + sonant. See Unison.] Being in unison; having the same degree of gravity or acuteness; sounded alike in pitch.

unisonous.c: Unisonous U*nis"o*nous (?), a. [See Unison.] Being in unison; unisonant. Busby.

unit.c: Unit U"nit (?), n. [Abbrev. from unity.] 1. A single thing or person.

unitable.c: Unitable U*nit"a*ble (?), a. Capable of union by growth or otherwise. Owen.

unitarian.c: Unitarian U`ni*ta"ri*an (?), n. [Cf. F. unitaire, unitairien, NL. unitarius. See Unity.] 1. (Theol.) One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, believing that God exists only in one person; a unipersonalist; also, one of a denomination of Christians holding this belief.
Unitarian U`ni*ta"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Unitarians, or their doctrines.

unitarianism.c: Unitarianism U`ni*ta"ri*an*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. unitairianisme.] The doctrines of Unitarians.

unitarianize.c: Unitarianize U`ni*ta"ri*an*ize (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Unitarianized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unitarianizing (?).] To change or turn to Unitarian views.

unitary.c: Unitary U"nit*a*ry (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a unit or units; relating to unity; as, the unitary method in arithmetic.

unite.c: Unite U*nite" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. United; p. pr. & vb. n. Uniting.] [L. unitus, p. p. of unire to unite, from unus one. See One.] 1. To put together so as to make one; to join, as two or more constituents, to form a whole; to combine; to connect; to join; to cause to adhere; as, to unite bricks by mortar; to unite iron bars by welding; to unite two armies.
Unite U*nite", v. i. 1. To become one; to be cemented or consolidated; to combine, as by adhesion or mixture; to coalesce; to grow together.
Unite U*nite", a. [L. unitus, p. p. See Unite, v. t.] United; joint; as, unite consent. [Obs.] J. Webster.

united.c: United U*nit"ed, a. Combined; joined; made one.

unitedly.c: Unitedly U*nit"ed*ly, adv. In an united manner. Dryden.

uniter.c: Uniter U*nit"er (?), n. One who, or that which, unites.

uniterable.c: Uniterable U*nit"er*a*ble (?), a. Not iterable; incapable of being repeated. [Obs.] “To play away an uniterable life.” Sir T. Browne.

unition.c: Unition U*ni"tion (?), n. [LL. unitio, from L. unire. See Unite,v. t.] The act of uniting, or the state of being united; junction. [Obs.] Wiseman.

unitive.c: Unitive U"ni*tive (?), a. [LL. unitivus: cf. F. unitif.] Having the power of uniting; causing, or tending to produce, union. Jer. Taylor.

unitively.c: Unitively U"ni*tive*ly, adv. In a unitive manner. Cudworth.

unitize.c: Unitize U"nit*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unitized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unitizing (?).] To reduce to a unit, or one whole; to form into a unit; to unify.

unity.c: Unity U"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Unities (#). [OE. unite, F. unité, L. unitas, from unus one. See One, and cf. Unit.] 1. The state of being one; oneness.
