univalence.c: Univalence U*niv"a*lence (?), n. (Chem.) The quality or state of being univalent.

univalent.c: Univalent U*niv"a*lent (?), a. [Uni- + L. valens, -entis, p. pr. See Valence.] (Chem.) Having a valence of one; capable of combining with, or of being substituted for, one atom of hydrogen; monovalent; -- said of certain atoms and radicals.

univalve.c: Univalve U"ni*valve (?), n. [Uni- + valve: cf. F. univalve.] (Zool.) A shell consisting of one valve only; a mollusk whose shell is composed of a single piece, as the snails and conchs.

univalved.c: Univalved Univalve { U"ni*valve (?), U"ni*valved (?), } a. [Cf. F. univalve.] (Bot. & Zool.) Having one valve; as, a univalve shell or pericarp.

univalvular.c: Univalvular U`ni*val"vu*lar (?), a. (Bot. & Zool.) Same as Univalve, a.

univariant.c: Univariant U`ni*va"ri*ant (?), a. (Chem.) Having one degree of freedom or variability.

universal.c: Universal U`ni*ver"sal (?), a. [L. universalis: cf. F. universel, OF. also universal. See Universe.] 1. Of or pertaining to the universe; extending to, including, or affecting, the whole number, quantity, or space; unlimited; general; all-reaching; all-pervading; as, universal ruin; universal good; universal benevolence or benefice. “Anointed universal King.” Milton.
Universal U`ni*ver"sal, n. 1. The whole; the general system of the universe; the universe. [Obs.]

universalian.c: Universalian U`ni*ver*sa"li*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Universalism; Universalist. [R.]

universalism.c: Universalism U`ni*ver"sal*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. universalisme.] (Theol.) The doctrine or belief that all men will be saved, or made happy, in the future state.

universalist.c: Universalist U`ni*ver"sal*ist (?), a. Of or pertaining to Unversalists of their doctrines.

universalistic.c: Universalistic U`ni*ver`sal*is"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the whole; universal.

universality.c: Universality U`ni*ver*sal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Universalties (#). [Cf. F. universalité.] The quality or state of being universal; unlimited extension or application; generality; -- distinguished from particularity; as, the unversality of a proposition; the unversality of sin; the unversality of the Deluge.

universalize.c: Universalize U`ni*ver"sal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Universalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Universalizing (?).] [Cf. F. universaliser.] To make universal; to generalize. Coleridge.

universally.c: Universally U`ni*ver"sal*ly, adv. In a universal manner; without exception; as, God's laws are universally binding on his creatures.

universalness.c: Universalness U`ni*ver"sal*ness, n. The quality or state of being universal; universality.

universe.c: Universe U"ni*verse (?), n. [L. universum, from universus universal; unus one + vertere, versum, to turn, that is, turned into one, combined into one whole; cf. F. univers. See One, and Verse.] All created things viewed as constituting one system or whole; the whole body of things, or of phenomena; the to~ pa^n of the Greeks, the mundus of the Latins; the world; creation.

university.c: University U`ni*ver"si*ty (?), n.; pl. Universities (#). [OE. universite, L. universitas all together, the whole, the universe, a number of persons associated into one body, a society, corporation, fr. universus all together, universal: cf. F. université. See Universe.] 1. The universe; the whole. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
University extension U`ni*ver"si*ty ex*ten"sion. The extension of the advantages of university{3} instruction by means of lectures and classes at various centers.

universological.c: Universological U`ni*ver`so*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to universology.

universologist.c: Universologist U`ni*ver*sol"o*gist (?), n. One who is versed in universology.

universology.c: Universology U`ni*ver*sol"o*gy (?), n. [Universe + -logy.] The science of the universe, and the relations which it involves.

univocacy.c: Univocacy U*niv"o*ca*cy (?), n. The quality or state of being univocal. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

univocal.c: Univocal U*niv"o*cal (?), a. [L. univocus; unus one + vox, vocis, a voice, word. See One, and Voice.] 1. Having one meaning only; -- contrasted with equivocal.
Univocal U*niv"o*cal, n. 1. (Aristotelian Logic) A generic term, or a term applicable in the same sense to all the species it embraces.

univocally.c: Univocally U*niv"o*cal*ly, adv. In a univocal manner; in one term; in one sense; not equivocally.

univocation.c: Univocation U*niv`o*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. univocation.] Agreement of name and meaning. [Obs.] Whiston.

unjoin.c: Unjoin Un*join" (?), v. t. [1st un- + join.] To disjoin.

unjoint.c: Unjoint Un*joint" (?), v. t. [1st un- + joint.] To disjoint.

unjointed.c: Unjointed Un*joint"ed, a. [Properly p. p. of unjoint.] 1. Disjointed; unconnected; hence, incoherent. Shak.

unjust.c: Unjust Un*just" (?), a. 1. Acting contrary to the standard of right; not animated or controlled by justice; false; dishonest; as, an unjust man or judge.

unjustice.c: Unjustice Un*jus"tice (?), n. Want of justice; injustice. [Obs.] Hales.

unlisted.c: Unlisted Un*list"ed (?), a. Not listed; specif. (a) (New York Stock Exchange), admitted to quotation in the unlisted department, that is, admitted to be dealt in on the floor, but not to the “regular list.” (b) not listed in the telephone directory; -- of telephone numbers; as, an unlisted number.

unke.c: Unke ‖Un"ke (?), n. [G. unke.] (Zool.) A European aquatic toad (Bombinator igneus). Its back is dark; its belly is marked with crimson. Called also feuerkröte.

unked.c: Unked Un"ked (?), a. [Corrupted fr. uncouth, or OE. unkid; un- + p. p. of AS. cȳðan to make known, fr. cūð known. See Uncouth.] 1. Odd; strange; ugly; old; uncouth. [Prov. Eng.]

unkempt.c: Unkempt Un*kempt" (?; 215), a. [Pref. un- not + kempt, p. p. of kemb.] 1. Not combed; disheveled; as, an urchin with unkempt hair.

unkent.c: Unkent Un*kent" (?), a. [Un- knot + ken to know.] Unknown; strange. [Obs. or Scot.] W. Browne.

unketh.c: Unketh Un*keth" (?), a. Uncouth. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

unkind.c: Unkind Un*kind" (?), a. [See Kin kindred.] Having no race or kindred; childless. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
Unkind Un*kind", a. 1. Not kind; contrary to nature, or the law of kind or kindred; unnatural. [Obs.] “Such unkind abominations.” Chaucer.

unkindly.c: Unkindly Un*kind"ly, a. 1. Not kindly; unkind; ungracious.

unkindred.c: Unkindred Un*kin"dred (?), a. Not kindred; not of the same kin. [Obs.] Rowe. -- Un*kin"dred*ly, a.

unking.c: Unking Un*king" (?), v. t. [1st un- + king.] To cause to cease to be a king. [R.]

unkingship.c: Unkingship Un*king"ship, n. The quality or condition of being unkinged; abolition of monarchy. [Obs.]

unkiss.c: Unkiss Un*kiss" (?), v. t. [1st un- + king.] To cancel or annul what was done or sealed by a kiss; to cancel by a kiss. [Obs.]

unknight.c: Unknight Un*knight" (?), v. t. [1st un- + knight.] To deprive of knighthood. Fuller.

unknit.c: Unknit Un*knit" (?), v. t. [1st un- + knit.] To undo or unravel what is knitted together.

unknot.c: Unknot Un*knot" (?), v. t. [1st un- + knot.] To free from knots; to untie.

unknow.c: Unknow Un*know", a. [See Un- not, Know.] Unknown. [Obs.] “French of Paris was to her unknow.” Chaucer.

unknowledged.c: Unknowledged Un*knowl"edged (?), a. Not acknowledged or recognized. [Obs.]

unknown.c: Unknown Un*known" (?), a. Not known; not apprehended. -- Un*known"ness, n. [R.] Camden.

unlabored.c: Unlabored Un*la"bored (?), a. 1. Not produced by labor or toil. “Unlabored harvests.” Dryden.

unlade.c: Unlade Un*lade" v. t. [1st un- + lade.] 1. To take the load from; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship or a wagon.

unlaid.c: Unlaid Un*laid" (?), a. 1. Not laid or placed; not fixed. Hooker.

unland.c: Unland Un*land" (?), v. t. [1st un- + land.] To deprive of lands.

unlap.c: Unlap Un*lap" (?), v. t. [1st un- + lap.] To unfold. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unlash.c: Unlash Un*lash" (?), v. t. [1st un- + lash.] (Naut.) To loose, as that which is lashed or tied down.

unlatch.c: Unlatch Un*latch" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Unlatched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unlatching.] [1st un- + latch.] To open or loose by lifting the latch; as, to unlatch a door.

unlaugh.c: Unlaugh Un*laugh" (?), v. t. [1st un- + laugh.] To recall, as former laughter. [Obs. & R.] Sir T. More.

unlaw.c: Unlaw Un*law" (?), v. t. [1st un- + law.] 1. To deprive of the authority or character of law. [Obs.]
Unlaw Un*law" (?), n. [Pref. un- + law.] (Scots Law) (a) Any transgression or offense against the law. (b) A fine imposed as a penalty for violation of the law.

unlawed.c: Unlawed Un*lawed" (?), a. [Pref. un- + lawed, p. p. of lawe.] Not having the claws and balls of the forefeet cut off; -- said of dogs.

unlawful.c: Unlawful Un*law"ful (?), a. Not lawful; contrary to law. -- Un*law"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*law"ful*ness, n.

unlawlike.c: Unlawlike Un*law"like` (?), a. Not according to law; being or done in violation of law; unlawful. Milton.

unlay.c: Unlay Un*lay" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + lay.] (Naut.) To untwist; as, to unlay a rope.

unlearn.c: Unlearn Un*learn" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + learn.]

unlearned.c: Unlearned Un*learn"ed, a. [Pref. un- + learned.] 1. Not learned; untaught; uneducated; ignorant; illiterate.

unleash.c: Unleash Un*leash" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + leash.] To free from a leash, or as from a leash; to let go; to release; as, to unleash dogs.

unleavened.c: Unleavened Un*leav"ened (?), a. Not leavened; containing no leaven; as, unleavened bread.

unless.c: Unless Un*less" (?), conj. [Formerly, onles, onlesse, onlesse that, that is, in less, in a less case. See On, and Less.] Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious.

unlicked.c: Unlicked Un*licked" (?), a. Not licked; hence, not properly formed; ungainly. Cf. To lick into shape, under Lick, v. Shak.

unlike.c: Unlike Un*like" (?), a. 1. Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance; as, the cases are unlike.

unlikeliness.c: Unlikeliness Un*like"li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being unlikely.

unlikely.c: Unlikely Un*like"ly, a. 1. Not likely; improbable; not to be reasonably expected; as, an unlikely event; the thing you mention is very unlikely.
Unlikely Un*like"ly, adv. In an unlikely manner.

unliken.c: Unliken Un*lik"en (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + liken.] To make unlike; to dissimilate. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unlikeness.c: Unlikeness Un*like"ness, n. The quality or state of being unlike; want of resemblance; dissimilarity. Tennyson.

unlimber.c: Unlimber Un*lim"ber (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + limber.] (Mil.) To detach the limber from; as, to unlimber a gun.

unlimited.c: Unlimited Un*lim"it*ed, a. 1. Not limited; having no bounds; boundless; as, an unlimited expanse of ocean.

unline.c: Unline Un*line" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + line.] To take the lining out of; hence, to empty; as, to unline one's purse.

unlink.c: Unlink Un*link" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + link.] To separate or undo, as links; to uncoil; to unfasten. Shak.

unliquidated.c: Unliquidated Un*liq"ui*da`ted (?), a. Not liquidated; not exactly ascertained; not adjusted or settled.

unliquored.c: Unliquored Un*liq"uored (?), a. 1. Not moistened or wet with liquor; dry. “Unliquored coach.” Bp. Hall.

unlive.c: Unlive Un*live" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + live.] To??ve in a contrary manner, as a life; to live in a manner contrary to. [R.] Glanvill.

unlived.c: Unlived Un*lived" (?), a. [See 1st pref. Un-, and Life, Live.] Bereft or deprived of life. [Obs.] Shak.

unload.c: Unload Un*load" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + load.] 1. To take the load from; to discharge of a load or cargo; to disburden; as, to unload a ship; to unload a beast.
Unload Un*load", v. i. To perform the act of unloading anything; as, let unload now.

unloader.c: Unloader Un*load"er (?), n. One who, or that which, unloads; a device for unloading, as hay from a wagon.

unlocated.c: Unlocated Un*lo"ca*ted (?), a. 1. Not located or placed; not fixed in a place.

unlock.c: Unlock Un*lock" (?), v. t. [Cf. AS. unl?can. See 1st Un-, and Lock, v. t.] 1. To unfasten, as what is locked; as, to unlock a door or a chest.

unlodge.c: Unlodge Un*lodge" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + lodge.] To dislodge; to deprive of lodgment. Carew.

unlook.c: Unlook Un*look" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + look.] To recall or retract, as a look. [R.] Richardson.

unlooked.c: Unlooked Un*looked" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + looked.] Not observed or foreseen; unexpected; -- generally with for. “Unlooked success.” Denham.

unlookedfor.c: Unlooked-for Un*looked"-for (?), a. Not looked for; unexpected; as, an unlooked-for event.

unloose.c: Unloose Un*loose" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + loose.] To make loose; to loosen; to set free. Shak.
Unloose Un*loose", v. i. To become unfastened; to lose all connection or union.

unloosen.c: Unloosen Un*loos"en (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + loosen.] To loosen; to unloose.

unlord.c: Unlord Un*lord" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + lord.] To deprive of the rank or position of a lord. Milton.

unlorded.c: Unlorded Un*lord"ed, a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unlord.] Deprived of the rank of a lord.

unlove.c: Unlove Un*love" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + love.] To cease to love; to hate. [Obs.]

unlovely.c: Unlovely Un*love"ly (?), a. Not lovely; not amiable; possessing qualities that excite dislike; disagreeable; displeasing; unpleasant. -- Un*love"li*ness (#), n.

unluckily.c: Unluckily Un*luck"i*ly (?), adv. In an unlucky manner.

unluckiness.c: Unluckiness Un*luck"i*ness, n. Quality or state of being unlucky.

unlucky.c: Unlucky Un*luck"y (?), a. 1. Not lucky; not successful; unfortunate; ill-fated; unhappy; as, an unlucky man; an unlucky adventure; an unlucky throw of dice; an unlucky game.

unlust.c: Unlust Un*lust" (?), n. Listlessness; disinclination. [Obs.] “Idleness and unlust.” Chaucer.

unlute.c: Unlute Un*lute" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + lute.] To separate, as things cemented or luted; to take the lute or the clay from. Boyle.

unmade.c: Unmade Un*made" (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + made.] Not yet made or formed; as, an unmade grave. Shak.

unmagistrate.c: Unmagistrate Un*mag"is*trate (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + magistrate.] To divest of the office or authority of a magistrate. [Obs.] Milton.

unmaiden.c: Unmaiden Un*maid"en (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + maiden.] To ravish; to deflower. [Obs.]

unmake.c: Unmake Un*make" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + make.] To destroy the form and qualities of; to deprive of being; to uncreate.

unman.c: Unman Un*man" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + man.]

unmanacle.c: Unmanacle Un*man"a*cle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + manacle.] To free from manacles. Tennyson.

unmanhood.c: Unmanhood Un*man"hood (?), n. Absence or lack of manhood. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unmanned.c: Unmanned Un*manned" (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unman.] Deprived of manly qualities; deficient in vigor, strength, courage, etc.; weak; effeminate.

unmannerly.c: Unmannerly Un*man"ner*ly (?), a. Not mannerly; ill-bred; rude. -- adv. Uncivilly; rudely. -- Un*man"ner*li*ness (#), n.

unmantle.c: Unmantle Un*man"tle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mantle.] To divest of a mantle; to uncover.

unmarry.c: Unmarry Un*mar"ry (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + marry.] To annul the marriage of; to divorce. Milton.

unmartyr.c: Unmartyr Un*mar"tyr (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + martyr.] To degrade from the rank of a martyr. [Obs.] Fuller.

unmasculate.c: Unmasculate Un*mas"cu*late (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + masculate.] To emasculate. [Obs.] Fuller.

unmask.c: Unmask Un*mask" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mask.] To strip of a mask or disguise; to lay open; to expose.
Unmask Un*mask", v. i. To put off a mask. Shak.

unmasterable.c: Unmasterable Un*mas"ter*a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being mastered or subdued. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

unmaterial.c: Unmaterial Un`ma*te"ri*al (?), a. Not material; immaterial. [Obs.] Daniel.

unmeaning.c: Unmeaning Un*mean"ing (?), a. 1. Having no meaning or signification; as, unmeaning words.

unmeant.c: Unmeant Un*meant" (?), a. Not meant or intended; unintentional. Dryden.

unmeasurable.c: Unmeasurable Un*meas"ur*a*ble (?), a. Immeasurable. Swift. -- Un*meas"ur*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*meas"ur*a*bly, adv.

unmechanize.c: Unmechanize Un*mech"an*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mechanize.]

unmechanized.c: Unmechanized Un*mech"an*ized (?), a. [Pref. un- + mechanized.] Not mechanized. Paley.

unmeet.c: Unmeet Un*meet" (?), a. Not meet or fit; not proper; unbecoming; unsuitable; -- usually followed by for. “Unmeet for a wife.” Tennyson.

unmember.c: Unmember Un*mem"ber (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + member.] To deprive of membership, as in a church.

unmentionables.c: Unmentionables Un*men"tion*a*bles (?), n. pl. The breeches; trousers. [Jocose]

unmerchantable.c: Unmerchantable Un*mer"chant*a*ble (?), a. (Com.) Not merchantable; not fit for market; being of a kind, quality, or quantity that is unsalable. McElrath.

unmercied.c: Unmercied Un*mer"cied (?), a. [Pref. un- not + mercy.] Unmerciful; merciless. [Obs.] Drayton.

unmerciful.c: Unmerciful Un*mer"ci*ful (?), a. Not merciful; indisposed to mercy or grace; cruel; inhuman; merciless; unkind. -- Un*mer"ci*ful*ly, adv. -- Un*mer"ci*ful*ness, n.

unmerciless.c: Unmerciless Un*mer"ci*less, a. [Pref. un- (intensive) + merciless.] Utterly merciless. [Obs.] Joye.

unmew.c: Unmew Un*mew" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mew to confine.] To release from confinement or restraint. Keats.

unmingle.c: Unmingle Un*min"gle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mingle.] To separate, as things mixed. Bacon.

unmistakable.c: Unmistakable Un`mis*tak"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being mistaken or misunderstood; clear; plain; obvious; evident. -- Un`mis*tak"a*bly, adv.

unmitre.c: Unmitre Unmiter { Un*mi"ter, Un*mi"tre (?) }, v. t. [1st pref. un- + miter.] To deprive of a miter; to depose or degrade from the rank of a bishop. Milton.

unmould.c: Unmould Unmold { Un*mold", Un*mould" } (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mold.] To change the form of; to reduce from any form. “Unmolding reason's mintage.” Milton.

unmoneyed.c: Unmoneyed Un*mon"eyed (?), a. Destitute of money; not rich. [Written also unmonied.] Shenstone.

unmonopolize.c: Unmonopolize Un`mo*nop"o*lize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + monopolize.] To recover or release from the state of being monopolized. [R.]

unmoor.c: Unmoor Un*moor" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + moor.] (Naut.) (a) To cause to ride with one anchor less than before, after having been moored by two or more anchors. (b) To loose from anchorage. See Moor, v. t.
Unmoor Un*moor", v. i. To weigh anchor. Sir W. Scott.

unmoral.c: Unmoral Un*mor"al (?), a. Having no moral perception, quality, or relation; involving no idea of morality; -- distinguished from both moral and immoral. -- Un`mo*ral"i*ty (#), n.

unmoralized.c: Unmoralized Un*mor"al*ized (?), a. Not restrained or tutored by morality. Norris.

unmorrised.c: Unmorrised Un*mor"rised (?), a. Not arrayed in the dress of a morris dancer. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

unmortise.c: Unmortise Un*mor"tise (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + mortise.] To loosen, unfix, or separate, as things mortised together. Tennyson.

unmosaic.c: Un-Mosaic Un`-Mo*sa"ic (?), a. Not according to Moses; unlike Moses or his works.

unmothered.c: Unmothered Un*moth"ered (?), [1st pref. un- + mother.] Deprived of a mother; motherless.

unmovable.c: Unmovable Un*mov"a*ble (?), a. Immovable. “Steadfast, unmovable.” 1 Cor. xv. 58. Locke.

unmoved.c: Unmoved Un*moved" (?), a. Not moved; fixed; firm; unshaken; calm; apathetic. -- Un*mov"ed*ly, adv.

unmuffle.c: Unmuffle Un*muf"fle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + muffle.]

unmuzzle.c: Unmuzzle Un*muz"zle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + muzzle.] To loose from a muzzle; to remove a muzzle from.

unnail.c: Unnail Un*nail" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nail.] To remove the nails from; to unfasten by removing nails.

unnapped.c: Unnapped Un*napped" (?), a. Finished without a nap.

unnatural.c: Unnatural Un*nat"u*ral (?; 135), a. Not natural; contrary, or not conforming, to the order of nature; being without natural traits; as, unnatural crimes.

unnaturalize.c: Unnaturalize Un*nat"u*ral*ize (?), v. t. To make unnatural. [R.] Hales.

unnature.c: Unnature Un*na"ture (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nature.] To change the nature of; to invest with a different or contrary nature. [Obs.]
Unnature Un*na"ture, n. [Pref. un- not + nature.] The contrary of nature; that which is unnatural. [R.]

unnear.c: Unnear Un*near" (?), prep. Not near; not close to; at a distance from. [Obs.] Davies (Muse's Sacrifice).

unnecessary.c: Unnecessary Un*nec"es*sa*ry (?), a. Not necessary; not required under the circumstances; unless; needless; as, unnecessary labor, care, or rigor. -- Un*nec"es*sa*ri*ly (#), adv. -- Un*nec"es*sa*ri*ness, n.

unnecessity.c: Unnecessity Un`ne*ces"si*ty (?), n. The state of being unnecessary; something unnecessary. [Obs.]

unneighbored.c: Unneighbored Un*neigh"bored (?), a. Being without neigbors. Cowper.

unneighborly.c: Unneighborly Un*neigh"bor*ly (?), a. Not neighborly; distant; reserved; solitary; exclusive. -- adv. Not in a neighborly manner. Shak.

unnerve.c: Unnerve Un*nerve" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nerve.] To deprive of nerve, force, or strength; to weaken; to enfeeble; as, to unnerve the arm.

unnest.c: Unnest Un*nest (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nest.] To eject from a nest; to unnestle. [R.] T. Adams.

unnestle.c: Unnestle Un*nes"tle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nestle.] Same as Unnest. [R.]

unnethes.c: Unnethes Unnethe { Un*nethe" (?), Un*nethes" (?), } adv. With difficulty. See Uneath. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unnooked.c: Unnooked Un*nooked" (?), a. Without nooks and corners; guileless. [Obs.] “Unnooked simplicity.” Marston.

unnotify.c: Unnotify Un*no"ti*fy (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + notify.] To retract or withdraw a notice of. Walpole.

unnumbered.c: Unnumbered Un*num"bered (?), a. Not numbered; not counted or estimated; innumerable. Dryden.

unnumerable.c: Unnumerable Un*nu"mer*a*ble (?), a. Innumerable. [Obs.] “An unnumerable multitude.” Udall.

unnun.c: Unnun Un*nun" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + nun.] To remove from condition of being a nun. [R.]

unobservance.c: Unobservance Un`ob*serv"ance (?), n. Want or neglect of observance; inobservance. Whitlock.

unobtrusive.c: Unobtrusive Un`ob*tru"sive (?), a. Not obtrusive; not presuming; modest. -- Un`ob*tru"sive*ly, adv. -- Un`ob*tru"sive*ness, n.

unoil.c: Unoil Un*oil" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + oil.] To remove the oil from. Dryden.

unoperative.c: Unoperative Un*op"er*a*tive (?), a. Producing no effect; inoperative. [Obs.] South.

unoperculated.c: Unoperculated Un`o*per"cu*la`ted (?), a. Destitute of an operculum, or cover.

unorder.c: Unorder Un*or"der (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + order.] To countermand an order for. [R.]

unordinate.c: Unordinate Un*or"di*nate (?), a. Disorderly; irregular; inordinate. [R.] -- Un*or"di*nate*ly, adv. [R.]

unorganized.c: Unorganized Un*or"gan*ized (?), a. Not organized; being without organic structure; specifically (Biol.), not having the different tissues and organs characteristic of living organisms, nor the power of growth and development; as, the unorganized ferments. See the Note under Ferment, n., 1.

unoriginated.c: Unoriginated Un`o*rig"i*na`ted (?), a. 1. Not originated; existing from all eternity. F. W. Newman.

unossified.c: Unossified Un*os"si*fied (?), a. (Zool.) Destitute of a bony structure.

unowned.c: Unowned Un*own"ed (?), a. [Pref. un- not + (sense 1) owned possessed, and (sense 2) owned granted, acknowledged.]

unpack.c: Unpack Un*pack" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pack.]

unpaganize.c: Unpaganize Un*pa"gan*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + paganize.] To cause to cease to be pagan; to divest of pagan character. [R.] Cudworth.

unpaint.c: Unpaint Un*paint" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + paint.] To remove the paint from; to efface, as a painting. Parnell.

unpaired.c: Unpaired Un*paired (?), a. Not paired; not suited or matched.

unpalped.c: Unpalped Un*palped" (?), a. (Zool.) Destitute of a palp.

unpannel.c: Unpannel Un*pan"nel (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pannel.] To take the saddle off; to unsaddle. [Obs.] Jervas.

unparadise.c: Unparadise Un*par"a*dise (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + paradise.] To deprive of happiness like that of paradise; to render unhappy. [R.] Young.

unparagoned.c: Unparagoned Un*par"a*goned (?), a. Having no paragon or equal; matchless; peerless. [R.]

unparalleled.c: Unparalleled Un*par"al*leled (?), a. Having no parallel, or equal; unequaled; unmatched.

unparched.c: Unparched Un*parched" (?), a. [Pref. un- not (intensive) parched.] Dried up; withered by heat. [Obs.] “My tongue... unparched.” Crashaw.

unpardonable.c: Unpardonable Un*par"don*a*ble (?), a. Not admitting of pardon or forgiveness; inexcusable.

unparented.c: Unparented Un*par"ent*ed (?), a. Having no parent, or no acknowledged parent. [R.]

unparliamentary.c: Unparliamentary Un*par`lia*men"ta*ry (?), a. Not parliamentary; contrary to the practice of parliamentary bodies. -- Un*par`lia*men"ta*ri*ness (#), n.

unpartial.c: Unpartial Un*par"tial (?), a. Impartial. [Obs.] Bp. Sanderson. -- Un*par"tial*ly, adv. [Obs.] Hooker.

unpassable.c: Unpassable Un*pass"a*ble (?), a. Impassable. E. A. Freeman. -- Un*pass"a*ble*ness, n. Evelyn.

unpassionate.c: Unpassionate Un*pas"sion*ate (?), a. Not passionate; dispassionate. -- Un*pas"sion*ate*ly, adv.

unpastor.c: Unpastor Un*pas"tor (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pastor.] To cause to be no longer pastor; to deprive of pastorship. [R.] Fuller.

unpathed.c: Unpathed Un*pathed" (?), a. Not having a path. Shak.

unpathwayed.c: Unpathwayed Un*path"wayed` (?), a. Pathless. [R.] “The smooth, unpathwayed plain.” Wordsworth.

unpaved.c: Unpaved Un*paved" (?), a. 1. Not paved; not furnished with a pavement. Hakewill.

unpay.c: Unpay Un*pay" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pay.] To undo, take back, or annul, as a payment. Shak.

unpeace.c: Unpeace Un*peace" (?), n. Absence or lack of peace. [Obs.] Testament of Love.

unpedigreed.c: Unpedigreed Un*ped"i*greed (?), a. Not distinguished by a pedigree. [R.] Pollok.

unpeeled.c: Unpeeled Un*peeled (?), a. 1. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + peel.] Thoroughly stripped; pillaged. [Obs.] Shak.

unpeerable.c: Unpeerable Un*peer"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of having a peer, or equal.

unpeered.c: Unpeered Un*peered (?), a. Having no peer; unequaled; unparalleled. “Unpeered excellence.” Marston.

unpeg.c: Unpeg Un*peg" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + peg.] To remove a peg or pegs from; to unfasten; to open. Shak.

unpen.c: Unpen Un*pen" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pen.] To release from a pen or from confinement. “If a man unpens another's water.” Blackstone.

unpeople.c: Unpeople Un*peo"ple (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + people.] To deprive of inhabitants; to depopulate. Shak.

unperegal.c: Unperegal Un`per*e"gal (?), a. [Pref. un- not + peregal.] Unequal. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unperfect.c: Unperfect Un*per"fect (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + perfect.] To mar or destroy the perfection of. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Unperfect Un*per"fect (?), a. [Pref. un- + perfect.] Imperfect. [Obs.] Holland. -- Un*per"fect*ly, adv. [Obs.] Hales. -- Un*per"fect*ness, n. [Obs.]

unperfection.c: Unperfection Un`per*fec"tion (?), n. Want of perfection; imperfection. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unperplex.c: Unperplex Un`per*plex" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + perplex.] To free from perplexity. [R.] Donne.

unpersuasion.c: Unpersuasion Un`per*sua"sion (?), n. The state of not being persuaded; disbelief; doubt. [R.] Abp. Leighton.

unpervert.c: Unpervert Un`per*vert (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pervert.] To free from perversion; to deliver from being perverted; to reconvert. [Obs.]

unphilosophize.c: Unphilosophize Un`phi*los"o*phize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + philosophize.] To degrade from the character of a philosopher. [R.] Pope.

unpick.c: Unpick Un*pick (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + pick.] To pick out; to undo by picking.

unpicked.c: Unpicked Un*picked" (?), a. [Properly p. p. of unpick.] Picked out; picked open.

unpin.c: Unpin Un*pin" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pin.] To loose from pins; to remove the pins from; to unfasten; as, to unpin a frock; to unpin a frame.

unpinion.c: Unpinion Un*pin"ion (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pinion.] To loose from pinions or manacles; to free from restraint. Goldsmith.

unpitious.c: Unpitious Un*pi"tious (?), a. 1. Impious; wicked. [Obs.] “The life of the unpitous.” Wyclif (Prov. xv. 8).

unplaid.c: Unplaid Un*plaid" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + plaid.] To deprive of a plaid.

unplained.c: Unplained Un*plained" (?), a. Not deplored or bewailed; unlamented. [Obs.] Spenser.

unplat.c: Unplat Un*plat" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + plat.] To take out the folds or twists of, as something previously platted; to unfold; to unwreathe.

unplausive.c: Unplausive Un*plau"sive (?), a. Not approving; disapproving. [Obs.] Shak.

unpleaded.c: Unpleaded Un*plead"ed (?), a. 1. Not used as a plea; not urged; as, an unpleaded excuse.

unpleasant.c: Unpleasant Un*pleas"ant (?), a. Not pleasant; not amiable or agreeable; displeasing; offensive. -- Un*pleas"ant*ly, adv. -- Un*pleas"ant*ness, n.

unpleasive.c: Unpleasive Un*pleas"ive (?), a. Unpleasant. [Obs.] “An unpleasive passion.” Bp. Hall.

unpleat.c: Unpleat Un*pleat" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pleat.] To remove the plaits of; to smooth. W. Browne.

unplight.c: Unplight Un*plight" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + plight.] To unfold; to lay open; to explain. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unplumb.c: Unplumb Un*plumb" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + plumb.] To deprive of lead, as of a leaden coffin. [R.] Burke.

unplume.c: Unplume Un*plume" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + plume.] To strip of plumes or feathers; hence, to humiliate.

unpoised.c: Unpoised Un*poised" (?), a. 1. Not poised or balanced.

unpoison.c: Unpoison Un*poi"son (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + poison.] To remove or expel poison from. [Obs.] South.

unpolicied.c: Unpolicied Un*pol"i*cied (?), a. 1. Not having civil polity, or a regular form of government.

unpolish.c: Unpolish Un*pol"ish (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + polish.] To deprive of polish; to make impolite.

unpolite.c: Unpolite Un`po*lite" (?), a. Not polite; impolite; rude. -- Un`po*lite"ly, adv. -- Un`po*lite"ness, n.

unpolled.c: Unpolled Un*polled" (?), a. Not polled. Specifically: (a) Not enumerated or registered; as, an unpolled vote or voter. (b) Not plundered. [Obs.] “Unpoll'd Arabian wealth.” Fanshawe.

unpope.c: Unpope Un*pope" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pope.] 1. To divest of the character, office, or authority of a pope.

unportunate.c: Unportunate Un*por"tu*nate (?), a. Importunate; troublesome with requests. [Obs.] Golden Boke.

unportuous.c: Unportuous Un*por"tu*ous (?), a. Having no ports. [Obs.] “An unportuous coast.” Burke.

unpossess.c: Unpossess Un`pos*sess" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + possess.] To be without, or to resign, possession of. [Obs.]

unpower.c: Unpower Un*pow"er (?), n. Want of power; weakness. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

unpowerful.c: Unpowerful Un*pow"er*ful (?), a. Not powerful; weak. Cowley.

unpractical.c: Unpractical Un*prac"ti*cal (?), a. Not practical; impractical. “Unpractical questions.” H. James.

unpraise.c: Unpraise Un*praise" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + praise.] To withhold praise from; to deprive of praise. [R.]

unpray.c: Unpray Un*pray (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pray.] To revoke or annul by prayer, as something previously prayed for. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

unprayable.c: Unprayable Un*pray"a*ble (?), a. Not to be influenced or moved by prayers; obdurate. [R.] Wyclif.

unprayed.c: Unprayed Un*prayed" (?), a. [With for.] Not prayed for. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

unpreach.c: Unpreach Un*preach" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + preach.] To undo or overthrow by preaching. [R.] De Foe.

unprecedented.c: Unprecedented Un*prec"e*dent*ed (?), a. Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled. -- Un*prec"e*dent*ed*ly, adv.

unpredict.c: Unpredict Un`pre*dict" (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + predict.] To retract or falsify a previous prediction. Milton.

unprejudiced.c: Unprejudiced Un*prej"u*diced (?), a. 1. Not prejudiced; free from undue bias or prepossession; not preoccupied by opinion; impartial; as, an unprejudiced mind; an unprejudiced judge.

unprelated.c: Unprelated Un*prel"a*ted (?), a. [1st pref. un- + prelate.] Deposed from the office of prelate.

unprevented.c: Unprevented Un`pre*vent"ed (?), a. 1. Not prevented or hindered; as, unprevented sorrows. Shak.

unpriced.c: Unpriced Un*priced" (?), a. Not priced; being without a fixed or certain value; also, priceless. “Amethyst unpriced.” Neale (Rhythm of St. Bernard).

unpriest.c: Unpriest Un*priest" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + priest.] To deprive of priesthood; to unfrock. [R.] Milton.

unprince.c: Unprince Un*prince" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + prince.] To deprive of the character or authority of a prince; to divest of principality of sovereignty. [R.] Swift.

unprinciple.c: Unprinciple Un*prin"ci*ple (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + principle.] To destroy the moral principles of. [R.]

unprincipled.c: Unprincipled Un*prin"ci*pled (?), a. [Pref. un- not + principled.] Being without principles; especially, being without right moral principles; also, characterized by absence of principle. -- Un*prin"ci*pled*ness, n.

unprison.c: Unprison Un*pris"on (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + prison.] To take or deliver from prison.

unprizable.c: Unprizable Un*priz"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not prized or valued; being without value. [Obs.]

unprobably.c: Unprobably Un*prob"a*bly (?), adv. [Pref. un- not + probably.] Improbably.
Unprobably Un*prob"a*bly, adv. [Un- + L. probabilis approvable, fr. probare to approve. Cf. Probable.] In a manner not to be approved of; improperly. [Obs. & R.]

unproficiency.c: Unproficiency Un`pro*fi"cien*cy (?), n. Want of proficiency or improvement. Bp. Hall.

unprofit.c: Unprofit Un*prof"it (?), n. Want of profit; unprofitableness. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unpromise.c: Unpromise Un*prom"ise (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + promise.] To revoke or annul, as a promise. Chapman.

unprop.c: Unprop Un*prop" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + prop.] To remove a prop or props from; to deprive of support.

unproper.c: Unproper Un*prop"er (?), a. Not proper or peculiar; improper. [Obs.] -- Un*prop"er*ly, adv. [Obs.]

unproselyte.c: Unproselyte Un*pros"e*lyte (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + proselyte.] To convert or recover from the state of a proselyte. Fuller.

unprotestantize.c: Unprotestantize Un*prot"es*tant*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + protestantize.] To render other than Protestant; to cause to change from Protestantism to some other form of religion; to deprive of some Protestant feature or characteristic.

unprovide.c: Unprovide Un`pro*vide (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + provide.] To deprive of necessary provision; to unfurnish.

unprovident.c: Unprovident Un*prov"i*dent (?), a. Improvident. [Obs.] “Who for thyself art so unprovident.” Shak.

unprudential.c: Unprudential Un`pru*den"tial (?), a. Imprudent. [Obs.] “The most unwise and unprudential act.” Milton.

unpucker.c: Unpucker Un*puck"er (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + pucker.] To smooth away the puckers or wrinkles of.

unqualify.c: Unqualify Un*qual"i*fy (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + quality.] To disqualify; to unfit. Swift.

unqualitied.c: Unqualitied Un*qual"i*tied (?), a. [1st pref. un- + quality.] Deprived of the usual faculties. [Obs.] Shak.

unqueen.c: Unqueen Un*queen" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + queen.] To divest of the rank or authority of queen. Shak.

unquestionable.c: Unquestionable Un*ques"tion*a*ble (?), a. 1. Not questionable; as, an unquestionable title.

unquestioned.c: Unquestioned Un*ques"tioned (?), a. 1. Not called in question; not doubted.

unquiet.c: Unquiet Un*qui"et (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + quiet.] To disquiet. [Obs.] Ld. Herbert.
Unquiet Un*qui"et, a. [Pref. un- + quiet.] Not quiet; restless; uneasy; agitated; disturbed. -- Un*qui"et*ly, adv. -- Un*qui"et*ness, n.

unravel.c: Unravel Un*rav"el (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + ravel.]
Unravel Un*rav"el, v. i. To become unraveled, in any sense.

unravelment.c: Unravelment Un*rav"el*ment (?), n. The act of unraveling, or the state of being unraveled.

unread.c: Unread Un*read" (?), a. 1. Not read or perused; as, an unread book. Hooker.

unreadiness.c: Unreadiness Un*read"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being unready.

unready.c: Unready Un*read"y (?), a. 1. Not ready or prepared; not prompt; slow; awkward; clumsy. Dryden.
Unready Un*read"y, v. t. [1st pref. un- + ready.] To undress. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

unreal.c: Unreal Un*re"al (?), a. Not real; unsubstantial; fanciful; ideal.

unreality.c: Unreality Un`re*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unreal; want of reality.

unrealize.c: Unrealize Un*re"al*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + realize.] To make unreal; to idealize.

unreally.c: Unreally Un*re"al*ly, adv. In an unreal manner; ideally.

unreason.c: Unreason Un*rea"son (?), n. [Pref. un- not + reason.] Want of reason; unreasonableness; absurdity.
Unreason Un*rea"son, v. t. [1st pref. un- + reason.] To undo, disprove, or refute by reasoning. [Obs.]

unreasonable.c: Unreasonable Un*rea"son*a*ble (?), a. Not reasonable; irrational; immoderate; exorbitant. -- Un*rea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*rea"son*a*bly, adv.

unreasoned.c: Unreasoned Un*rea"soned (?), a. Not supported by reason; unreasonable. “Unreasoned habits.” Burke.

unreave.c: Unreave Un*reave" (?), v. t. [See Unreeve.] To unwind; to disentangle; to loose. [Obs.] Spenser.

unreaved.c: Unreaved Un*reaved" (?), a. [See Un- not, and, for -reaved, cf. Rive, and AS. reófan to break.] Not torn, split, or parted; not torn to pieces. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

unrebukable.c: Unrebukable Un`re*buk"a*ble (?), a. Not deserving rebuke or censure; blameless. 1 Tim. vi. 14.

unrecuring.c: Unrecuring Un`re*cur"ing (?), a. Incurable. [Obs.] “Some unrecuring wound.” Shak.

unreeve.c: Unreeve Un*reeve" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + reeve, v. t.] (Naut.) To withdraw, or take out, as a rope from a block, thimble, or the like.

unreformation.c: Unreformation Un*ref`or*ma"tion (?), n. Want of reformation; state of being unreformed. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

unregeneracy.c: Unregeneracy Un`re*gen"er*a*cy (?), n. The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill.

unregenerated.c: Unregenerated Unregenerate { Un`re*gen"er*ate (?), Un`re*gen"er*a`ted (?), } a. Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.

unrein.c: Unrein Un*rein" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + rein.] To loosen the reins of; to remove restraint from. Addison.

unrelenting.c: Unrelenting Un`re*lent"ing (?), a. Not relenting; unyielding; rigid; hard; stern; cruel. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ly, adv. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ness, n.

unreliable.c: Unreliable Un`re*li"a*ble (?), a. Not reliable; untrustworthy. See Reliable. -- Un`re*li"a*ble*ness, n.

unremembrance.c: Unremembrance Un`re*mem"brance (?), n. Want of remembrance; forgetfulness. I. Watts.

unremitting.c: Unremitting Un`re*mit"ting (?), a. Not remitting; incessant; continued; persevering; as, unremitting exertions. Cowper. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ly, adv. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ness, n.

unremorseless.c: Unremorseless Un`re*morse"less (?), a. [Pref. un- not (intensive) + remorseless.] Utterly remorseless. [Obs. & R.] “Unremorseless death.” Cowley.

unreprievable.c: Unreprievable Un`re*priev"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being reprieved. Shak.

unreproachable.c: Unreproachable Un`re*proach"a*ble (?), a. Not liable to be reproached; irreproachable.

unreserve.c: Unreserve Un`re*serve" (?), n. Absence of reverse; frankness; freedom of communication. T. Warton.

unreserved.c: Unreserved Un`re*served" (?), a. Not reserved; not kept back; not withheld in part; unrestrained. -- Un`re*serv"ed*ly (#), adv. -- Un`re*serv"ed*ness, n.

unresistance.c: Unresistance Un`re*sist"ance (?), n. Nonresistance; passive submission; irresistance. Bp. Hall.

unresisted.c: Unresisted Un`re*sist"ed, a. 1. Not resisted; unopposed. Bentley.

unrespect.c: Unrespect Un`re*spect" (?), n. Disrespect. [Obs.] “Unrespect of her toil.” Bp. Hall.

unresponsible.c: Unresponsible Un`re*spon"si*ble (?), a. Irresponsible. Fuller. -- Un`re*spon"si*ble*ness, n.

unrest.c: Unrest Un*rest" (?), n. Want of rest or repose; unquietness; sleeplessness; uneasiness; disquietude.

unrestraint.c: Unrestraint Un`re*straint" (?), n. Freedom from restraint; freedom; liberty; license.

unresty.c: Unresty Un*rest"y (?), a. Causing unrest; disquieting; as, unresty sorrows. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unrevenued.c: Unrevenued Un*rev"e*nued (?), a. Not furnished with a revenue. [R.] Milton.

unreverence.c: Unreverence Un*rev"er*ence (?), n. Absence or lack of reverence; irreverence. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unriddle.c: Unriddle Un*rid"dle (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + riddle.] To read the riddle of; to solve or explain; as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay.

unriddler.c: Unriddler Un*rid"dler (?), n. One who unriddles. Lovelace.

unrig.c: Unrig Un*rig" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + rig.] (Naut.) To strip of rigging; as, to unrig a ship. Totten.

unright.c: Unright Un*right" (?), a. [AS. unriht. See Un- not, and Right.] Not right; wrong. [Obs.] Gower.
Unright Un*right" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + right.] To cause (something right) to become wrong. [Obs.] Gower.

unrighteous.c: Unrighteous Un*right"eous (?), a. [OE. unrightwise, AS. unrihtwīs. See Un- not, and Righteous.]

unrightwise.c: Unrightwise Un*right"wise` (?), a. Unrighteous. [Obs.] Wyclif. -- Un*right"wise`ly, adv. [Obs.]

unringed.c: Unringed Un*ringed" (?), a. Not having a ring, as in the nose. “Pigs unringed.” Hudibras.

unrioted.c: Unrioted Un*ri"ot*ed (?), a. Free from rioting. [Obs.] “A chaste, unrioted house.” May (Lucan).

unrip.c: Unrip Un*rip" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- (intensive) + rip.] To rip; to cut open. Bacon.

unripe.c: Unripe Un*ripe" (?), a. 1. Not ripe; as, unripe fruit.

unripeness.c: Unripeness Un*ripe"ness, n. Quality or state of being unripe.

unrivaled.c: Unrivaled Un*ri"valed (?), a. Having no rival; without a competitor; peerless. [Spelt also unrivalled.] Pope.

unrivet.c: Unrivet Un*riv"et (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + rivet.] To take out, or loose, the rivets of; as, to unrivet boiler plates.

unrobe.c: Unrobe Un*robe" (?), v. t. & i. [1st pref. un- + robe.] To disrobe; to undress; to take off the robes.

unroll.c: Unroll Un*roll" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + roll.] [Written also unrol.]

unromanized.c: Un-Romanized Un-Ro"man*ized (?), a. 1. Not subjected to Roman arms or customs. J. Whitaker.

unroof.c: Unroof Un*roof" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + roof.] To strip off the roof or covering of, as a house. Shak.

unroofed.c: Unroofed Un*roofed" (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of unroof.] Stripped of a roof, or similar covering.

unroost.c: Unroost Un*roost" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + roost.] To drive from the roost. Shak.

unroot.c: Unroot Un*root" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + root.] To tear up by the roots; to eradicate; to uproot.
Unroot Un*root", v. i. To be torn up by the roots. Beau. & Fl.

unrude.c: Unrude Un*rude" (?), a. [Pref. un- + rude. In sense 2 un- is intensive.]

unruffle.c: Unruffle Un*ruf"fle (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + ruffle.] To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.

unruffled.c: Unruffled Un*ruf"fled (?), a. [Pref. un- not + ruffled.] Not ruffled or agitated; smooth; calm; tranquil; quiet.

unruinated.c: Unruinated Unruinate { Un*ru"in*ate (?), Un*ru"in*a`ted (?), } a. Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] “Unruinated towers.” Bp. Hall.

unruled.c: Unruled Un*ruled" (?), a. 1. Not governed or controlled. “Unruled and undirected.” Spenser.

unruliment.c: Unruliment Un*rul"i*ment (?), n. Unruliness. [Obs.] “Breaking forth with rude unruliment.” Spenser.

unruliness.c: Unruliness Un*rul"i*ness, n. Quality or state unruly.

unruly.c: Unruly Un*rul"y (?), a. [Compar. Unrulier (?), superl. Unruliest.] [Pref. un- not + rule. Cf. Ruly.] Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct.

unrumple.c: Unrumple Un*rum"ple (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + rumple.] To free from rumples; to spread or lay even,

unsacrament.c: Unsacrament Un*sac"ra*ment (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sacrament.] To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy; as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. [Obs.]

unsad.c: Unsad Un*sad" (?), a. [AS. unsæd unsated, insatiable. See Un- not, and Sad.] Unsteady; fickle. [Obs.]

unsadden.c: Unsadden Un*sad"den (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sadden.] To relieve from sadness; to cheer. [R.] Whitlock.

unsaddle.c: Unsaddle Un*sad"dle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + saddle.]

unsadness.c: Unsadness Un*sad"ness, n. [From Unsad.] Infirmity; weakness. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unsafety.c: Unsafety Un*safe"ty (?), n. The quality or state of being in peril; absence of safety; insecurity. Bacon.

unsaint.c: Unsaint Un*saint" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + saint.] To deprive of saintship; to deny sanctity to. [R.] South.

unsaintly.c: Unsaintly Un*saint"ly, a. Unbecoming to a saint. Gauden.

unsalable.c: Unsalable Un*sal"a*ble (?), a. Not salable; unmerchantable. -- n. That which can not be sold. Byron.

unsanctification.c: Unsanctification Un*sanc`ti*fi*ca"tion (?), n. Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.

unsatiability.c: Unsatiability Un*sa`ti*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being unsatiable; insatiability. [Obs.]

unsatiable.c: Unsatiable Un*sa"ti*a*ble (?), a. Insatiable. [Obs.] Hooker. -- Un*sa"ti*a*ble*ness, n. [Obs.] -- Un*sa"ti*a*bly, adv. [Obs.]

unsatiate.c: Unsatiate Un*sa"ti*ate (?), a. Insatiate. Dr. H. More.

unsaturated.c: Unsaturated Un*sat"u*ra`ted (?), a. 1. Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree; as, an unsaturated solution.

unsaturation.c: Unsaturation Un*sat`u*ra"tion (?), n. The quality or state of being unsaturated.

unsay.c: Unsay Un*say (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + say.] To recant or recall, as what has been said; to refract; to take back again; to make as if not said.

unscale.c: Unscale Un*scale" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + scale.] To divest of scales; to remove scales from.

unscapable.c: Unscapable Un*scap"a*ble (?), a. Not be escaped; inevitable. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unsceptred.c: Unsceptred Unsceptered { Un*scep"tered, Un*scep"tred } (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + sceptered.] Having no scepter.

unscience.c: Unscience Un*sci"ence (?), n. Want of science or knowledge; ignorance. [Obs.]

unscrew.c: Unscrew Un*screw" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + screw.] To draw the screws from; to loose from screws; to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.

unscrupulous.c: Unscrupulous Un*scru"pu*lous (?), a. Not scrupulous; unprincipled. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ly, adv. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ness, n.

unscutcheoned.c: Unscutcheoned Un*scutch"eoned (?), a. Destitute of an escutcheon. [R.] Pollock.

unseal.c: Unseal Un*seal" (ŭn*sēl"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + seal.] 1. To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed; as, to unseal a letter.

unseam.c: Unseam Un*seam (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + seam.] To open the seam or seams of; to rip; to cut; to cut open. Shak.

unsearchable.c: Unsearchable Un*search"a*ble (?), a. Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious.

unseason.c: Unseason Un*sea"son (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + season.]

unseasonable.c: Unseasonable Un*sea"son*a*ble (?), a. Not seasonable; being, done, or occurring out of the proper season; ill-timed; untimely; too early or too late; as, he called at an unseasonable hour; unseasonable advice; unseasonable frosts; unseasonable food. -- Un*sea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*sea"son*a*bly, adv.

unseat.c: Unseat Un*seat" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + seat.]

unseconded.c: Unseconded Un*sec"ond*ed (?), a. 1. Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted; as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded.

unsecret.c: Unsecret Un*se"cret (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + secret.] To disclose; to divulge. [Obs.] Bacon.
Unsecret Un*se"cret, a. [Pref. un- not + secret.] Not secret; not close; not trusty; indiscreet. [Obs.] “We are unsecret to ourselves.” Shak.

unsecularize.c: Unsecularize Un*sec"u*lar*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + secularize.] To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.

unseel.c: Unseel Un*seel" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + seel.] To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled; hence, to give light to; to enlighten. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

unseem.c: Unseem Un*seem" (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + seem.] Not to seem. [Obs.] Shak.

unseeming.c: Unseeming Un*seem"ing, a. Unbeseeming; not fit or becoming.

unseemliness.c: Unseemliness Un*seem"li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being unseemly; unbecomingness. Udall.

unseemly.c: Unseemly Un*seem"ly, a. Not seemly; unbecoming; indecent.
Unseemly Un*seem"ly, adv. In an unseemly manner.

unseen.c: Unseen Un*seen" (?), a. 1. Not seen or discovered.

unsely.c: Unsely Un*se"ly (?), a. [AS. uns?lig. See Un- not, and Silly.] Not blessed or happy; wretched; unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Un*se"li*ness, n. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unseminared.c: Unseminared Un*sem"i*nared (?), a. [See 1st Un-, and Semen.] Deprived of virility, or seminal energy; made a eunuch. [Obs.]

unsensed.c: Unsensed Un*sensed (?), a. Wanting a distinct meaning; having no certain signification. [R.] Puller.

unsensualize.c: Unsensualize Un*sen"su*al*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sensualize.] To elevate from the domain of the senses; to purify. Coleridge.

unseparable.c: Unseparable Un*sep"a*ra*ble (?), a. Inseparable. [Obs.] “In love unseparable.” Shak.

unservice.c: Unservice Un*serv"ice (?), n. Neglect of duty; idleness; indolence. [Obs.] Massinger.

unset.c: Unset Un*set" (?), a. Not set; not fixed or appointed.

unsettle.c: Unsettle Un*set"tle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + settle.] To move or loosen from a settled position or state; to unfix; to displace; to disorder; to confuse.
Unsettle Un*set"tle, v. i. To become unsettled or unfixed; to be disordered. Shak.

unsettledness.c: Unsettledness Un*set"tled*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being unsettled.

unsettlement.c: Unsettlement Un*set"tle*ment (?), n. The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled; disturbance. J. H. Newman.

unseven.c: Unseven Un*sev"en (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + seven.] To render other than seven; to make to be no longer seven. [Obs. & R.] “To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome.” Fuller.

unsew.c: Unsew Un*sew" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sew.] To undo, as something sewn, or something inclosed by sewing; to rip apart; to take out the stitches of.

unsex.c: Unsex Un*sex" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unsexed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Unsexing.] [1st pref. un- + sex.] To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.

unsexual.c: Unsexual Un*sex"u*al (?), a. Not sexual; not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De Quincey.

unshackle.c: Unshackle Un*shac"kle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shackle.] To loose from shackles or bonds; to set free from restraint; to unfetter. Addison.

unshakable.c: Unshakable Un*shak"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being shaken; firm; fixed. Shak. J. S. Mill.

unshale.c: Unshale Un*shale" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shale.] To strip the shale, or husk, from; to uncover. [Obs.]

unshape.c: Unshape Un*shape (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shape.] To deprive of shape, or of proper shape; to disorder; to confound; to derange. [R.] Shak.

unshapen.c: Unshapen Unshaped { Un*shaped" (?), Un*shap"en (?), } a. [Pref. un- not + shaped, shapen.] Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.

unsheathe.c: Unsheathe Un*sheathe" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sheath.] To deprive of a sheath; to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword.

unshed.c: Unshed Un*shed" (?), a. 1. Not parted or divided, as the hair. [Obs.] Spenser.

unshell.c: Unshell Un*shell" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shell.] To strip the shell from; to take out of the shell; to hatch.

unshelve.c: Unshelve Un*shelve" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shelve.] To remove from, or as from, a shelf.

unshent.c: Unshent Un*shent (?), a. Not shent; not disgraced; blameless. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

unsheriff.c: Unsheriff Un*sher"iff (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sheriff.] To depose from the office of sheriff. [R.]

unshet.c: Unshet Un*shet" (?), v. t. To unshut. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unshiftable.c: Unshiftable Un*shift"a*ble (?), a. 1. That may?ot be shifted.

unship.c: Unship Un*ship" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + ship.]

unshipment.c: Unshipment Un*ship"ment (?), n. The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped; displacement.

unshot.c: Unshot Un*shot" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shot.] To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun; to unload.
Unshot Un*shot", a. [Pref. un- + shot.] Not hit by a shot; also, not discharged or fired off.

unshout.c: Unshout Un*shout" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shout.] To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.

unshroud.c: Unshroud Un*shroud" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shroud.] To remove the shroud from; to uncover. P. Fletcher.

unshut.c: Unshut Un*shut" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shut.] To open, or throw open. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unshutter.c: Unshutter Un*shut"ter (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + shutter.] To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.

unsight.c: Unsight Un*sight" (?), a. Doing or done without sight; not seeing or examining. [Colloq.]

unsighted.c: Unsighted Un*sight"ed, a. 1. Not sighted, or seen. Suckling.

unsimplicity.c: Unsimplicity Un`sim*plic"i*ty (?), n. Absence of simplicity; artfulness. C. Kingsley.

unsin.c: Unsin Un*sin" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sin.] To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin; to make sinless. [Obs.] Feltham.

unsincere.c: Unsincere Un`sin*cere" (?), a. Not sincere or pure; insincere. [Obs.] Dryden. -- Un`sin*cere"ness, n. [Obs.]

unsincerity.c: Unsincerity Un`sin*cer"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unsincere or impure; insincerity. [Obs.] Boyle.

unsinew.c: Unsinew Un*sin"ew (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sinew.] To deprive of sinews or of strength. [R.] Dryden.

unsister.c: Unsister Un*sis"ter (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sister.] To separate, as sisters; to disjoin. [Poetic & R.] Tennyson.

unsisting.c: Unsisting Un*sist"ing (?), a. Unresisting. [Obs.] “The unsisting postern.” Shak.

unsitting.c: Unsitting Un*sit"ting (?), a. Not sitting well; unbecoming. [Obs.] “Unsitting words.” Sir T. More.

unskill.c: Unskill Un*skill" (?), n. Want of skill; ignorance; unskillfulness. [Obs.] Sylvester.

unslacked.c: Unslacked Un*slacked" (?), a. Not slacked; unslaked; as, unslacked lime.

unslaked.c: Unslaked Un*slaked" (?), a. Not slaked; unslacked; as, an unslaked thirst; unslaked lime.

unsling.c: Unsling Un*sling" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sling.] (Naut.) To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like; to release from the slings. Totten.

unsluice.c: Unsluice Un*sluice" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sluice.] To sluice; to open the sluice or sluices of; to let flow; to discharge. Dryden.

unsociability.c: Unsociability Un*so`cia*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being unsociable; unsociableness.

unsociable.c: Unsociable Un*so"cia*ble (?), a. Not sociable; not inclined to society; averse to companionship or conversation; solitary; reserved; as, an unsociable person or temper. -- Un*so"cia*ble*ness, n. -- Un*so"cia*bly, adv.

unsocket.c: Unsocket Un*sock"et (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + socket.] To loose or take from a socket.

unsoft.c: Unsoft Un*soft" (?; 115), a. Not soft; hard; coarse; rough. [Obs.] “Bristles of his beard unsoft.” Chaucer.
Unsoft Un*soft", adv. [AS. uns?fte. See Un- not, and Soft.] Not softly. [Obs.]

unsolder.c: Unsolder Un*sol"der (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + solder.] To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered; hence, to divide; to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.

unsoldiered.c: Unsoldiered Un*sol"diered (?; 106), a. Not equipped like a soldier; unsoldierlike. [Obs.] J. Fletcher.

unsolemnize.c: Unsolemnize Un*sol"em*nize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + solemnize.] To divest of solemnity.

unsonable.c: Unsonable Un*so"na*ble (?), a. [Pref. un- + L. sonabilis sounding, from sonare to sound.] Incapable of being sounded. [Obs.]

unsonsy.c: Unsonsy Un*son"sy (?), a. [See Un- not, and Soncy.] Not soncy (sonsy); not fortunate. [Scot.]

unsoot.c: Unsoot Un*soot" (?), a. [AS. unsw?te. See Un- not, and Sweet.] Not sweet. [Obs.] Spenser.

unsophisticated.c: Unsophisticated Unsophisticate { Un`so*phis"ti*cate (?), Un`so*phis"ti*ca`ted (?), } a. Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine.

unsorrowed.c: Unsorrowed Un*sor"rowed (?), a. Not sorrowed for; unlamented. Beau. & Fl.

unsorted.c: Unsorted Un*sort"ed (?), a. 1. Not sorted; not classified; as, a lot of unsorted goods.

unsoul.c: Unsoul Un*soul" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + soul.] To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. [R.] Shelton.

unsound.c: Unsound Un*sound" (?), a. Not sound; not whole; not solid; defective; infirm; diseased.

unspar.c: Unspar Un*spar" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spar.] To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

unsparing.c: Unsparing Un*spar"ing (?), a. [Pref. un- not + sparing, p. pr. of spare.]

unspeak.c: Unspeak Un*speak" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + speak.] To retract, as what has been spoken; to recant; to unsay. [R.] Shak.

unspeakable.c: Unspeakable Un*speak"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. un- not + speakable.] Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable grief or rage. -- Un*speak"a*bly, adv.

unspecialized.c: Unspecialized Un*spe"cial*ized (?), a. Not specialized; specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function; as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.

unsped.c: Unsped Un*sped" (?), a. Not performed; not dispatched. [Obs.] Garth.

unspell.c: Unspell Un*spell" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spell.] To break the power of (a spell); to release (a person) from the influence of a spell; to disenchant. [R.]

unsphere.c: Unsphere Un*sphere" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sphere.] To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.

unspike.c: Unspike Un*spike" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spike.] To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.

unspilt.c: Unspilt Un*spilt" (?), a. Not spilt or wasted; not shed.

unspin.c: Unspin Un*spin" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spin.] To untwist, as something spun.

unspirit.c: Unspirit Un*spir"it (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spirit.] To dispirit. [Obs.] Sir W. Temple.

unspiritalize.c: Unspiritalize Un*spir"it*al*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + spiritualize.] To deprive of spiritually. South.

unspleened.c: Unspleened Un*spleened" (?), a. [1st pref. un- + spleen.] Deprived of a spleen.

unspotted.c: Unspotted Un*spot"ted (?), a. Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation. -- Un*spot"ted*ness, n.

unsquire.c: Unsquire Un*squire" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + squire.] To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.

unstable.c: Unstable Un*sta"ble (?), a. [Cf. Instable.] Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or overthrow. -- Un*sta"ble*ness, n. Chaucer.

unstack.c: Unstack Un*stack" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + stack.] To remove, or take away, from a stack; to remove, as something constituting a stack.

unstarch.c: Unstarch Un*starch" (?), v. t. [Pref. un- + starch.] To free from starch; to make limp or pliable.

unstate.c: Unstate Un*state" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + state.] To deprive of state or dignity. [R.]

unsteel.c: Unsteel Un*steel" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + steel.] To disarm; to soften. Richardson.

unstep.c: Unstep Un*step" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + step.] (Naut.) To remove, as a mast, from its step.

unstick.c: Unstick Un*stick" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + stick.] To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.

unstill.c: Unstill Un*still" (?), a. [AS. unstille. See Un- not, and Still, a.] Not still; restless. [R.]

unsting.c: Unsting Un*sting" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sting.] To disarm of a sting; to remove the sting of. [R.] “Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice... will not unsting calamity.” J. M. Mason.

unstitch.c: Unstitch Un*stitch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + stitch.] To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.

unstock.c: Unstock Un*stock" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + stock.]

unstockinged.c: Unstockinged Un*stock"inged (?), a. 1. [Pref. un- not + stocking.] Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott.

unstop.c: Unstop Un*stop" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + stop.]

unstrain.c: Unstrain Un*strain" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + strain.] To relieve from a strain; to relax. B. Jonson.

unstrained.c: Unstrained Un*strained" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + strain.] 1. Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining; as, unstrained oil or milk.

unstratified.c: Unstratified Un*strat"i*fied (?), a. (Geol.) Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.

unstrength.c: Unstrength Un*strength" (?), n. Want of strength; weakness; feebleness. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unstring.c: Unstring Un*string" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + string.]

unstudied.c: Unstudied Un*stud"ied (?), a. 1. Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural.

unsubstantial.c: Unsubstantial Un`sub*stan"tial (?), a. Lacking in matter or substance; visionary; chimerical.

unsubstantialize.c: Unsubstantialize Un`sub*stan"tial*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + substantialize.] To make unsubstantial. [R.]

unsubstantiation.c: Unsubstantiation Un`sub*stan`ti*a"tion (?), n. [1st pref. un- + substantiation.] A divesting of substantiality.

unsucceedable.c: Unsucceedable Un`suc*ceed"a*ble (?), a. Not able or likely to succeed. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

unsuccess.c: Unsuccess Un`suc*cess" (?), n. Want of success; failure; misfortune. Prof. Wilson.

unsuccessful.c: Unsuccessful Un`suc*cess"ful (?), a. Not successful; not producing the desired event; not fortunate; meeting with, or resulting in, failure; unlucky; unhappy. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ly, adv. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ness, n.

unsufferable.c: Unsufferable Un*suf"fer*a*ble (?), a. Insufferable. [Obs.] Hooker. -- Un*suf"fer*a*bly, adv. [Obs.]

unsuffering.c: Unsuffering Un*suf"fer*ing, n. Inability or incapability of enduring, or of being endured. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unsufficiency.c: Unsufficiency Unsufficience { Un`suf*fi"cience (?), Un`suf*fi"cien*cy (?), } n. Insufficiency. [Obs.] Hooker.

unsuit.c: Unsuit Un*suit" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + suit.] Not to suit; to be unfit for. [Obs.] Quarles.

unsupportable.c: Unsupportable Un`sup*port"a*ble (?), a. Insupportable; unendurable. -- Un`sup*port"a*ble*ness, n. Bp. Wilkins. -- Un`sup*port"a*bly, adv.

unsurety.c: Unsurety Un*sure"ty (?), n. Want of surety; uncertainty; insecurity; doubt. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

unsuspicion.c: Unsuspicion Un`sus*pi"cion (?), n. The quality or state of being unsuspecting. Dickens.

unswaddle.c: Unswaddle Un*swad"dle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + swaddle.] To take a swaddle from; to unswathe.

unswathe.c: Unswathe Un*swathe" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + swathe.] To take a swathe from; to relieve from a bandage; to unswaddle. Addison.

unswayable.c: Unswayable Un*sway"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being swayed. Shak.

unswear.c: Unswear Un*swear" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + swear.] To recant or recall, as an oath; to recall after having sworn; to abjure. J. Fletcher.
Unswear Un*swear", v. i. To recall an oath. Spenser.

unsweat.c: Unsweat Un*sweat" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + sweat.] To relieve from perspiration; to ease or cool after exercise or toil. [R.] Milton.

unswell.c: Unswell Un*swell" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + swell.] To sink from a swollen state; to subside. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unsymmetrical.c: Unsymmetrical Un`sym*met"ric*al (?), a. 1. Wanting in symmetry, or due proportion of parts.

unsympathy.c: Unsympathy Un*sym"pa*thy (?), n. Absence or lack of sympathy.

untack.c: Untack Un*tack" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tack.] To separate, as what is tacked; to disjoin; to release.

untackle.c: Untackle Un*tac"kle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tackle.] To unbitch; to unharness. [Colloq.] Tusser.

untalked.c: Untalked Un*talked" (?), a. Not talked; not mentioned; -- often with of. Shak.

untangle.c: Untangle Un*tan"gle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tangle.] To loose from tangles or intricacy; to disentangle; to resolve; as, to untangle thread.

untappice.c: Untappice Un*tap"pice (?), v. i. [1st pref. un- + tappice.] to come out of concealment. [Obs.] Massinger.

untaste.c: Untaste Un*taste" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + taste.] To deprive of a taste for a thing. [R.] Daniel.

unteach.c: Unteach Un*teach" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + teach.]

unteam.c: Unteam Un*team" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + team.] To unyoke a team from. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

untemper.c: Untemper Un*tem"per (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + temper.] To deprive of temper, or of the proper degree of temper; to make soft.

untempter.c: Untempter Un*tempt"er (?; 215), n. One who does not tempt, or is not a tempter. [Obs.] Wyclif.

untenant.c: Untenant Un*ten"ant (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tenant.] To remove a tenant from. [R.] Coleridge.

untent.c: Untent Un*tent" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tent.] To bring out of a tent. [R.] Shak.

untented.c: Untented Un*tent"ed, a. [Pref. un- not + tent a covering.] Having no tent or tents, as a soldier or a field.
Untented Un*tent"ed, a. [Pref. un- not + tented, p. p. of tent to probe.] Not tended; not dressed. See 4th Tent.

unthank.c: Unthank Un*thank" (?), n. [AS. unpank. See Un- not, Thank.] No thanks; ill will; misfortune. [Obs.]

unthink.c: Unthink Un*think" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + think.] To recall or take back, as something thought. Shak.

unthinker.c: Unthinker Un*think"er (?), n. [Pref. un- + thinker.] A person who does not think, or does not think wisely.

unthinking.c: Unthinking Un*think"ing, a. 1. Not thinking; not heedful; thoughtless; inconsiderate; as, unthinking youth.

unthread.c: Unthread Un*thread" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + thread.]

unthrift.c: Unthrift Un"thrift` (?), n. 1. Want of thrift; unthriftiness; prodigality.

unthriftfully.c: Unthriftfully Un*thrift"ful*ly (?), adv. Not thriftily. [Obs.] “Unthriftfully spent.” Sir J. Cheke.

unthriftihood.c: Unthriftihood Unthriftihead { Un*thrift"i*head (?), Un*thrift"i*hood (?) }, n. Unthriftiness. [Obs.] Spenser.

unthriftiness.c: Unthriftiness Un*thrift"i*ness, n. The quality or state or being unthrifty; profuseness; lavishness. Udall.

unthrifty.c: Unthrifty Un*thrift"y (?), a. Not thrifty; profuse. Spenser.

unthrone.c: Unthrone Un*throne" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + throne.] To remove from, or as from, a throne; to dethrone. Milton.

untidy.c: Untidy Un*ti"dy (?), a. 1. Unseasonable; untimely. [Obs.] “Untidy tales.” Piers Plowman.

untie.c: Untie Un*tie" (?), v. t. [AS. untȳgan. See 1st Un-, and Tie, v. t.]
Untie Un*tie", v. i. To become untied or loosed.

untighten.c: Untighten Un*tight"en (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tighten.] To make less tight or tense; to loosen.

until.c: Until Un*til" (?), prep. [OE. until, ontil; un- (as in unto) + til till; cf. Dan. indtil, Sw. intill. See Unto, and Till, prep.]
Until Un*til", conj. As far as; to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; till. See Till, conj.

untile.c: Untile Un*tile" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tile.] To take the tiles from; to uncover by removing the tiles.

untimely.c: Untimely Un*time"ly, a. Not timely; done or happening at an unnatural, unusual, or improper time; unseasonable; premature; inopportune; as, untimely frosts; untimely remarks; an untimely death.
Untimely Un*time"ly, adv. Out of the natural or usual time; inopportunely; prematurely; unseasonably. “Let them know... what's untimely done.” Shak.

untimeous.c: Untimeous Un*time"ous (?), a. Untimely. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

untitled.c: Untitled Un*ti"tled (?), a. 1. Not titled; having no title, or appellation of dignity or distinction. Spenser.

unto.c: Unto Un"to (?), prep. [OE. unto; un- (only in unto, until) unto, as far as + to to; this un- is akin to AS.?? until, OFries. und OS. und until, conj. (cf. OS. unt? unto, OHG. unzi), Goth. und unto, until. See To, and cf. Until.]
Unto Un"to, conj. Until; till. [Obs.] “Unto this year be gone.” Chaucer.

untold.c: Untold Un*told" (?), a. 1. Not told; not related; not revealed; as, untold secrets.

untomb.c: Untomb Un*tomb" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tomb.] To take from the tomb; to exhume; to disinter. Fuller.

untongue.c: Untongue Un*tongue (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tongue.] To deprive of a tongue, or of voice. [Obs.] Fuller.

untooth.c: Untooth Un*tooth" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tooth.] To take out the teeth of. Cowper.

untowardly.c: Untowardly Un*to"ward*ly, a. Perverse; froward; untoward. “Untowardly tricks and vices.” Locke.

untraded.c: Untraded Un*trad"ed (?), a. 1. Not dealt with in trade; not visited for purposes of trade. [Obs.] Hakluyt

untrammeled.c: Untrammeled Un*tram"meled (?), a. Not hampered or impeded; free. [Written also untrammelled.]

untread.c: Untread Un*tread" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tread.] To tread back; to retrace. Shak.

untreasure.c: Untreasure Un*treas"ure (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + treasure.] To bring forth or give up, as things previously treasured. “The quaintness with which he untreasured, as by rote, the stores of his memory.” J. Mitford.

untreasured.c: Untreasured Un*treas"ured (?), a. 1. [Properly p. p. of untreasure.] Deprived of treasure. [Obs.] Shak.

untreatable.c: Untreatable Un*treat"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being treated; not practicable. [R.] Dr. H. More.

untrenched.c: Untrenched Un*trenched" (?), a. Being without trenches; whole; intact. [Obs.]

untressed.c: Untressed Un*tressed" (?), a. Not tied up in tresses; unarranged; -- said of the hair. Chaucer.

untrue.c: Untrue Un*true" (?), a. 1. Not true; false; contrary to the fact; as, the story is untrue.
Untrue Un*true, adv. Untruly. [Obs. or Poetic] Chaucer.

untruism.c: Untruism Un*tru"ism (?), n. Something not true; a false statement. [Recent & R.] A. Trollope.

untrunked.c: Untrunked Un*trunked" (?), a. [1st pref. un- + trunk.] Separated from its trunk or stock. [Obs.]

untruss.c: Untruss Un*truss" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + truss.] To loose from a truss, or as from a truss; to untie or unfasten; to let out; to undress. [R.] Dryden.

untrusser.c: Untrusser Untruss { Un*truss" (?), Un*truss"er (?), } n. One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them; a public whipper. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

untrustful.c: Untrustful Un*trust"ful (?), a. 1. Not trustful or trusting.

untruth.c: Untruth Un*truth" (?), n. 1. The quality of being untrue; contrariety to truth; want of veracity; also, treachery; faithlessness; disloyalty. Chaucer.

untruthful.c: Untruthful Un*truth"ful (?), a. Not truthful; unveracious; contrary to the truth or the fact. -- Un*truth"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*truth"ful*ness, n.

untuck.c: Untuck Un*tuck" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tuck.] To unfold or undo, as a tuck; to release from a tuck or fold.

untune.c: Untune Un*tune" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + tune.] To make incapable of harmony, or of harmonious action; to put out of tune. Shak.

unturn.c: Unturn Un*turn" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + turn.] To turn in a reserve way, especially so as to open something; as, to unturn a key. Keats.

unturned.c: Unturned Un*turned" (?), a. [Pref. un- + turned.] Not turned; not revolved or reversed.

untwain.c: Untwain Un*twain" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + twain.] To rend in twain; to tear in two. [Obs.] Skelton.

untwine.c: Untwine Un*twine" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + twine.] To untwist; to separate, as that which is twined or twisted; to disentangle; to untie.
Untwine Un*twine", v. i. To become untwined. Milton.

untwirl.c: Untwirl Un*twirl" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + twirl.] To untwist; to undo. Ash.

untwist.c: Untwist Un*twist" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + twist.]

unty.c: Unty Un*ty" (?), v. t. To untie. [Archaic] Young.

unusage.c: Unusage Un*us"age (?; 48), n. Want or lack of usage. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unused.c: Unused Un*used" (?), a. 1. Not used; as, an unused book; an unused apartment.

unusual.c: Unusual Un*u"su*al (?), a. Not usual; uncommon; rare; as, an unusual season; a person of unusual grace or erudition. -- Un*u"su*al*ly, adv. -- Un*u"su*al*ness, n.

unutterable.c: Unutterable Un*ut"ter*a*ble (?), a. Not utterable; incapable of being spoken or voiced; inexpressible; ineffable; unspeakable; as, unutterable anguish.

unvail.c: Unvail Un*vail" (?), v. t. & i. See Unveil.

unvaluable.c: Unvaluable Un*val"u*a*ble (?), a. 1. Invaluable; being beyond price. [Obs.] South.

unvalued.c: Unvalued Un*val"ued (?), a. 1. Not valued; not appraised; hence, not considered; disregarded; valueless; as, an unvalued estate. “Unvalued persons.” Shak.

unveil.c: Unveil Un*veil" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + veil.] To remove a veil from; to divest of a veil; to uncover; to disclose to view; to reveal; as, she unveiled her face.
Unveil Un*veil", v. i. To remove a veil; to reveal one's self.

unveiler.c: Unveiler Un*veil"er (?), n. One who removes a veil.

unveracity.c: Unveracity Un`ve*rac"i*ty (?), n. Want of veracity; untruthfulness; as, unveracity of heart. Carlyle.

unvessel.c: Unvessel Un*ves"sel (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + vessel.] To cause to be no longer a vessel; to empty. [Obs.] Ford.

unvicar.c: Unvicar Un*vi"car (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + vicar.] To deprive of the position or office a vicar. [R.] Strype.

unvisard.c: Unvisard Un*vis"ard (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + vizard.] To take the vizard or mask from; to unmask. [Written also unvizard.] [Obs.] Milton.

unvote.c: Unvote Un*vote" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + vote.] To reverse or annul by vote, as a former vote. [R.] Bp, Burnet.

unvoweled.c: Unvoweled Un*vow"eled (?), a. Having no vowel sounds or signs. [Written also unvowelled.] Skinner.

unvulgarize.c: Unvulgarize Un*vul"gar*ize (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + vulgarize.] To divest of vulgarity; to make to be not vulgar. Lamb.

unware.c: Unware Un*ware" (?), a. [AS. unwær unwary. See Un- not, and Wary.]

unwares.c: Unwares Un*wares" (?), adv. Unawares; unexpectedly; -- sometimes preceded by at. [Obs.] Holinshed.

unwarily.c: Unwarily Un*wa"ri*ly (?), adv. In an unwary manner.

unwariness.c: Unwariness Un*wa"ri*ness, n. The quality or state of being unwary; carelessness; heedlessness.

unwarm.c: Unwarm Un*warm" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + warm.] To lose warmth; to grow cold. [R.]

unwarp.c: Unwarp Un*warp" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + warp.] To restore from a warped state; to cause to be linger warped.

unwarped.c: Unwarped Un*warped" (?), a. [Pref. un- not + warped.] Not warped; hence, not biased; impartial.

unwarrantable.c: Unwarrantable Un*war"rant*a*ble (?), a. Not warrantable; indefensible; not vindicable; not justifiable; illegal; unjust; improper. -- Un*war"rant*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*war"rant*a*bly, adv.

unwarranted.c: Unwarranted Un*war"rant*ed, a. Not warranted; being without warrant, authority, or guaranty; unwarrantable.

unwashed.c: Unwashed Un*washed" (?), a. Not washed or cleansed; filthy; unclean.

unwashen.c: Unwashen Un*wash"en (?), a. Not washed. [Archaic] “To eat with unwashen hands.” Matt. xv. 20.

unwayed.c: Unwayed Un*wayed" (?), a. 1. Not used to travel; as, colts that are unwayed. [Obs.] Suckling.

unwearied.c: Unwearied Un*wea"ried (?), a. Not wearied; not fatigued or tired; hence, persistent; not tiring or wearying; indefatigable. -- Un*wea"ried*ly, adv. -- Un*wea"ried*ness, n.

unweary.c: Unweary Un*wea"ry (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + weary.] To cause to cease being weary; to refresh. [Obs.] Dryden.

unweave.c: Unweave Un*weave" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + weave.] To unfold; to undo; to ravel, as what has been woven.

unwedgeable.c: Unwedgeable Un*wedge"a*ble (?), a. Not to be split with wedges. [Obs.] Shak.

unweeting.c: Unweeting Un*weet"ing (?), a. [See Un- not, and Weet, Wit.] Unwitting. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser.

unweighed.c: Unweighed Un*weighed" (?), a. Not weighed; not pondered or considered; as, an unweighed statement.

unweighing.c: Unweighing Un*weigh"ing (?), a. Not weighing or pondering; inconsiderate. Shak.

unweldy.c: Unweldy Unweld { Un*weld" (?), Un*weld"y (?) }, a. Unwieldy; unmanageable; clumsy. [Obs.]

unwell.c: Unwell Un*well" (?), a. 1. Not well; indisposed; not in good health; somewhat ill; ailing.

unwellness.c: Unwellness Un*well"ness, n. Quality or state of being unwell.

unwemmed.c: Unwemmed Un*wemmed" (?), a. Not blemished; undefiled; pure. [Obs.] Wyclif.

unwhole.c: Unwhole Un*whole" (?), a. [AS. unhāl. See Un- not, and Whole.] Not whole; unsound. [Obs.]

unwieldy.c: Unwieldy Un*wield"y (?), a. Not easily wielded or carried; unmanageable; bulky; ponderous. “A fat, unwieldy body of fifty-eight years old.” Clarendon.

unwild.c: Unwild Un*wild" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wild.] To tame; to subdue. [Obs. & R.] Sylvester.

unwill.c: Unwill Un*will" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + will.] To annul or reverse by an act of the will. Longfellow.

unwilled.c: Unwilled Un*willed" (?), a. [1st pref. un- + will.] Deprived of the faculty of will or volition. Mrs. Browning.

unwilling.c: Unwilling Un*will"ing (?), a. Not willing; loath; disinclined; reluctant; as, an unwilling servant.

unwind.c: Unwind Un*wind" (?), v. t. [AS. unwindan. See 1st Un-, and Wind to coil.]
Unwind Un*wind", v. i. To be or become unwound; to be capable of being unwound or untwisted.

unwisdom.c: Unwisdom Un*wis"dom (?), n. Want of wisdom; unwise conduct or action; folly; simplicity; ignorance.

unwise.c: Unwise Un*wise" (?), a. [AS. unwīs. See Un- not, and Wise, a.] Not wise; defective in wisdom; injudicious; indiscreet; foolish; as, an unwise man; unwise kings; unwise measures.

unwisely.c: Unwisely Un*wise"ly, adv. [AS. unwīslice.] In an unwise manner; foolishly.

unwish.c: Unwish Un*wish" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wish.] To wish not to be; to destroy by wishing. [Obs.]

unwist.c: Unwist Un*wist" (?), a. 1. Not known; unknown. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser.

unwit.c: Unwit Un*wit" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wit.] To deprive of wit. [Obs.] Shak.
Unwit Un*wit", n. [Pref. un- not + wit.] Want of wit or understanding; ignorance. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unwitch.c: Unwitch Un*witch" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + witch.] To free from a witch or witches; to fee from witchcraft. [R.] B. Jonson.

unwitting.c: Unwitting Un*wit"ting (?), a. Not knowing; unconscious; ignorant. -- Un*wit"ting*ly, adv.

unwoman.c: Unwoman Un*wom"an (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + woman.] To deprive of the qualities of a woman; to unsex. [R.] R. Browning.

unwonder.c: Unwonder Un*won"der (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wonder.] To divest of the quality of wonder or mystery; to interpret; to explain. [R.] Fuller.

unwont.c: Unwont Un*wont" (ŭn*wŭnt"), a. Unwonted; unused; unaccustomed. [Archaic] Sir W. Scott.

unwonted.c: Unwonted Un*wont"ed (ŭn*wŭnt"ĕd), a. 1. Not wonted; unaccustomed; unused; not made familiar by practice; as, a child unwonted to strangers. Milton.

unwork.c: Unwork Un*work" (ŭn*wûk"), v. t. [1st pref. un- + work.] To undo or destroy, as work previously done.

unworldly.c: Unworldly Un*world"ly (?), a. Not worldly; spiritual; holy. Hawthorne. -- Un*world"li*ness (#), n.

unwormed.c: Unwormed Un*wormed" (?), a. Not wormed; not having had the worm, or lytta, under the tongue cut out; -- said of a dog.

unworship.c: Unworship Un*wor"ship (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + worship.] To deprive of worship or due honor; to dishonor. [Obs.] Wyclif.
