Unworship Un*wor"ship, n. [Pref. un- not + worship.] Lack of worship or respect; dishonor. [Obs.] Gower.

unworthy.c: Unworthy Un*wor"thy (?), a. Not worthy; wanting merit, value, or fitness; undeserving; worthless; unbecoming; -- often with of. -- Un*wor"thi*ly (#), adv. -- Un*wor"thi*ness, n.

unwrap.c: Unwrap Un*wrap" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wrap.] To open or undo, as what is wrapped or folded. Chaucer.

unwreathe.c: Unwreathe Un*wreathe" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wreathe.] To untwist, uncoil, or untwine, as anything wreathed.

unwrie.c: Unwrie Un*wrie" (?), v. t. [AS. onwreón; on- (see 1st Un-) + wreón to cover.] To uncover. [Obs.] Chaucer.

unwrinkle.c: Unwrinkle Un*wrin"kle (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + wrinkle.] To reduce from a wrinkled state; to smooth.

unwrite.c: Unwrite Un*write" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + write.] To cancel, as what is written; to erase. Milton.

unwritten.c: Unwritten Un*writ"ten (?), a. 1. Not written; not reduced to writing; oral; as, unwritten agreements.

unwroken.c: Unwroken Un*wro"ken (?), a. [See Un- not, and Wreak.] Not revenged; unavenged. [Obs.] Surrey.

unyoke.c: Unyoke Un*yoke" (?), v. t. [1st pref. un- + yoke.]

unyoked.c: Unyoked Un*yoked" (?), a. [In sense 1 pref. un- not + yoked; in senses 2 and 3 properly p. p. of unyoke.]

unyolden.c: Unyolden Un*yold"en (?), a. Not yielded. [Obs.] “[By] force... is he taken unyolden.” Sir T. Browne.

unzoned.c: Unzoned Un*zoned" (?), a. Not zoned; not bound with a girdle; as, an unzoned bosom. Prior.

up.c: Up Up (ŭp), adv. [AS. up, upp, ūp; akin to OFries. up, op, D. op, OS. ūp, OHG. ūf, G. auf, Icel. & Sw. upp, Dan. op, Goth. iup, and probably to E. over. See Over.]
Up Up, prep. 1. From a lower to a higher place on, upon, or along; at a higher situation upon; at the top of.
Up Up, n. The state of being up or above; a state of elevation, prosperity, or the like; -- rarely occurring except in the phrase ups and downs. [Colloq.]
Up Up, a. Inclining up; tending or going up; upward; as, an up look; an up grade; the up train.

upas.c: Upas U"pas (ū"pȧs), n. [Malay pūhn-ūpas; pūhn a tree + ūpas poison.]

upbar.c: Upbar Up*bar" (?), v. t. 1. To fasten with a bar. [R.]

upbear.c: Upbear Up*bear" (?), v. t. To bear up; to raise aloft; to support in an elevated situation; to sustain. Spenser.

upbind.c: Upbind Up*bind" (?), v. t. To bind up. [R.] Collins.

upblow.c: Upblow Up*blow", v. t. To inflate. [Obs.] Spenser.
Upblow Up*blow", v. i. To blow up; as, the wind upblows from the sea. [Obs.] Spenser.

upbraid.c: Upbraid Up*braid" (ŭp*brād"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Upbraided; p. pr. & vb. n. Upbraiding.] [OE. upbreiden; AS. upp up + bregdan to draw, twist, weave, or the kindred Icel. bregða to draw, brandish, braid, deviate from, change, break off, upbraid. See Up, and Braid, v. t.]
Upbraid Up*braid", v. i. To utter upbraidings. Pope.
Upbraid Up*braid", n. The act of reproaching; contumely. [Obs.] “ Foul upbraid.” Spenser.

upbreak.c: Upbreak Up*break" (ŭp*brāk"), v. i. To break upwards; to force away or passage to the surface.
Upbreak Up"break` (ŭp"brāk`), n. A breaking upward or bursting forth; an upburst. Mrs. Browning.

upbreathe.c: Upbreathe Up*breathe" (ŭp*brēth"), v. i. To breathe up or out; to exhale. [Obs.] Marston.

upbreed.c: Upbreed Up*breed" (ŭp*brēd"), v. t. To rear, or bring up; to nurse. “Upbred in a foreign country.” Holinshed.

upbrought.c: Upbrought Up*brought" (?), a. Brought up; educated. [Obs.] Spenser.

upbuoyance.c: Upbuoyance Up*buoy"ance (?), n. The act of buoying up; uplifting. [R.] Coleridge.

upburst.c: Upburst Up"burst` (?), n. The act of bursting upwards; a breaking through to the surface; an upbreak or uprush; as, an upburst of molten matter.

upcast.c: Upcast Up"cast` (?), a. Cast up; thrown upward; as, with upcast eyes. Addison.
Upcast Up"cast` (?), n. 1. (Bowling) A cast; a throw. Shak.
Upcast Up*cast" (?), v. t. 1. To cast or throw up; to turn upward. [Obs.] Chaucer.

upcaught.c: Upcaught Up"caught` (?), a. Seized or caught up. “ She bears upcaught a mariner away.” Cowper.

upcheer.c: Upcheer Up*cheer" (?), v. t. To cheer up. Spenser.

upclimb.c: Upclimb Up*climb" (?), v. t. & i. To climb up; to ascend.

upcoil.c: Upcoil Up*coil" (?), v. t. & i. To coil up; to make into a coil, or to be made into a coil.

upcountry.c: Upcountry Up"coun`try (?), adv. In an upcountry direction; as, to live upcountry. [Colloq.]
Upcountry Up"coun`try, a. Living or situated remote from the seacoast; as, an upcountry residence. [Colloq.] -- n. The interior of the country. [Colloq.]

upcurl.c: Upcurl Up*curl" (?), v. t. To curl up. [R.] Tennyson.

updive.c: Updive Up*dive" (?), v. i. To spring upward; to rise. [R.] Davies (Microcosmos).

updraw.c: Updraw Up*draw" (?), v. t. To draw up. [R.] Milton.

upend.c: Upend Up*end" (?), v. t. To end up; to set on end, as a cask.

upfill.c: Upfill Up*fill" (?), v. t. To fill up. [Obs.]

upflow.c: Upflow Up*flow" (?), v. i. To flow or stream up. Southey.

upflung.c: Upflung Up*flung" (?), a. Flung or thrown up.

upgather.c: Upgather Up*gath"er (?), v. t. To gather up; to contract; to draw together. [Obs.]

upgaze.c: Upgaze Up*gaze" (?), v. i. To gaze upward. Byron.

upgive.c: Upgive Up*give" (?), v. t. To give up or out. [Obs.]

upgrow.c: Upgrow Up*grow" (?), v. i. To grow up. [R.] Milton.

upgrowth.c: Upgrowth Up"growth` (?), n. The process or result of growing up; progress; development.

upgush.c: Upgush Up"gush` (?), n. A gushing upward. Hawthorne.
Upgush Up*gush" (?), v. i. To gush upward.

uphaf.c: Uphaf Up*haf" (?), obs. imp. of Upheave. Chaucer.

uphand.c: Uphand Up"hand` (?), a. Lifted by the hand, or by both hands; as, the uphand sledge. [R.] Moxon.

uphang.c: Uphang Up*hang" (?), v. t. To hang up. Spenser.

uphasp.c: Uphasp Up*hasp" (?), v. t. To hasp or faster up; to close; as, sleep uphasps the eyes. [R.] Stanyhurst.

upheaval.c: Upheaval Up*heav"al (?), n. The act of upheaving, or the state of being upheaved; esp., an elevation of a portion of the earth's crust. Lubbock.

upheave.c: Upheave Up*heave", v. t. To heave or lift up from beneath; to raise. Milton.

upheld.c: Upheld Up*held" (?), imp. & p. p. of Uphold.

upher.c: Upher Up"her (?), n. (Arch.) A fir pole of from four to seven inches diameter, and twenty to forty feet long, sometimes roughly hewn, used for scaffoldings, and sometimes for slight and common roofs, for which use it is split. [Spelt also ufer.] [Eng.] Gwilt.

uphill.c: Uphill Up*hill" (?), adv. Upwards on, or as on, a hillside; as, to walk uphill.
Uphill Up"hill` (?), a. 1. Ascending; going up; as, an uphill road.

uphilt.c: Uphilt Up*hilt" (?), v. t. To thrust in up to the hilt; as, to uphilt one's sword into an enemy. [R.] Stanyhurst.

uphoard.c: Uphoard Up*hoard" (?), v. t. To hoard up. [Obs.] Shak.

uphold.c: Uphold Up*hold" (?), v. t. 1. To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.

upholster.c: Upholster Up*hol"ster (?), v. t. [See Upholsterer.] To furnish (rooms, carriages, bedsteads, chairs, etc.) with hangings, coverings, cushions, etc.; to adorn with furnishings in cloth, velvet, silk, etc.; as, to upholster a couch; to upholster a room with curtains.

upholsterer.c: Upholsterer Up*hol"ster*er (?), n. [A substitution for older upholder, in OE., broker, tradesman, and formerly also written upholster, upholdster. See Upholder, and -ster.] One who provides hangings, coverings, cushions, curtains, and the like; one who upholsters.

upholstery.c: Upholstery Up*hol"ster*y (?), n. The articles or goods supplied by upholsterers; the business or work of an upholsterer.

upkeep.c: Upkeep Up"keep` (?), n. 1. The act of keeping up, or maintaining; maintenance of persons, organizations, or objects such as machinery, by providing a location, repairs, and consumable items when necessary. “Horse artillery... expensive in the upkeep.” Scribner's Mag.

upland.c: Upland Up"land (?), n. 1. High land; ground elevated above the meadows and intervals which lie on the banks of rivers, near the sea, or between hills; land which is generally dry; -- opposed to lowland, meadow, marsh, swamp, interval, and the like.
Upland Up"land, a. 1. Of or pertaining to uplands; being on upland; high in situation; as, upland inhabitants; upland pasturage.

uplander.c: Uplander Up"land*er (?), n. 1. One dwelling in the upland; hence, a countryman; a rustic. [Obs.]

uplandish.c: Uplandish Up*land"ish (?), a. Of or pertaining to uplands; dwelling on high lands. [Obs.] Chapman.

uplay.c: Uplay Up*lay" (?), v. t. To hoard. [Obs.] Donne.

uplead.c: Uplead Up*lead" (?), v. t. To lead upward. [Obs.]

uplean.c: Uplean Up*lean" (?), v. i. To lean or incline upon anything. [Obs.] Spenser.

uplift.c: Uplift Up*lift" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Uplifting.] To lift or raise aloft; to raise; to elevate; as, to uplift the arm; to uplift a rock. Cowper.
Uplift Up"lift` (?), n. (Geol.) A raising or upheaval of strata so as to disturb their regularity and uniformity, and to occasion folds, dislocations, and the like.

upline.c: Up-line Up"-line` (?), n. (Railroad) A line or track leading from the provinces toward the metropolis or a principal terminus; the track upon which up-trains run. See Up-train. [Eng.]

uplock.c: Uplock Up*lock" (?), v. t. To lock up. [Obs.] Shak.

uplook.c: Uplook Up*look" (?), v. i. To look or gaze up. [Obs.]

upmost.c: Upmost Up"most` (?), a. [Cf. Uppermost.] Highest; topmost; uppermost. Spenser. Dryden.

upokororo.c: Upokororo U`po*ko*ro"ro (?), n. [From the native Maori name.] (Zool.) An edible fresh-water New Zealand fish (Prototroctes oxyrhynchus) of the family Haplochitonidae. In general appearance and habits, it resembles the northern lake whitefishes and trout. Called also grayling.

upon.c: Upon Up*on" (?), prep.[AS. uppan, uppon; upp up + on, an, on. See Up, and On.] On; -- used in all the senses of that word, with which it is interchangeable. “Upon an hill of flowers.” Chaucer.

upover.c: Up-over Up"-o`ver, a. (Mining & Civil Eng.) Designating a method of shaft excavation by drifting to a point below, and then raising instead of sinking.

uppent.c: Uppent Up*pent` (?), a. A Pent up; confined. [Obs.]

upper.c: Upper Up"per (?), a.; comp. of Up. Being further up, literally or figuratively; higher in place, position, rank, dignity, or the like; superior; as, the upper lip; the upper side of a thing; the upper house of a legislature.
Upper Up"per, n. The upper leather for a shoe; a vamp.

uppermost.c: Uppermost Up"per*most` (?), a. [From Up, Upper; formed like aftermost. Cf. Upmost.] Highest in place, position, rank, power, or the like; upmost; supreme.

uppertendom.c: Uppertendom Up`per*ten"dom (?), n. [Upper ten + -dom.] The highest class in society; the upper ten. See Upper ten, under Upper. [Colloq.]

uppile.c: Uppile Up*pile" (?), v. t. To pile, or heap, up. Southey.

uppish.c: Uppish Up"pish (?), a. [From Up.] Proud; arrogant; assuming; putting on airs of superiority. [Colloq.] T. Brown. -- Up"pish*ly, adv. [Colloq.] -- Up"pish*ness, n. [Colloq.]

upplight.c: Upplight Up*plight" (?), obs. imp. & p. p. of Uppluck.

uppluck.c: Uppluck Up*pluck" (?), v. t. To pull or pluck up. [Obs.]

uppricked.c: Uppricked Up*pricked" (?), a. Upraised; erect; -- said of the ears of an animal. Mason.

upprop.c: Upprop Up*prop" (?), v. t. To prop up. Donne.

upraise.c: Upraise Up*raise" (?), v. t. To raise; to lift up.

uprear.c: Uprear Up*rear" (?), v. t. To raise; to erect. Byron.

upridged.c: Upridged Up*ridged" (?), a. Raised up in a ridge or ridges; as, a billow upridged. Cowper.

upright.c: Upright Up"right` (?), a. [AS. upright, uppriht. See Up, and Right, a.] 1. In an erect position or posture; perpendicular; vertical, or nearly vertical; pointing upward; as, an upright tree.
Upright Up"right`, n. 1. Something standing upright, as a piece of timber in a building. See Illust. of Frame.

uprighteously.c: Uprighteously Up*right"eous*ly (?), adv. [See Righteous.] In an upright or just manner. [Obs.] Shak.

uprightly.c: Uprightly Up"right`ly (ŭp"rīt`ly̆), adv. In an upright manner.

uprightness.c: Uprightness Up"right`ness (ŭp"rīt`nĕs), n. the quality or state of being upright.

uprise.c: Uprise Up*rise" (ŭp*rīz"), v. i. 1. To rise; to get up; to appear from below the horizon. “Uprose the sun.” Cowley.
Uprise Up*rise", n. The act of rising; appearance above the horizon; rising. [R.]

uprising.c: Uprising Up*ris"ing, n. 1. Act of rising; also, a steep place; an ascent. “The steep uprising of the hill.” Shak.

uprist.c: Uprist Up*rist", obs. imp. of Uprise. Uprose. Chaucer.

uproar.c: Uproar Up"roar (ŭp"rōr`), n. [D. oproer; akin to G. aufruhr, Dan. oprör, Sw. uppror; D. op up + roeren to stir; akin to AS. hrēran to stir, hrōr stirring, active, G. rühren to stir, OHG. ruoren, Icel. hræra, Dan. röre, Sw. röra. Cf. Rearmouse.] Great tumult; violent disturbance and noise; noisy confusion; bustle and clamor.
Uproar Up*roar" (?), v. t. To throw into uproar or confusion. [Obs.] “Uproar the universal peace.” Shak.
Uproar Up*roar", v. i. To make an uproar. [R.] Carlyle.

uproarious.c: Uproarious Up*roar"i*ous (?), a. Making, or accompanied by, uproar, or noise and tumult; as, uproarious merriment.

uproll.c: Uproll Up*roll" (?), v. t. To roll up. Milton.

uproot.c: Uproot Up*root" (?), v. t. To root up; to tear up by the roots, or as if by the roots; to remove utterly; to eradicate; to extirpate.

uprouse.c: Uprouse Up*rouse" (?), v. t. To rouse up; to rouse from sleep; to awake; to arouse. Shak.

uprun.c: Uprun Up*run" (?), v. i. To run up; to ascend.

uprush.c: Uprush Up*rush" (?), v. i. To rush upward. Southey.
Uprush Up"rush` (?), n. Act of rushing upward; an upbreak or upburst; as, an uprush of lava. R. A. Proctor.

upseek.c: Upseek Up*seek" (?), v. i. To seek or strain upward. “Upseeking eyes suffused with... tears.” Southey.

upsend.c: Upsend Up*send" (?), v. t. To send, cast, or throw up.

upset.c: Upset Up*set" (?), v. t. 1. To set up; to put upright. [Obs.] “With sail on mast upset.” R. of Brunne.
Upset Up*set", v. i. To become upset.

Upset Up"set` (?), a. Set up; fixed; determined; -- used chiefly or only in the phrase upset price; that is, the price fixed upon as the minimum for property offered in a public sale, or, in an auction, the price at which property is set up or started by the auctioneer, and the lowest price at which it will be sold.
Upset Up"set`, n. The act of upsetting, or the state of being upset; an overturn; as, the wagon had an upset.

upsetting.c: Upsetting Up*set"ting (?), a. 1. Conceited; assuming; as, an upsetting fellow. [Scot.] Jamieson.

Upsetting thermometer Up*set"ting ther*mom"e*ter. A thermometer by merely inverting which the temperature may be registered. The column of mercury is broken and, as it remains until the instrument is reset, the reading may be made at leisure.

upshoot.c: Upshoot Up*shoot" (?), v. i. To shoot upward. “Trees upshooting high.” Spenser.

upshot.c: Upshot Up"shot` (?), n. [Up + shot, equivalent to scot share, reckoning. Cf. the phrase to cast up an account.] Final issue; conclusion; the sum and substance; the end; the result; the consummation.

upside.c: Upside Up"side` (?), n. 1. The upper side; the part that is uppermost.

upsidown.c: Upsidown Up"si*down` (?), adv. See Upsodown. [Obs. or Colloq.] Spenser.

upsilon.c: Upsilon Up"si*lon (?), n. [Gr. 'y^ psilo`n bare, mere, simple y.] The 20th letter (Υ, υ) of the Greek alphabet, a vowel having originally the sound of ōo as in room, becoming before the 4th century b. c. that French u or Ger. ü. Its equivalent in English is u or y.

upsitting.c: Upsitting Up"sit`ting (?), n. A sitting up of a woman after her confinement, to receive and entertain her friends. [Obs.]

upsnatch.c: Upsnatch Up*snatch" (?), v. t. To snatch up. [R.]

upsoar.c: Upsoar Up*soar" (?), v. i. To soar or mount up. Pope.

upsodown.c: Upsodown Up"so*down` (?), adv. [Up + so as + down.] Upside down. [Obs. or Colloq.] Wyclif.

upspear.c: Upspear Up*spear" (?), v. i. To grow or shoot up like a spear; as, upspearing grass. [R.] Cowper.

upspring.c: Upspring Up*spring" (?), v. i. To spring up. Tennyson.
Upspring Up"spring` (?), n. 1. An upstart. [Obs.] “The swaggering upspring.” Shak.

upspurner.c: Upspurner Up"spurn`er (?), n. A spurner or contemner; a despiser; a scoffer. [Obs.] Joye.

upstairs.c: Upstairs Up*stairs" (?), adv. Up the stairs; in or toward an upper story.
Upstairs Up"stairs` (?), a. Being above stairs; as, an upstairs room.

upstand.c: Upstand Up*stand" (?), v. i. To stand up; to be erected; to rise. Spenser. Milton.

upstare.c: Upstare Up*stare" (?), v. i. To stare or stand upward; hence, to be uplifted or conspicuous. “Rearing fiercely their upstaring crests.” Spenser.

upstart.c: Upstart Up*start" (?), v. i. To start or spring up suddenly. Spenser. Tennyson.
Upstart Up"start` (?), n. 1. One who has risen suddenly, as from low life to wealth, power, or honor; a parvenu. Bacon.
Upstart Up"start`, a. Suddenly raised to prominence or consequence. “A race of upstart creatures.” Milton.

upstay.c: Upstay Up*stay" (?), v. t. To sustain; to support. [Obs.] “His massy spear upstayed.” Milton.

upsterte.c: Upsterte Up*stert"e (?), obs. imp. & p. p. of Upstart.

upstir.c: Upstir Up"stir` (?), n. Insurrection; commotion; disturbance. [Obs.] Sir J. Cheke.

upstream.c: Upstream Up*stream" (?), adv. Toward the higher part of a stream; against the current.

upstreet.c: Upstreet Up*street" (?), adv. Toward the higher part of a street; as, to walk upstreet. G. W. Gable.

upstroke.c: Upstroke Up"stroke` (?), n. An upward stroke, especially the stroke, or line, made by a writing instrument when moving upward, or from the body of the writer, or a line corresponding to the part of a letter thus made.

upsun.c: Upsun Up"sun` (?), n. (Scots Law) The time during which the sun is up, or above the horizon; the time between sunrise and sunset.

upswarm.c: Upswarm Up*swarm" (?), v. i. & i. To rise, or cause to rise, in a swarm or swarms. [R.] Shak. Cowper.

upsway.c: Upsway Up*sway" (?), v. t. To sway or swing aloft; as, to upsway a club. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

upswell.c: Upswell Up*swell" (?), v. i. To swell or rise up.

upsyturvy.c: Upsyturvy Up"sy*tur"vy (?), adv. [Cf. Upside down, under Upside, and Topsy-turvy.] Upside down; topsy-turvy. [Obs.] Robert Greene.

uptails.c: Uptails all Up"tails` all" (?). 1. An old game at cards. [Obs.]

uptake.c: Uptake Up*take" (?), v. t. To take into the hand; to take up; to help. [Obs.] Wyclif. Spenser.

uptear.c: Uptear Up*tear" (?), v. t. To tear up. Milton.

upthrow.c: Upthrow Up*throw" (?), v. t. To throw up. Drayton.

upthunder.c: Upthunder Up*thun"der (?), v. i. To send up a noise like thunder. [R.] Coleridge.

uptie.c: Uptie Up*tie" (?), v. t. To tie up. Spenser.

uptodate.c: Up-to-date Up`-to-date" (?), a. Extending to the present time; having style, manners, knowledge, or other qualities that are abreast of the times. “A general up-to-date style of presentment.” Nature. “Everything's up-to-date in Kansas City.”

uptown.c: Uptown Up*town" (?), adv. To or in the upper part of a town; as, to go uptown. [Colloq. U. S.]
Uptown Up"town` (?), a. Situated in, or belonging to, the upper part of a town or city; as, a uptown street, shop, etc.; uptown society. [Colloq. U. S.]

uptrace.c: Uptrace Up*trace" (?), v. t. To trace up or out.

uptrain.c: Uptrain Up*train" (?), v. t. To train up; to educate. [Obs.] “Daughters which were well uptrained.” Spenser.
Up-train Up"-train` (?). 1. A train going in the direction of the metropolis or the main terminus. [Eng.]

upturn.c: Upturn Up*turn" (?), v. t. To turn up; to direct upward; to throw up; as, to upturn the ground in plowing. “A sea of upturned faces.” D. Webster.

upupa.c: Upupa U"pu*pa (?; 277), n. [L., the hoopoe.] (Zool.) A genus of birds which includes the common hoopoe.

upwaft.c: Upwaft Up*waft" (?), v. t. To waft upward. Cowper.

upwards.c: Upwards Upward { Up"ward (?), Up"wards (?), } adv. [AS. upweardes. See Up-, and -wards.]

upward.c: Upward Up"ward, a. [AS. upweard. See Up, and -ward.] Directed toward a higher place; as, with upward eye; with upward course.
Upward Up"ward, n. The upper part; the top. [Obs.]

upwhirl.c: Upwhirl Up*whirl" (?), v. t. & i. To rise upward in a whirl; to raise upward with a whirling motion.

upwind.c: Upwind Up*wind" (?), v. t. To wind up. Spenser.
Up-wind Up"-wind`, adv. Against the wind; toward the direction from which the wind is blowing.

upwreath.c: Upwreath Up*wreath" (?), v. i. To rise with a curling motion; to curl upward, as smoke. Longfellow.

upyat.c: Upyat Up*yat" (?), obs. imp. of Upgive. Chaucer.

ure.c: Ure Ur { Ur (?), Ure }, n. (Zool.) The urus.
Ure Ure (?), n. [OE. ure, OF. oevre, ovre, ouvre, work, F. œuvre, L. opera. See Opera, Operate, and cf. Inure, Manure.] Use; practice; exercise. [Obs.] Fuller.
Ure Ure, v. t. To use; to exercise; to inure; to accustom by practice. [Obs.]

urachus.c: Urachus ‖U"ra*chus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? urine +? to hold.] (Anat.) A cord or band of fibrous tissue extending from the bladder to the umbilicus.

uraemia.c: Uraemia ‖U*rae"mi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? urine +? blood.] (Med.) Accumulation in the blood of the principles of the urine, producing dangerous disease.

uraemic.c: Uraemic U*rae"mic (?), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to uraemia; as, uraemic convulsions.

uraeum.c: Uraeum ‖U*rae"um (?), n. [NL., from Gr.??, fr.? of the tail; cf. L. uraeus, adj.] (Zool.) The posterior half of an animal.

uraeus.c: Uraeus ‖U*rae"us (?), n. [NL., fr. L. uraeus pertaining to a tail, Gr.?, fr.? tail.] (Egypt. Archaeol.) A serpent, or serpent's head and neck, represented on the front of the headdresses of divinities and sovereigns as an emblem of supreme power.

ural.c: Ural U"ral (?), a. Pertaining to, or designating, the Urals, a mountain range between Europe and Asia.

uralaltaic.c: Ural-Altaic U"ral-Al*ta"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Urals and the Altai; as the Ural-Altaic, or Turanian, languages.

uralic.c: Uralic Uralian { U*ra"li*an (?), U*ral"ic (?), } a. Of or relating to the Ural Mountains.

uralite.c: Uralite U"ral*ite (?), n. [So called because first observed in the Ural Mountains.] (Min.) Amphibole resulting from the alternation of pyroxene by paramorphism. It is not uncommon in massive eruptive rocks.

uralitization.c: Uralitization U`ral*i`ti*za"tion (?), n. (Geol.) The change of pyroxene to amphibole by paramorphism.

uranate.c: Uranate U"ra*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of uranic acid.

urania.c: Urania U*ra"ni*a (?), n. [L., from Gr.?, i. e., the Heavenly, fr.? heavenly, fr.? heaven.]

uranian.c: Uranian U*ra"ni*an (?), a. (Astron.) Of or pertaining to the planet Uranus; as, the Uranian year.

uranic.c: Uranic U*ran"ic (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to the heavens; celestial; astronomical.

uranin.c: Uranin U"ra*nin (?), n. (Chem.) An alkaline salt of fluorescein, obtained as a brownish red substance, which is used as a dye; -- so called from the peculiar yellowish green fluorescence (resembling that of uranium glass) of its solutions. See Fluorescein.

uraninite.c: Uraninite U*ran"i*nite (?), n. (Min.) A mineral consisting chiefly of uranium oxide with some lead, thorium, etc., occurring in black octahedrons, also in masses with a pitchlike luster; pitchblende.

uraniscoplasty.c: Uraniscoplasty U`ra*nis"co*plas`ty (?), n. [Gr.? top of a tent, plate (fr.? sky) + -plasty.] (Surg.) The process of forming an artificial palate.

uraniscorrhaphy.c: Uraniscorrhaphy Uraniscoraphy { U`ra*nis*cor"a*phy, U`ra*nis*cor"rha*phy } (?), n. [Gr.? the top of a tent, the palate (fr.? sky) +? a seam.] (Surg.) Suture of the palate. See Staphyloraphy.

uranite.c: Uranite U"ra*nite (?), n. [Cf. G. uranit, F. uranite.] (Min.) A general term for the uranium phosphates, autunite, or lime uranite, and torbernite, or copper uranite.

uranitic.c: Uranitic U`ra*nit"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to uranium; containing uranium.

uranium.c: Uranium U*ra"ni*um (?), n. [NL., from Uranus the planet. See Uranus.] (Chem.) An element of the chromium group, found in certain rare minerals, as pitchblende, uranite, etc., and reduced as a heavy, hard, nickel-white metal which is quite permanent. Its yellow oxide is used to impart to glass a delicate greenish-yellow tint which is accompanied by a strong fluorescence, and its black oxide is used as a pigment in porcelain painting. Symbol U. Atomic weight 239.

uranochre.c: Uran-ochre Uran-ocher { U"ran-o`cher, U"ran-o`chre } (?), n. [Cf. F. uranochre.] (Min.) (a) A yellow, earthy incrustation, consisting essentially of the oxide of uranium, but more or less impure.

uranographical.c: Uranographical Uranographic { U`ra*no*graph"ic (?), U`ra*no*graph"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to uranography; as, an uranographic treatise.

uranographist.c: Uranographist U`ra*nog"ra*phist (?), n. One practiced in uranography.

uranography.c: Uranography U`ra*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.?;? heaven +? to write.] A description or plan of the heavens and the heavenly bodies; the construction of celestial maps, globes, etc.; uranology.

uranolite.c: Uranolite U*ran"o*lite (?), n. [Gr.? heaven + -lite.] A meteorite or aerolite. [Obs.] Hutton.

uranology.c: Uranology U`ra*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? heaven + -logy.] A discourse or treatise on the heavens and the heavenly bodies; the study of the heavens; uranography.

uranometry.c: Uranometry U`ra*nom"e*try (?), n. [Gr.? heaven + -metry.] (Astron.) A chart or catalogue of fixed stars, especially of stars visible to the naked eye.

uranoplasty.c: Uranoplasty U"ra*no*plas`ty (?), n. [See Uraniscoplasty.] (Surg.) The plastic operation for closing a fissure in the hard palate.

uranoscopy.c: Uranoscopy U`ra*nos"co*py (?), n. [Gr.? + -scopy.] Observation of the heavens or heavenly bodies.

uranoso.c: Uranoso- U`ra*no"so- (?), a. (Chem.) A combining form (also used adjectively) from uranium; -- used in naming certain complex compounds; as in uranoso-uranic oxide, uranoso-uranic sulphate.

uranous.c: Uranous U"ra*nous (ū"rȧ*nŭs), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or containing, uranium; designating those compounds in which uranium has a lower valence as contrasted with the uranic compounds.

uranus.c: Uranus U"ra*nus (-nŭs), n. [L. Uranus, Gr. O'yrano`s Uranus, o'yrano`s heaven, sky. Cf. Uranium.]

uranyl.c: Uranyl U"ra*nyl (?), n. [Uranium + -yl.] (Chem.) The radical UO2, conveniently regarded as a residue of many uranium compounds.

urari.c: Urari Urare { U*ra"re (?), U*ra"ri }, n. See Curare.

urate.c: Urate U"rate (?), n. [Cf. F. urate.] (Physiol. Chem.) A salt of uric acid; as, sodium urate; ammonium urate.

uratic.c: Uratic U*rat"ic (?), (Physiol. Chem.) Of or containing urates; as, uratic calculi.

urban.c: Urban Ur"ban (?), a. [L. urbanus belonging to the?ity or town, refined, polished, fr. urbs, urbis, a city: cf. F. urbain. Cf. Urbane.]

urbane.c: Urbane Ur*bane" (?), a. [See Urban.] Courteous in manners; polite; refined; elegant.

urbaniste.c: Urbaniste Ur"ban*iste (?), n. (Bot.) A large and delicious pear or Flemish origin.

urbanity.c: Urbanity Ur*ban"i*ty (?), n. [L. urbanitas; cf. F. urbanité.]

urbanize.c: Urbanize Ur"ban*ize (?), v. t. To render urban, or urbane; to refine; to polish. Howell.

urbicolae.c: Urbicolae ‖Ur*bic"o*lae (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. L. urbs, urbis, a city + colere to inhabit.] (Zool.) An extensive family of butterflies (Hesperidae), including those known as skippers.

urbicolous.c: Urbicolous Ur*bic"o*lous (?), a. Of or pertaining to a city; urban. [R.]

urceolate.c: Urceolate Ur"ce*o*late (?), a. [L. urceolus, dim. of urceus a pitcher or waterpot.] (Nat. Hist.) Shaped like a pitcher or urn; swelling below, and contracted at the orifice, as a calyx or corolla.

urceole.c: Urceole Ur"ce*ole (?), n. [See Urceolate.] (R. C. Ch.) A vessel for water for washing the hands; also, one to hold wine or water.

urceolus.c: Urceolus ‖Ur*ce"o*lus (?), n.; pl. Urceoli (#). [L., a little pitcher.] (Bot.) Any urn-shaped organ of a plant.

urchin.c: Urchin Ur"chin (û"chĭn), n. [OE. urchon, irchon, a hedgehog, OF. ireçon, eriçon, heriçon, herichon, F. hérisson, a derivative fr. L. ericius, from er a hedgehog, for her; akin to Gr. chh`r. Cf. Herisson.]
Urchin Ur"chin, a. Rough; pricking; piercing. [R.] “Helping all urchin blasts.” Milton.

urchon.c: Urchon Ur"chon (?), n. (Zool.) The urchin, or hedgehog.

urdu.c: Urdu Ur"du (?), n. [Hind. urdū.] The language more generally called Hindustanee.

urea.c: Urea U"re*a (?), a. [NL. See Urine.] (Physiol. Chem.) A very soluble crystalline body which is the chief constituent of the urine in mammals and some other animals. It is also present in small quantity in blood, serous fluids, lymph, the liver, etc.

ureal.c: Ureal U"re*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to urea; containing, or consisting of, urea; as, ureal deposits.

ureameter.c: Ureameter U`re*am"e*ter (?), n. [Urea + -meter.] (Physiol. Chem.) An apparatus for the determination of the amount of urea in urine, in which the nitrogen evolved by the action of certain reagents, on a given volume of urine, is collected and measured, and the urea calculated accordingly.

urechitin.c: Urechitin U`re*chi"tin (?), n. (Chem.) A glucoside extracted from the leaves of a certain plant (Urechitis suberecta) as a bitter white crystalline substance.

urechitoxin.c: Urechitoxin U`re*chi*tox"in (?), n. [Urechitin + toxic + -in.] (Chem.) A poisonous glucoside found accompanying urechitin, and extracted as a bitter white crystalline substance.

uredo.c: Uredo ‖U*re"do (?), n. [L., a blast, blight, a burning itch, fr. urere to burn, to scorch.]

uredospore.c: Uredospore U*re"do*spore (?), n. (Bot.) The thin-walled summer spore which is produced during the so-called Uredo stage of certain rusts. See (in the Supplement) Uredinales, Heterœcious, etc.

ureide.c: Ureide U"re*ide (?), n. (Chem.) Any one of the many complex derivatives of urea; thus, hydantoin, and, in an extended dense, guanidine, caffeine, et., are ureides. [Written also ureid.]

uret.c: -uret -u*ret (?). A suffix with the same meaning as -ide. See -ide. [Obs.]

ureter.c: Ureter ‖U*re"ter (?; 277), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?. See Urine.] (Anat.) The duct which conveys the urine from the kidney to the bladder or cloaca. There are two ureters, one for each kidney.

ureteritis.c: Ureteritis ‖U*re`ter*i"tis (?), n. [NL. See Ureter, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the ureter. Dunglison.

urethane.c: Urethane U*reth"ane (?), n. [F. uréthane. See Urea; Ether.] 1. (Org. Chem.) A white crystalline substance, NH2.CO.OC2H5, produced by the action of ammonia on ethyl carbonate or by heating urea nitrate and ethyl alcohol. It is used as a hypnotic, antipyretic, and antispasmodic. Hence, any ester of carbamic acid.

urethra.c: Urethra ‖U*re"thra (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?. See Urine.] (Anat.) The canal by which the urine is conducted from the bladder and discharged.

urethral.c: Urethral U*re"thral (?), a. Of or pertaining to the urethra.

urethritis.c: Urethritis ‖U`re*thri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Urethra, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the urethra.

urethroplasty.c: Urethroplasty U*re"thro*plas`ty (?), n. [Urethra + -plasty.] (Surg.) An operation for the repair of an injury or a defect in the walls of the urethra. -- U*re`thro*plas"tic (#), a.

urethroscope.c: Urethroscope U*re"thro*scope (?), n. [Urethra + -scope.] (Med.) An instrument for viewing the interior of the urethra.

urethroscopy.c: Urethroscopy U`re*thros"co*py (?), n. (Med.) Examination of the urethra by means of the urethroscope.

urethrotome.c: Urethrotome U*re"thro*tome (?), n. [Urethra + Gr.? to cut.] An instrument for cutting a urethral stricture.

urethrotomy.c: Urethrotomy U`re*throt"o*my (?), n. [Urethra + Gr.? to cut.] (Surg.) An incision of the urethra, esp. incision for relief of urethral stricture.

uretic.c: Uretic U*ret"ic (?), a. [L. ureticus, Gr.?. See Urine.] (Med.) Of or pertaining to the urine; diuretic; urinary; as, uretic medicine.

urge.c: Urge Urge (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Urged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Urging (?).] [L. urgere; akin to E. wreak. See Wreak, v. t.]
Urge Urge (?), v. i. 1. To press onward or forward. [R.]

urgency.c: Urgency Ur"gen*cy (?), n. [Cf. F. urgence.] The quality or condition of being urgent; insistence; pressure; as, the urgency of a demand or an occasion.

urgent.c: Urgent Ur"gent (?), a. [L. urgens, p. pr. of urgere: cf. F. urgent. See Urge.] Urging; pressing; besetting; plying, with importunity; calling for immediate attention; instantly important. “The urgent hour.” Shak.

urgently.c: Urgently Ur"gent*ly, adv. In an urgent manner.

urger.c: Urger Ur"ger (?), n. One who urges. Beau. & Fl.

uric.c: Uric U"ric (?), a. [Gr.? urine: cf. F. urique. See Urine.] (Physiol. Chem.) Of or pertaining to urine; obtained from urine; as, uric acid.

urim.c: Urim ‖U"rim (?), n. [Heb.?rīm, pl. of?r, fire?r light.] A part or decoration of the breastplate of the high priest among the ancient Jews, by which Jehovah revealed his will on certain occasions. Its nature has been the subject of conflicting conjectures.

urinal.c: Urinal U"ri*nal (?), n. [L. urinal, fr. urina urine: cf. F. urinal.]

urinarium.c: Urinarium U`ri*na"ri*um (?), n. [LL. urinarium.] (Agric.) A reservoir for urine, etc., for manure.

urinary.c: Urinary U"ri*na*ry (?), a. [L. urina urine: cf. F. urinaire.]
Urinary U"ri*na*ry, n. A urinarium; also, a urinal.

urinate.c: Urinate U"ri*nate (?), v. i. [LL. urinare.] To discharge urine; to make water.

urination.c: Urination U`ri*na"tion (?), n. The act or process of voiding urine; micturition.

urinative.c: Urinative U"ri*na*tive (?), a. Provoking the flow of urine; uretic; diuretic. [R.] Bacon.

urinator.c: Urinator U"ri*na`tor (?), n. [L., from urinari to plunge under water, to dive.] One who dives under water in search of something, as for pearls; a diver. [R.] Ray.

urine.c: Urine U"rine (?), n. [F. urine, L. urina; akin to urinari to plunge under water, to dive, Gr.? urine; cf. Skr. vār water, Icel.?r drizzling rain, AS. wær the sea.] (Physiol.) In mammals, a fluid excretion from the kidneys; in birds and reptiles, a solid or semisolid excretion.
Urine U"rine, v. i. To urinate. [Obs.] Bacon.

uriniferous.c: Uriniferous U`ri*nif"er*ous (?), a. [Urine + -ferous.] Bearing or conveying urine; as, uriniferous tubules.

uriniparous.c: Uriniparous U`ri*nip"a*rous (?), a. [Urine + L. parere to produce: cf. F. urinipare.] (Physiol.) Producing or preparing urine; as, the uriniparous tubes in the cortical portion of the kidney.

urinogenital.c: Urinogenital U`ri*no*gen"i*tal (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to the urinary and genital organs; genitourinary; urogenital; as, the urinogenital canal.

urinometer.c: Urinometer U`ri*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Urine + -meter.] A small hydrometer for determining the specific gravity of urine.

urinometry.c: Urinometry U`ri*nom"e*try (?), n. The estimation of the specific gravity of urine by the urinometer.

urinous.c: Urinous Urinose { U"ri*nose (?), U"ri*nous (?), } a. [Cf. F. urineux. See Urine.] Of or pertaining to urine, or partaking of its qualities; having the character or odor of urine; similar to urine. Arbuthnot.

urite.c: Urite U"rite (?), n. [Gr.? tail.] (Zool.) One of the segments of the abdomen or post-abdomen of arthropods.

urith.c: Urith U"rith (?), n. The bindings of a hedge. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

urn.c: Urn Urn (?), n. [OE. urne, L. urna; perhaps fr. urere to burn, and sop called as being made of burnt clay (cf. East): cf. F. urne.]
Urn Urn, v. t. To inclose in, or as in, an urn; to inurn.

urnal.c: Urnal Urn"al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an urn; effected by an urn or urns. “Urnal interments.” Sir T. Browne.

urnful.c: Urnful Urn"ful (?), n.; pl. Urnfuls (?). As much as an urn will hold; enough to fill an urn.

urnshaped.c: Urn-shaped Urn"-shaped` (?), a. Having the shape of an urn; as, the urn-shaped capsules of some mosses.

uro.c: Uro- U"ro- (?). A combining form fr. Gr. o'y^ron, urine.
Uro- U"ro-. A combining form from Gr. o'yra`, the tail, the caudal extremity.

urobilin.c: Urobilin U`ro*bi"lin (?), n. [1st uro- + bile + -in.] (Physiol. Chem.) A yellow pigment identical with hydrobilirubin, abundant in the highly colored urine of fever, and also present in normal urine. See Urochrome.

urocele.c: Urocele U"ro*cele (?), n. [1st uro + Gr.? tumor.] (Med.) A morbid swelling of the scrotum due to extravasation of urine into it.

urocerata.c: Urocerata ‖U`ro*cer"a*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? tail +?,?, horn.] (Zool.) A division of boring Hymenoptera, including Tremex and allied genera. See Illust. of Horntail.

urochord.c: Urochord U"ro*chord (?), n. [2d uro- + chord.] (Zool.) The central axis or cord in the tail of larval ascidians and of certain adult tunicates. [Written also urocord.]

urochordata.c: Urochordata Urochorda U`ro*chor"da, U`ro*chor`da"ta (?), prop. n. pl. [NL. See Urochord.] (Zool.) Same as Tunicata.

urochordal.c: Urochordal U`ro*chor"dal (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Urochorda.

urochrome.c: Urochrome U"ro*chrome (?), n. [1st uro- + Gr.? color.] (Physiol. Chem.) A yellow urinary pigment, considered by Thudichum as the only pigment present in normal urine. It is regarded by Maly as identical with urobilin.

urocyst.c: Urocyst U"ro*cyst (?), n. [1st uro- + cyst.] (Anat.) The urinary bladder.

urodela.c: Urodela ‖U`ro*de"la (?), n. pl. [NL.; Gr.? tail +? visible.] (Zool.) An order of amphibians having the tail well developed and often long. It comprises the salamanders, tritons, and allied animals.

urodele.c: Urodele U"ro*dele (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Urodela.

urodelian.c: Urodelian U`ro*de"li*an (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Urodela. -- n. One of the Urodela.

uroerythrin.c: Uroerythrin U`ro*e*ryth"rin (?), n. [See 1st Uro-, and Erythrin.] (Physiol. Chem.) A reddish urinary pigment, considered as the substance which gives to the urine of rheumatism its characteristic color. It also causes the red color often seen in deposits of urates.

urogastric.c: Urogastric U`ro*gas"tric (?), a. [2d uro- + gastric.] (Zool.) Behind the stomach; -- said of two lobes of the carapace of certain crustaceans.

urogenital.c: Urogenital U`ro*gen"i*tal (?), a. [1st uro- + genital.] (Anat.) Same as Urinogenital.

uroglaucin.c: Uroglaucin U`ro*glau"cin (?), n. [1st uro- + L. glaucus bright.] (Physiol. Chem.) A body identical with indigo blue, occasionally found in the urine in degeneration of the kidneys. It is readily formed by oxidation or decomposition of indican.

urohaematin.c: Urohaematin U`ro*haem"a*tin (?), n. [1st uro- + haematin.] (Physiol. Chem.) Urinary haematin; -- applied to the normal coloring matter of the urine, on the supposition that it is formed either directly or indirectly (through bilirubin) from the haematin of the blood. See Urochrome, and Urobilin.

urohyal.c: Urohyal U`ro*hy"al (?), a. [2d uro- + the Gr. letter Υ.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to one or more median and posterior elements in the hyoidean arch of fishes. -- n. A urohyal bone or cartilage.

uromere.c: Uromere U"ro*mere (?), n. [2d uro- + -mere.] (Zool.) Any one of the abdominal segments of an arthropod.

uronology.c: Uronology U`ro*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? urine + -logy.] (Med.) That part of medicine which treats of urine. Dunglison.

uropod.c: Uropod U"ro*pod (?), n. [2d uro- + -pod.] (Zool.) Any one of the abdominal appendages of a crustacean, especially one of the posterior ones, which are often larger than the rest, and different in structure, and are used chiefly in locomotion. See Illust. of Crustacea, and Stomapoda.

uropodal.c: Uropodal U*rop"o*dal (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to a uropod.

uropoetic.c: Uropoetic U`ro*po*et"ic (?), a. [1st uro- + Gr.? to make.]

uropygial.c: Uropygial U`ro*pyg"i*al (?), a. [See Uropygium.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the uropygium, or prominence at the base of the tail feathers, in birds.

uropygium.c: Uropygium ‖U`ro*pyg"i*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, (corrupted form)?;? the end of the os sacrum +? rump.] (Anat.) The prominence at the posterior extremity of a bird's body, which supports the feathers of the tail; the rump; -- sometimes called pope's nose.

urosacral.c: Urosacral U`ro*sa"cral (?), a. [2d uro- + sacral.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to both the caudal and sacral parts of the vertebral column; as, the urosacral vertebrae of birds.

uroscopy.c: Uroscopy U*ros"co*py (?), n. [1st uro- + -scopy: cf. F. uroscopie.] The diagnosis of diseases by inspection of urine. Sir T. Browne.

urosome.c: Urosome U"ro*some (?), n. [2d uro- + -some body.] (Zool.) The abdomen, or post-abdomen, of arthropods.

urostege.c: Urostege U"ro*stege (?), n. [2d uro- + Gr.? roof.] (Zool.) One of the plates on the under side of the tail of a serpent.

urosteon.c: Urosteon ‖U*ros"te*on (?), n.; pl. L. Urostea (#), E. Urosteons (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? the tail +? a bone.] (Anat.) A median ossification back of the lophosteon in the sternum of some birds.

urosternite.c: Urosternite U`ro*ster"nite (?), n. [2d uro- + sternum.] (Zool.) The sternal, or under piece, of any one of the uromeres of insects and other arthropods.

urostyle.c: Urostyle U"ro*style (?), n. [2d uro- + Gr.? a pillar.] (Anat.) A styliform process forming the posterior extremity of the vertebral column in some fishes and amphibians.

urox.c: Urox U"rox (?), n. [See Aurochs, and cf. Urus.] (Zool.) The aurochs.

uroxanate.c: Uroxanate U*rox"a*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of uroxanic acid.

uroxanic.c: Uroxanic U`rox*an"ic (?), a. [Uric + alloxan.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C5H8N4O6, which is obtained, as a white crystalline substance, by the slow oxidation of uric acid in alkaline solution.

uroxanthin.c: Uroxanthin U`ro*xan"thin (?), n. [1st uro- + xanthin.] (Physiol. Chem.) Same as Indican.

urrhodin.c: Urrhodin Ur*rho"din (?), n. [1st uro- + Gr.? a rose.] (Physiol. Chem.) Indigo red, a product of the decomposition, or oxidation, of indican. It is sometimes found in the sediment of pathological urines. It is soluble in ether or alcohol, giving the solution a beautiful red color. Also called indigrubin.

urry.c: Urry Ur"ry (?), n. [Cf. Gael. uir, uireach, mold, clay.] A sort of blue or black clay lying near a vein of coal.

ursa.c: Ursa Ur"sa (?), n. [L. ursa a she-bear, also, a constellation, fem. of ursus a bear. Cf. Arctic.] (Astron.) Either one of the Bears. See the Phrases below.

ursal.c: Ursal Ur"sal (?), n. (Zool.) The ursine seal. See the Note under 1st Seal.

ursiform.c: Ursiform Ur"si*form (?), a. [L. ursus, ursa, a bear + -form.] Having the shape of a bear.

ursine.c: Ursine Ur"sine (?), a. [L. ursinus, from ursus a bear. See Ursa.] Of or pertaining to a bear; resembling a bear.

urson.c: Urson Ur"son (?), n. [Cf. Urchin.] (Zool.) The Canada porcupine. See Porcupine.

ursula.c: Ursula Ur"su*la (?), n. (Zool.) A beautiful North American butterfly (Basilarchia astyanax syn. Limenitis astyanax). Its wings are nearly black with red and blue spots and blotches. Called also red-spotted purple.

ursuline.c: Ursuline Ur"su*line (?), n. [Cf. F. ursuline.] (R. C. Ch.) One of an order of nuns founded by St. Angela Merici, at Brescia, in Italy, about the year 1537, and so called from St. Ursula, under whose protection it was placed. The order was introduced into Canada as early as 1639, and into the United States in 1727. The members are devoted entirely to education.
Ursuline Ur"su*line, a. Of or pertaining to St. Ursula, or the order of Ursulines; as, the Ursuline nuns.

ursus.c: Ursus ‖Ur"sus (?), n. [L., a bear.] (Zool.) A genus of Carnivora including the common bears.

urtica.c: Urtica ‖Ur*ti"ca (?), n. [L., a nettle.] (Bot.) A genus of plants including the common nettles. See Nettle, n.

urticaceous.c: Urticaceous Ur`ti*ca"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to a natural order (Urticaceae) of plants, of which the nettle is the type. The order includes also the hop, the elm, the mulberry, the fig, and many other plants.

urtical.c: Urtical Ur"tic*al (?), a. Resembling nettles; -- said of several natural orders allied to urticaceous plants.

urticaria.c: Urticaria ‖Ur`ti*ca"ri*a (?), n. [NL. See Urtica.] (Med.) The nettle rash, a disease characterized by a transient eruption of red pimples and of wheals, accompanied with a burning or stinging sensation and with itching; uredo.

urticate.c: Urticate Ur"ti*cate (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Urticated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Urticating.] To sting with, or as with, nettles; to irritate; to annoy. G. A. Sala.

urtication.c: Urtication Ur`ti*ca"tion (?), n. (Med.) The act or process of whipping or stinging with nettles; -- sometimes used in the treatment of paralysis.

urubu.c: Urubu U*ru*bu" (?), n. [Cf. Pg. urubú a certain Brazilian bird.] (Zool.) The black vulture (Catharista atrata). It ranges from the Southern United States to South America. See Vulture.

urus.c: Urus ‖U"rus (?), n. [L.; of Teutonic origin. See Aurochs.] (Zool.) A very large, powerful, and savage extinct bovine animal (Bos urus or Bos primigenius) anciently abundant in Europe. It appears to have still existed in the time of Julius Caesar. It had very large horns, and was hardly capable of domestication. Called also, ur, ure, and tur.

urva.c: Urva Ur"va (?), n. [NL.] (Zool.) The crab-eating ichneumon (Herpestes urva), native of India. The fur is black, annulated with white at the tip of each hair, and a white streak extends from the mouth to the shoulder.

us.c: Us Us (?), pron. [OE. us, AS.?s; akin to OFries. & OS.?s, D. ons, G. uns, Icel. & Sw. oss, Dan. os, Goth. uns, L. nos we, us, Gr.? we, Skr. nas us.????. Cf. Nostrum, Our.] The persons speaking, regarded as an object; ourselves; -- the objective case of we. See We. “Tell us a tale.” Chaucer.

usable.c: Usable Us"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being used.

usage.c: Usage Us"age (?), n. [F. usage, LL. usaticum. See Use.]

usager.c: Usager Us"a*ger (?), n. [F. usager.] One who has the use of anything in trust for another. [Obs.] Daniel.

usance.c: Usance Us"ance (?), n. [F. See Use, v. t.]

usant.c: Usant Us"ant (?), a. [OF.] Using; accustomed. [Obs.] “Usant for to steal.” Chaucer.

usbeks.c: Usbeks Usbegs { Us"begs (?), Us"beks (?), } n. pl. (Ethnol.) A Turkish tribe which about the close of the 15th century conquered, and settled in, that part of Asia now called Turkestan. [Written also Uzbecks, and Uzbeks.]

use.c: Use Use (?), n. [OE. us use, usage, L. usus, from uti, p. p. usus, to use. See Use, v. t.]

Use Use (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Used (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Using.] [OE. usen, F. user to use, use up, wear out, LL. usare to use, from L. uti, p. p. usus, to use, OL. oeti, oesus; of uncertain origin. Cf. Utility.]

Use Use (?), v. i. 1. To be wont or accustomed; to be in the habit or practice; as, he used to ride daily; -- now disused in the present tense, perhaps because of the similarity in sound, between “use to,” and “used to.”

useful.c: Useful Use"ful (?), a. Full of use, advantage, or profit; producing, or having power to produce, good; serviceable for any end or object; helpful toward advancing any purpose; beneficial; profitable; advantageous; as, vessels and instruments useful in a family; books useful for improvement; useful knowledge; useful arts.

usefully.c: Usefully Use"ful*ly, adv. In a useful manner.

usefulness.c: Usefulness Use"ful*ness, n. The quality or state of being useful; utility; serviceableness; advantage. Addison.

useless.c: Useless Use"less, a. Having, or being of, no use; unserviceable; producing no good end; answering no valuable purpose; not advancing the end proposed; unprofitable; ineffectual; as, a useless garment; useless pity.

user.c: User Us"er (?), n. 1. One who uses. Shak.

ushaped.c: U-shaped U"-shaped` (?), a. Having the form of the letter U; specif. (Phys. Geog.), of valleys, resembling a broad U in cross profile.

usher.c: Usher Ush"er (?), n. [OE. ussher, uschere, OF. ussier, uisser, oissier, hussier, huissier, fr. L. ostiarius a doorkeeper, fr. ostium a door, entrance, fr. os mouth. See Oral, and cf. Ostiary.]

Usher Ush"er, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ushered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ushering.] To introduce or escort, as an usher, forerunner, or harbinger; to forerun; -- sometimes followed by in or forth; as, to usher in a stranger; to usher forth the guests; to usher a visitor into the room.

usherance.c: Usherance Ush"er*ance (?), n. The act of ushering, or the state of being ushered in. [Obs.] Shaftesbury.

usherdom.c: Usherdom Ush"er*dom (?), n. The office or position of an usher; ushership; also, ushers, collectively. [R.]

usherless.c: Usherless Ush"er*less, a. Destitute of an usher. Marston.

ushership.c: Ushership Ush"er*ship, n. The office of an usher; usherdom.

usitative.c: Usitative Us"i*ta*tive (?), a. [L. usitari to use often.] Denoting usual or customary action. “The usitative aorist.” Alford.

usnea.c: Usnea ‖Us"ne*a (?), n. [NL., from Ar. usnah moss.] (Bot.) A genus of lichens, most of the species of which have long, gray, pendulous, and finely branched fronds. Usnea barbata is the common bearded lichen which grows on branches of trees in northern forests.

usnic.c: Usnic Us"nic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a complex acid obtained, as a yellow crystalline substance, from certain genera of lichens (Usnea, Parmelia, etc.).

usquebaugh.c: Usquebaugh Us"que*baugh (?), n. [Ir. or Gael. uisge beatha, literally, water of life; uisge water + beatha life; akin to Gr. bi`os life. See Quick, a., and cf. Whisky.]

usself.c: Usself Us`self" (?), n. pl. Ourselves. [Obs.] Wyclif. Piers Plowman. Chaucer.

ustion.c: Ustion Us"tion (?), n. [L. ustio, fr. urere, ustum, to burn: cf. F. ustion.] The act of burning, or the state of being burned. [R.] Johnson.

ustorious.c: Ustorious Us*to"ri*ous (?), a. [L. urere, ustum, to burn.] Having the quality of burning. [R.] I. Watts.

ustulate.c: Ustulate Us"tu*late (?), a. [L. ustulatus, p. p. of ustulare to scorch, urere to burn.] Blackened as if burned.

usual.c: Usual U"su*al (?), a. [L. usualis, from usus use: cf. F. usuel. See Use, n.] Such as is in common use; such as occurs in ordinary practice, or in the ordinary course of events; customary; ordinary; habitual; common.

usucaption.c: Usucaption U`su*cap"tion (?; 277), n. [L. usucapere, usucaptum, to acquire by long use; usu (ablative of usus use) + capere to take: cf. usucapio usucaption.] (Roman Law) The acquisition of the title or right to property by the uninterrupted possession of it for a certain term prescribed by law; -- the same as prescription in common law.

usufruct.c: Usufruct U"su*fruct (?; 277), n. [L. usufructus, ususfructus, usus et fructus; usus use + fructus fruit.] (Law) The right of using and enjoying the profits of an estate or other thing belonging to another, without impairing the substance. Burrill.

usufructuary.c: Usufructuary U`su*fruc"tu*a*ry (?), n. [L. usufructuarius.] (Law) A person who has the use of property and reaps the profits of it. Wharton.
Usufructuary U`su*fruc"tu*a*ry, a. (Law) Of or pertaining to a usufruct; having the nature of a usufruct.

usurary.c: Usurary Usurarious { U`su*ra"ri*ous (?), U"su*ra*ry (?), } a. [L. usurarius that serves for use, that pays interest. See Usurer.] Usurious. [Obs.] “Usurarious contracts.” Jer. Taylor. Bp. Hall.

usure.c: Usure U"sure (?; 115), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Usured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Usuring.] [Cf. OF. usurer, LL. usurare.] To practice usury; to charge unlawful interest. [Obs.] “The usuringb senate.” Shak.

usurer.c: Usurer U"su*rer (?), n. [F. usurier, LL. usurarius. See Usury, and cf. Usurarious.]

usurp.c: Usurp U*surp" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Usurped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Usurping.] [L. usurpare, usurpatum, to make use of, enjoy, get possession of, usurp; the first part of usurpare is akin to usus use (see Use, n.): cf. F. usurper.] To seize, and hold in possession, by force, or without right; as, to usurp a throne; to usurp the prerogatives of the crown; to usurp power; to usurp the right of a patron is to oust or dispossess him.
Usurp U*surp", v. i. To commit forcible seizure of place, power, functions, or the like, without right; to commit unjust encroachments; to be, or act as, a usurper.

usurpant.c: Usurpant U*surp"ant (?), a. [L. usurpans, p. pr.] Usurping; encroaching. [Obs.] Gauden.

usurpation.c: Usurpation U`sur*pa"tion (?), n. [L. usurpatio? making use, usurpation: cf. F. usurpation.]

usurpatory.c: Usurpatory U*surp"a*to*ry (?), a. [L. usurpatorius.] Marked by usurpation; usurping. [R.]

usurpature.c: Usurpature U*surp"a*ture (?), n. Usurpation. [R.] “Beneath man's usurpature.” R. Browning.

usurper.c: Usurper U*surp"er (?), n. One who usurps; especially, one who seizes illegally on sovereign power; as, the usurper of a throne, of power, or of the rights of a patron.

usurpingly.c: Usurpingly U*surp"ing*ly, adv. In a usurping manner.

usury.c: Usury U"su*ry (?), n. [OE. usurie, usure, F. usure, L. usura use, usury, interest, fr. uti, p. p. usus, to use. See Use, v. t.]

ut.c: Ut Ut (?), n. (Min.) The first note in Guido's musical scale, now usually superseded by do. See Solmization.

utas.c: Utas U"tas (?), n. [OF. huitieves, witieves, witaves, oitieves, pl. of huitieve, witieve, etc., eighth, L. octavus. See Octave, n.] [Written also utis.]

utensil.c: Utensil U*ten"sil (?; 277), n. [F. utensile, ustensile, L. utensile, fr. utensilis that may be used, fit for use, fr. uti, p. p. usus, to use. See Use, v. t.] That which is used; an instrument; an implement; especially, an instrument or vessel used in a kitchen, or in domestic and farming business.

uterine.c: Uterine U"ter*ine (?; 277), a. [L. uterinus born of the same mother, from uterus womb: cf. F. utérin.]

uterogestation.c: Uterogestation U`te*ro*ges*ta"tion (?), n. [Uterus + gestation.] Gestation in the womb from conception to birth; pregnancy. Pritchard.

uterovaginal.c: Uterovaginal U`te*ro*vag"i*nal (?), n. [Uterus + vaginal.] Pertaining to both the uterus and the vagina.

uterus.c: Uterus U"te*rus (?), n. [L.] 1. (Anat.) The organ of a female mammal in which the young are developed previous to birth; the womb.

utes.c: Utes Utes (?), n. pl.; sing. Ute. (Ethnol.) An extensive tribe of North American Indians of the Shoshone stock, inhabiting Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, Arizona, and adjacent regions. They are subdivided into several subordinate tribes, some of which are among the most degraded of North American Indians.

utia.c: Utia U"ti*a (?), n. [NL.] (Zool.) Any species of large West Indian rodents of the genus Capromys, or Utia. In general appearance and habits they resemble rats, but they are as large as rabbits.

utica.c: Utica U"ti*ca (?), a. [So called from Utica, in New York.] (Geol.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a subdivision of the Trenton Period of the Lower Silurian, characterized in the State of New York by beds of shale.

utile.c: Utile U"tile (?), a. [L. utilis, fr. uti to use: cf. F. utile. See Use, v. t.] Profitable; useful. [Obs.]

utilitarian.c: Utilitarian U*til`i*ta"ri*an (?), n. One who holds the doctrine of utilitarianism.

utilitarianism.c: Utilitarianism U*til`i*ta"ri*an*ism (?), n. 1. The doctrine that the greatest happiness of the greatest number should be the end and aim of all social and political institutions. Bentham.

utility.c: Utility U*til"i*ty (?), n. [OE. utilite, F. utilité, L. utilitas, fr. utilis useful. See Utile.]

utilizable.c: Utilizable U"til*i`za*ble (?), a. Capable of being utilized; as, the utilizable products of the gas works.

utilization.c: Utilization U`til*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. utilization.] The act of utilizing, or the state of being utilized.

utilize.c: Utilize U"til*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Utilized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Utilizing (?).] [Cf. F. utiliser.] To make useful; to turn to profitable account or use; to make use of; as, to utilize the whole power of a machine; to utilize one's opportunities.

utmost.c: Utmost Ut"most` (?), a. [OE. utmeste, utemest, AS.?temest, a superlative fr.?te out.????. See Out, and cf. Aftermost, Outmost, Uttermost.]
Utmost Ut"most`, n. The most that can be; the farthest limit; the greatest power, degree, or effort; as, he has done his utmost; try your utmost.

utopia.c: Utopia U*to"pi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. not +? a place.]

utopian.c: Utopian U*to"pi*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Utopia; resembling Utopia; hence, ideal; chimerical; fanciful; founded upon, or involving, imaginary perfections; as, Utopian projects; Utopian happiness.
Utopian U*to"pi*an, n. An inhabitant of Utopia; hence, one who believes in the perfectibility of human society; a visionary; an idealist; an optimist. Hooker.

utopianism.c: Utopianism U*to"pi*an*ism (?), n. The ideas, views, aims, etc., of a Utopian; impracticable schemes of human perfection; optimism.

utopianist.c: Utopianist U*to"pi*an*ist, n. An Utopian; an optimist.

utopical.c: Utopical U*to"pic*al (?), a. Utopian; ideal. [Obs.] “Utopical perfection.” Bp. Hall.

utraquist.c: Utraquist U"tra*quist (?), n. [L. uterque, fem. utraque, both.] One who receives the eucharist in both kinds; esp., one of a body of Hussites who in the 15th century fought for the right to do this. Called also Calixtines.

utricle.c: Utricle U"tri*cle (?), n. [L. utriculus a little womb, a calycle, dim. of uter, utris, a bag or bottle made of an animal's hide: cf. F. utricule.]

utricularia.c: Utricularia ‖U*tric`u*la"ri*a (?), n. [NL.] (Bot.) A genus of aquatic flowering plants, in which the submersed leaves bear many little utricles, or ascidia. See Ascidium,

utriculate.c: Utriculate U*tric"u*late (?), a. Resembling a bladder; swollen like a bladder; inflated; utricular. Dana.

utriculoid.c: Utriculoid U*tric"u*loid (?), a. [L. utriculus a little womb, a calycle + -oid.] Resembling a bladder; utricular; utriculate. Dana.

utriculus.c: Utriculus U*tric"u*lus (?), n. [L., a little womb or matrix, a calycle.] (Anat.) A little sac, or bag; a utricle; especially, a part of the membranous labyrinth of the ear. See the Note under Ear.

utro.c: Utro- U"tro- (?). A combining form used in anatomy to indicate connection with, or relation to, the uterus; as in utro-ovarian.

utter.c: Utter Ut"ter (?), a. [OE. utter, originally the same word as outer. See Out, and cf. Outer, Utmost.]
Utter Ut"ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Uttered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Uttering.] [OE. outren, freq. of outen to utter, put out, AS. ūtian to put out, eject, fr. ūt out. √198. See Out, and cf. Utter, a.]

utterable.c: Utterable Ut"ter*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being uttered.

utterance.c: Utterance Ut"ter*ance (?), n. 1. The act of uttering. Specifically: --
Utterance Ut"ter*ance, n. [F. outrance. See Outrance.] The last extremity; the end; death; outrance. [Obs.]

utterer.c: Utterer Ut"ter*er (?), n. One who utters. Spenser.

utterest.c: Utterest Ut"ter*est, obs. superl. of Utter. Uttermost.

utterless.c: Utterless Ut"ter*less, a. Incapable of being uttered. [Obs.]

utterly.c: Utterly Ut"ter*ly, adv. In an utter manner; to the full extent; fully; totally; as, utterly ruined; it is utterly vain.

uttermore.c: Uttermore Ut"ter*more` (?), a. [Cf. Uttermost.] Further; outer; utter. [Obs. & R.] Holland.

uttermost.c: Uttermost Ut"ter*most (?), a. [From Utter, a.; cf. Utmost, and Outermost.] Extreme; utmost; being; in the farthest, greatest, or highest degree; as, the uttermost extent or end. “In this uttermost distress.” Milton.
Uttermost Ut"ter*most` (?), n. The utmost; the highest or greatest degree; the farthest extent. Tennyson.

utterness.c: Utterness Ut"ter*ness, n. The quality or state of being utter, or extreme; extremity; utmost; uttermost. [R.]

uva.c: Uva ‖U"va (?), n. [L., a grape.] (Bot.) A small pulpy or juicy fruit containing several seeds and having a thin skin, as a grape.

uvate.c: Uvate U"vate (?), n. [L. uva grape.] A conserve made of grapes.

uvaursi.c: Uva-ursi ‖U`va-ur"si (?), n. [NL., fr. L. uva grape + ursus bear.] (Bot.) The bearberry.

uvea.c: Uvea ‖U"ve*a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. uva grape.] (Anat.) The posterior pigmented layer of the iris; -- sometimes applied to the whole iris together with the choroid coat.

uveous.c: Uveous U"ve*ous (?), a. [See Uvea.] Resembling a grape.

uvic.c: Uvic U"vic (?), a. [L. uva grape.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, grapes; specifically, designating an organic acid, C7H8O3 (also called pyrotritartaric acid), obtained as a white crystalline substance by the decomposition of tartaric and pyrotartaric acids.

uvitic.c: Uvitic U*vit"ic (?), a. [From L. uva a grape. So called because it may be produced indirectly from tartaric acid, which is found in the grape.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, CH3C6H3(CO2H)2, obtained as a white crystalline substance by the partial oxidation of mesitylene; -- called also mesitic acid.

uvitonic.c: Uvitonic U`vi*ton"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid which is obtained as a white crystalline substance by the action of ammonia on pyrotartaric acid.

uvula.c: Uvula ‖U"vu*la (?), n. [NL., dim of L. uva a grape, the uvula.] (Anat.) The pendent fleshy lobe in the middle of the posterior border of the soft palate.

uvular.c: Uvular U"vu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a uvula.

uvulatome.c: Uvulatome U"vu*la*tome (?), n. [Uvula + Gr.? to cut.] (Surg.) An instrument for removing the uvula.

uvulatomy.c: Uvulatomy U`vu*lat"o*my (?), n. (Surg.) The operation of removing the uvula.

uvulitis.c: Uvulitis ‖U`vu*li"tis (?), n. [NL. See Uvula, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the uvula.

uxorial.c: Uxorial Ux*o"ri*al (?), a. [See Uxorious.] Dotingly fond of, or servilely submissive to, a wife; uxorious; also, becoming a wife; pertaining to a wife. [R.]

uxoricidal.c: Uxoricidal Ux*or"i*ci`dal (?), a. Of or pertaining to uxoricide; tending to uxoricide.

uxoricide.c: Uxoricide Ux*or"i*cide (?), n. [L. uxor wife + caedere to kill.]

uxorious.c: Uxorious Ux*o"ri*ous (?), a. [L. uxorius, fr. uxor a wife.] Excessively fond of, or submissive to, a wife; being a dependent husband. “Uxorious magistrates.” Milton.

uzema.c: Uzema ‖U"ze*ma (?), n. A Burman measure of twelve miles.
